entries.question: Alexander attacks with 4 [Wild Beastmaster]. What is the greatest amount of damage that can be dealt to Nathalie in total?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that the four Wild Beastmasters can deal 49 damage total by ordering their attack triggers optimally and give the same final power/toughness progression and assumptions.
entries.answer:
49 damage, if all four Wild Beastmaster are unblocked and their attack triggers are ordered optimally.

Each Wild Beastmaster has "Whenever this creature attacks, each other creature you control gets +X/+X until end of turn, where X is this creature's power." All four trigger when attackers are declared (an attack trigger triggers on the declaration of attackers, per [508.3d]), and Alexander, as their controller, chooses the order they go on the stack. X is locked in as that Wild Beastmaster's power at the moment its ability resolves, so each resolution feeds the next.

Call them A, B, C, D (all start 1/1):
- A resolves: X=1, so B, C, D become 2/2.
- B resolves: X=2, so A becomes 3/3, C and D become 4/4.
- C resolves: X=4, so A becomes 7/7, B becomes 6/6, D becomes 8/8.
- D resolves: X=8, so A becomes 15/15, B becomes 14/14, C becomes 12/12.

Final powers: 15 + 14 + 12 + 8 = 49 combat damage to Nathalie.

Assumptions: Nathalie is the defending player, she declares no blockers ([509.1]), no other creatures Alexander controls are attacking, and no other pump or damage effects are involved. If Nathalie blocks any of the four Wild Beastmaster, that creature's damage goes to the blocking creature instead and the total to Nathalie drops accordingly.

Multiplayer note: the provided rules only cover choosing blockers by the defending player; in a game with more than two players the same math holds as long as Nathalie is the player being attacked by all four Wild Beastmaster, since the pump triggers don't depend on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
49. Let's look at the 4 Wild Beastmaster's powers in the order their triggers resolve:
1 1 1 1
The first trigger resolves and adds 1 to the power of each other Wild Beastmaster:
1 2 2 2
The second trigger resolves and adds 2 to the power of each other Wild Beastmaster:
3 2 4 4
The third trigger, adding 4:
7 6 4 8
And the fourth trigger, adding 8:
15 14 12 8

entries.question: Aubrie attacks with a [Scrounger of Souls]. Nico blocks with a [Barony Vampire]. How much life does Aubrie gain?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Scrounger of Souls deals 3 damage and, because it has lifelink, Aubrie gains 3 life.
entries.answer:
Aubrie gains 3 life.

Scrounger of Souls is a 3/4 with lifelink. Because it's blocked by exactly one creature, Barony Vampire, Scrounger of Souls assigns all 3 of its combat damage to Barony Vampire [510.1c]. Lifelink means damage dealt by that source causes its controller to gain that much life, in addition to the damage's other results [702.15b], [120.3f] — so the 3 damage dealt to Barony Vampire (which is lethal to a 3/2 and destroys it) also gives Aubrie 3 life.

Notes: Barony Vampire deals 3 damage back to Scrounger of Souls, which survives with 4 toughness; Barony Vampire has no lifelink, so Nico gains nothing. If some effect had prevented or reduced Scrounger of Souls's damage, Aubrie would only gain life equal to the damage actually dealt [120.4d]. This single life gain event is one trigger for "whenever you gain life" abilities [119.9], [702.15e].

This works the same whether it's a two-player or multiplayer game — the damage assignment and life gain don't depend on the number of players (except in Two-Headed Giant, where the life gain applies to the team's shared life total [810.9]).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 3. Lifelink means that damage the creature deals also causes its controller to gain that much life. Scrounger of Souls deals damage equal to its power to the Barony Vampire in combat, regardless of the Barony Vampire's toughness.

entries.question: Albert controls a [Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle] and 5 [Mountain]s. They plays a [Steam Vents] and targets Nia with Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle's trigger. In response, Nia activates their [Keldon Arsonist], targeting the Steam Vents. Will they still be dealt 3 damage?
entries.reason: Both conclude the trigger still resolves and Valakut checks for five other Mountains on resolution, and because Steam Vents was the entering Mountain its removal leaves Albert with five other Mountains so the 3 damage can still be dealt.
entries.answer:
Yes — Nia will still be dealt 3 damage (if Albert chooses to have Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle deal it).

Why: Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle's ability has an intervening "if" clause — it checks the condition both when it would trigger and again on resolution, and does nothing if the condition is false at resolution [603.4 via Intervening "If" Clause; 608.2a; Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle ruling #3]. The condition is "you control at least five other Mountains," i.e., five Mountains other than the one that entered. Steam Vents is a Mountain (its type line is Island Mountain), so its entry triggered the ability, and Albert's 5 basic Mountains satisfy the "five other Mountains" requirement.

When Keldon Arsonist destroys Steam Vents in response, the destroyed land is the very Mountain that caused the trigger, so Albert's count of "other Mountains" is not reduced — it stays at 5 [Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle ruling #1]. Had Nia instead destroyed one of Albert's five basic Mountains, the count would drop to 4, the intervening "if" check would fail on resolution, and the ability would do nothing.

Two other points: the target (Nia) was chosen when the ability triggered and is still a legal target, so the ability resolves normally [608.2b], and the "may" means Albert decides at resolution whether to deal the damage [Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle ruling #0]. Also, the two lands Nia sacrifices to pay Keldon Arsonist's cost are Nia's own lands, so they don't affect Albert's Mountain count either.

This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table — Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle's trigger targets "any target," and only Albert's own Mountains are counted regardless of how many opponents there are.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Removing the object that caused an ability to trigger does not affect that ability on the stack. Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle checks how many other cards with the "mountain" subtype are on the battlefield when the trigger resolves. There are 5, so the damage will still be dealt.

entries.question: Alanna controls [Mikaeus, the Lunarch] with 2 +1/+1 counters. Nicolas casts Mikaeus, the Lunarch with X=0. What happens when the second Mikaeus, the Lunarch enters the battlefield?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the legend rule doesn't apply because the two Mikaeus are controlled by different players and Nicolas's Mikaeus dies from having 0 toughness as a result of state-based actions.
entries.answer:
Nothing happens from the legend rule — both copies of Mikaeus, the Lunarch stay on the battlefield. The legend rule (rule 704.5j, and the Legend Rule glossary entry) is a state-based action that only applies when *the same player* controls two or more legendary permanents with the same name. Here Alanna controls one Mikaeus, the Lunarch and Nicolas controls the other, so no one has to choose one to put into a graveyard.

Separately, note that Nicolas cast Mikaeus, the Lunarch with X=0, and Mikaeus, the Lunarch is a 0/0 that "enters with X +1/+1 counters on it." With X=0 it enters with no counters, so it is a 0/0. The state-based action that puts a creature with toughness 0 or less into its owner's graveyard is not among the rules provided in this context, so I can't cite it here — but be aware Nicolas's Mikaeus, the Lunarch will not survive on its own unless something else raises its toughness. Alanna's Mikaeus, the Lunarch, with 2 +1/+1 counters, is a 2/2 and is unaffected.

This answer is the same at a multiplayer table: rule 704.5j is per-player, so any number of different players may each control a Mikaeus, the Lunarch simultaneously. Only if one player somehow gained control of both would that player choose one to keep and put the other into its owner's graveyard.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Nicolas's Mikaeus, the Lunarch will be put into the graveyard as a result of state-based actions, since it has 0 toughness. The legend rule does not apply, since the two Mikaeus, the Lunarchs are controlled by different players.

entries.question: Armani controls a [Platinum Angel] and has -1 life. Norah has 4 life. Armani casts [Pulse of the Forge] targeting Norah. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final outcome as the reference: Pulse of the Forge returns to Armani's hand and Norah loses the game, while Armani does not lose due to Platinum Angel.
entries.answer:
Pulse of the Forge deals 4 damage to Norah, dropping Norah from 4 life to 0. Still during Pulse of the Forge's resolution, its second sentence checks life totals: Norah has 0 life and Armani has -1 life, so Norah has more life than Armani, and Pulse of the Forge returns to Armani's hand. Then, when a player would next receive priority, state-based actions are checked: Norah has 0 or less life and loses the game, while Armani does not lose despite being at -1 life, because Platinum Angel says "You can't lose the game and your opponents can't win the game."

Details:
- Damage causes loss of life, so Norah's life total is adjusted to 0 [119.3, 120.4c].
- State-based actions pay no attention to what happens mid-resolution, so nobody loses the game before Pulse of the Forge finishes resolving and makes its "more life than you" comparison [704.4]. That comparison uses the totals at that moment: 0 versus -1, so Pulse of the Forge does return to Armani's hand.
- After resolution, before any player gets priority, state-based actions are performed [117.5, 704.1, 704.5a, 119.6]. Norah at 0 life loses the game.
- Armani at -1 life would normally lose to the same state-based action, but Platinum Angel's static ability overrides that general rule — no game effect can make Armani lose while Platinum Angel is on the battlefield, regardless of 0 or less life [Platinum Angel ruling #3]. If Platinum Angel later leaves the battlefield while Armani is still at -1 or less life, Armani loses immediately the next time state-based actions are checked.

Assumption on timing: I'm treating the damage and the return check as one resolution of Pulse of the Forge, which is how the card is written; there is no window between them for state-based actions or priority.

Two players vs. more: the question names only Armani and Norah. In a multiplayer game the outcome for these two is the same — Norah leaves the game, Armani keeps playing — and any other players are unaffected; note also that Platinum Angel only stops Armani from losing and stops Armani's opponents from winning, it does not protect anyone else.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Norah goes to 0 life and Pulse of the Forge returns to Armani's hand, since -1 is less than 0. When state-based actions are checked after the spell finishes resolving, Norah loses the game.

entries.question: Aden casts [Stomping Slabs] targeting Nico. As it resolves, they reveal 5 [Mountain]s and 2 Stomping Slabs from the top of their library. How much damage is dealt to Nico?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly concludes that revealing any number of Stomping Slabs only triggers the spell's single 7-damage effect once, matching the reference.
entries.answer:
Nico is dealt 7 damage, not 14.

Stomping Slabs reads: "Reveal the top seven cards of your library, then put those cards on the bottom of your library in any order. If a card named Stomping Slabs was revealed this way, Stomping Slabs deals 7 damage to any target." That damage clause is a single conditional check, not a per-card count — it asks only whether at least one card named Stomping Slabs was among the revealed cards. Revealing two copies satisfies the condition exactly the same as revealing one, so the spell deals its fixed 7 damage once to the target, Nico.

The five Mountains are irrelevant except that they go to the bottom of Aden's library along with the two revealed Stomping Slabs cards, in any order Aden chooses. Card names are determined by the Oracle card reference, so the revealed cards must actually be named Stomping Slabs for the condition to be met [108.1], [201.4g].

If no card named Stomping Slabs had been revealed, Stomping Slabs would deal no damage to Nico at all [Stomping Slabs ruling #0].

This result doesn't change with the number of players: Stomping Slabs has a single target chosen when it was cast, and that target is Nico regardless of table size.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 7. A card named Stomping Slabs was revealed, so Stomping Slabs deals 7 damage to Nico. Nothing would cause it to deal any more damage based on how many Stomping Slabs are revealed.

entries.question: Asher has no cards in their library and controls a [Keranos, God of Storms]. What happens at the beginning of their draw step?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same ruling that Asher cannot draw, Keranos's triggers do not occur, and Asher loses the game when state-based actions are next checked.
entries.answer:
Asher loses the game. At the beginning of the draw step, the active player draws a card as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [504.1, 703.4d]. With no cards in Asher's library, Asher attempts to draw from an empty library and no card is actually drawn; Asher loses the game the next time a player would receive priority, which is a state-based action checked at that moment [121.4, 704.5b, 104.3c, 704.1].

Keranos, God of Storms does nothing here. Its ability says to reveal the first card you draw on each of your turns; since no card was actually drawn, there's nothing to reveal, so neither the "reveal a land card" nor the "reveal a nonland card" trigger of Keranos, God of Storms occurs. Note that Keranos, God of Storms is not a replacement effect for a draw 
therefore rule 121.6a / 614.11 (replacement effects apply even with an empty library) doesn't rescue it 

Also note Keranos, God of Storms is indestructible and stays on the battlefield, but that doesn't prevent Asher's loss.

This works the same whether the game has two players or more than two: Asher alone loses when state-based actions are checked, and in a multiplayer game the remaining players continue.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Asher can't draw a card, so no card is revealed and neither trigger triggers. Asher loses the game before they would next get priority.

entries.question: Addison activates [Nicol Bolas, the Ravager]'s ability while it's in their graveyard. Will it return to the battlefield transformed?
entries.reason: Both conclude the ability is a permanent's activated ability that functions only on the battlefield, so it can't be activated from the graveyard and won't return transformed.
entries.answer:
No — Addison can't activate that ability at all from the graveyard, so nothing returns transformed.

Nicol Bolas, the Ravager's ability, "{4}{U}{B}{R}: Exile Nicol Bolas, then return him to the battlefield transformed under his owner's control," is an activated ability of a permanent card. Abilities of objects that aren't instants or sorceries function only while the object is on the battlefield [113.6m]. The narrow exception is for an ability whose cost or effect moves the object out of a particular zone — that ability functions in that zone (the example given is Reassembling Skeleton returning itself from the graveyard) [113.6m]. Nicol Bolas, the Ravager's ability moves the card out of the battlefield (exiling it), not out of the graveyard, so it functions only on the battlefield. In the graveyard it's simply not activatable, and the mana cost of {4}{U}{B}{R} (four generic plus one blue, one black, and one red) never comes into play.

Related note on how the ability behaves when it is legally activated from the battlefield: if Nicol Bolas, the Ravager leaves the battlefield after the ability is activated but before it resolves, the card stays in whatever zone it went to and is neither exiled nor returned transformed [Nicol Bolas, the Ravager // Nicol Bolas, the Arisen ruling #9]. That ruling covers the case where the card is in the graveyard on resolution — again, no transformed return.

Separately, "transformed" means put onto the battlefield with the back face (here Nicol Bolas, the Arisen) up; a double-faced card put onto the battlefield from a zone other than the stack enters with its front face up unless an effect says transformed, and a card that isn't double-faced told to enter transformed just stays put [712.14a].

This answer doesn't depend on player count — it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: This can't happen as described. Nicol Bolas, the Ravager's ability can only be activated when it is on the battlefield.

entries.question: Ariel attacks Nala with an [Ayli, Eternal Pilgrim], which is their only creature. Nala blocks with their [Canyon Minotaur] and [Eager Cadet]. Will both blockers die, or just one? If there's a choice, who makes it, and when?
entries.reason: Both answers state the attacking player (Ariel) chooses how Ayli's combat damage is divided in the combat damage step and can assign 1 damage to each blocker (deathtouch) to have both die.
entries.answer:
Ariel chooses, and Ariel can kill both Canyon Minotaur and Eager Cadet.

Ayli, Eternal Pilgrim is a 2/3, so it assigns combat damage equal to its power: 2 damage total [510.1a]. Because Ayli, Eternal Pilgrim is blocked by two or more creatures (Canyon Minotaur and Eager Cadet), Ayli, Eternal Pilgrim's controller — Ariel, the active/attacking player — divides that 2 damage as they choose among Canyon Minotaur and Eager Cadet [510.1c]. There is no longer any "damage assignment order," and Ariel is not required to assign lethal damage to one blocker before the other (that lethal-damage requirement only applies to trample, which Ayli, Eternal Pilgrim doesn't have) [Damage Assignment Order (Obsolete)], [702.19b].

Ayli, Eternal Pilgrim has deathtouch: "Any amount of damage this deals to a creature is enough to destroy it." So if Ariel assigns 1 damage to Canyon Minotaur and 1 damage to Eager Cadet, both are destroyed. If Ariel instead assigns all 2 to one blocker, only that one dies (and Eager Cadet's 1 damage plus Canyon Minotaur's 3 damage — 4 total — would still be assigned to Ayli, Eternal Pilgrim by Nala, killing it, since Ayli, Eternal Pilgrim has 3 toughness) [510.1d].

When: the choice is made as a turn-based action immediately at the start of the combat damage step, before damage is dealt; it doesn't use the stack, and nobody can respond to it. Ariel (active player) announces assignments for Ayli, Eternal Pilgrim first, then Nala announces how Canyon Minotaur and Eager Cadet assign their damage [510.1], [703.4k]. Each player's total assignment is checked for legality once announced [510.1e].

This works the same at a multiplayer table: the attacking creature's controller still makes the division, with the defending player being the one Ayli, Eternal Pilgrim is attacking. (Exception not present here: if a blocker had banding, the defending player would choose the attacker's damage division instead [702.22j].)

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Ariel can choose to have either blocking creature die, or to have both of them die. They make this choice as damage is assigned in the combat damage step.

entries.question: Nico controls a 1/1 Thopter token. Angelique targets the token with [Release the Gremlins] (X=1). In response, Nico casts [Smash to Smithereens] targeting the token. Does Angelique create a gremlin token?
entries.reason: Both conclude Smash to Smithereens destroys the token before Release the Gremlins resolves, making its sole target illegal so the spell is removed from the stack and no Gremlin token is created.
entries.answer:
No — Angelique creates no Gremlin tokens.

Smash to Smithereens resolves first (it was cast in response, so it's on top of the stack) and destroys Nico's Thopter token. As a token that's put into a graveyard, it leaves the battlefield, so it is no longer in the zone it was in when Release the Gremlins targeted it. Note also that Smash to Smithereens deals 3 damage to that artifact's controller — Nico himself.

When Release the Gremlins (X=1) then tries to resolve, it checks its targets. A target that's no longer in the zone it was in when targeted is an illegal target [608.2b]. Since X=1, the Thopter token was its only target, so every target is illegal and Release the Gremlins doesn't resolve at all — it's removed from the stack and put into Angelique's graveyard, and none of its effects happen, including the token-creation clause [608.2b], [Release the Gremlins ruling #1].

Contrast: if X had been 2 or more and at least one other target artifact were still legal, Release the Gremlins would resolve and still create the full X Gremlin tokens — losing a target doesn't reduce the number of tokens [Release the Gremlins ruling #1].

Timing note: I'm assuming Smash to Smithereens actually resolves before Release the Gremlins, which is the normal stack order for a spell cast in response. If instead the Thopter token were still on the battlefield when Release the Gremlins resolved, Release the Gremlins would destroy it and create one 2/2 red Gremlin token.

This analysis is the same at any table size; nothing here depends on the number of players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. A targeted spell is countered upon resolution if all of its targets are illegal.

entries.question: Ariella casts [Unlicensed Disintegration], targeting their [Phyrexian Walker], which is their only artifact. Is Ariella dealt any damage?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Unlicensed Disintegration destroys Phyrexian Walker first, so Ariella no longer controls an artifact and takes no damage.
entries.answer:
No — Ariella takes no damage. Unlicensed Disintegration destroys Phyrexian Walker first, and only afterward checks whether Ariella controls an artifact [Unlicensed Disintegration ruling #1]. Since Phyrexian Walker (an artifact creature) was Ariella's only artifact and it's now in the graveyard, the condition fails and the 3 damage is never dealt.

Notes: Phyrexian Walker is a legal target, so Unlicensed Disintegration does resolve and does destroy it [608.2b]. Had Phyrexian Walker survived (e.g., indestructible) or had Ariella controlled some other artifact, then 3 damage would be dealt to that creature's controller — Ariella herself, since Ariella controls Phyrexian Walker [Unlicensed Disintegration ruling #0]. Also, if Phyrexian Walker had become an illegal target before resolution, Unlicensed Disintegration wouldn't resolve at all and no damage would happen [608.2b], [Unlicensed Disintegration ruling #0].

This outcome doesn't depend on the number of players; the damage clause only ever hits the destroyed creature's controller.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The instructions of a resolving spell are carried out in the order written. The Phyrexian Walker has been destroyed by the time Unlicensed Disintegration checks to see if Ariella controls an artifact.

entries.question: Arielle casts [Sram's Expertise]. As it resolves, they would like tap the tokens it created to cast [Collective Effort] escalated twice. Can they?
entries.reason: Both conclude Sram's Expertise creates the Servos before the free cast, so Arielle can pay the escalate additional costs by tapping two of them even though the spell's mana cost is waived.
entries.answer:
Yes. Arielle can tap two of the three Servo tokens to escalate Collective Effort twice and choose all three modes, paying no mana for it.

Why it works:

1. Sram's Expertise resolves by following its instructions in the order written [608.2c]. The first instruction creates the three 1/1 Servo tokens; the second lets Arielle cast a spell with mana value 3 or less from hand without paying its mana cost. So the Servos are already on the battlefield when Collective Effort (mana value 3) is cast during that resolution.

2. A spell cast during the resolution of Sram's Expertise is cast by following the normal casting steps 601.2a\u2013i, except no player gets priority afterward; Collective Effort goes on the stack above Sram's Expertise, which continues resolving [608.2g].

3. Escalate is an additional cost: "Escalate\u2014Tap an untapped creature you control," paid for each mode beyond the first. Additional costs must still be paid even when the mana cost is waived, and they're announced and paid as part of casting [118.8a]. Choosing all three modes means paying escalate twice, i.e., tapping two untapped creatures Arielle controls.

4. Summoning sickness is not an obstacle. The escalate cost is "tap an untapped creature you control," not a {T} symbol in the Servo tokens' own ability, and Collective Effort ruling #1 explicitly says you can tap any untapped creature you control, including one you haven't controlled since the beginning of the turn. [Collective Effort ruling #1]

5. Total cost paid for Collective Effort: {0} in mana (the {1}{W}{W} is waived by Sram's Expertise), plus tapping two untapped Servo tokens.

Timing note: any abilities that triggered while Sram's Expertise created the tokens don't go on the stack until Arielle has finished casting Collective Effort, and they're put on the stack together with anything that triggered during that casting [Sram's Expertise ruling #2]. Note also that no player gets priority to respond between the token creation and the free cast [608.2g].

Multiplayer: nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same at a two-player or multiplayer table, though the "target player" mode of Collective Effort simply has more legal choices with more opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The instructions of a resolving spell are carried out in the order written, so the tokens will be on the battlefield at that time. Tapping creatures for escalate is an additional cost. ([702.120a]) Arielle may still pay an additional cost for Collective Effort while casting it for the alternative cost given to it by Sram's Expertise.

entries.question: Addison casts [Sram's Expertise]. As it resolves, they would like sacrifice one of the tokens it created to cast [Carrion]. Can they?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference conclude the Servo tokens are created before casting Carrion and that Carrion's sacrifice additional cost must be paid, so the candidate reaches the same ruling.
entries.answer:
Yes. Sram's Expertise creates the three 1/1 Servo tokens first, and those tokens are already on the battlefield by the time Addison uses the second instruction, so one of them is available to sacrifice as Carrion's additional cost.

How it works step by step:

1. Sram's Expertise resolves and its instructions are followed in the order written [608.2c]. The first instruction creates three 1/1 colorless Servo artifact creature tokens, which are put onto the battlefield immediately [701.7a].
2. The second instruction lets Addison cast a spell with mana value 3 or less from hand without paying its mana cost. Casting a spell during another spell's resolution follows the normal steps of 601.2a–i, except no player receives priority after it's cast [608.2g].
3. Carrion has mana value 3, so it's legal. "Without paying its mana cost" only waives the {1}{B}{B}; it does not waive additional costs. Carrion's additional cost — sacrifice a creature — is still determined and paid as part of casting [601.2h]. Addison sacrifices one Servo token at that time.
4. Carrion goes on the stack above Sram's Expertise. No one gets priority yet; Sram's Expertise finishes resolving and is put into Addison's graveyard [608.2g], [608.2n], [Sram's Expertise ruling #1]. Carrion then resolves later, creating X 0/1 black Insect tokens where X is the sacrificed Servo's power — 1, since Servos are 1/1.

Note that no opponent can respond in between: Carrion's costs, including the sacrifice, are paid as part of casting, and players can only respond after the spell is fully cast [Carrion ruling #1] — and here they don't even get priority until Sram's Expertise has finished resolving [608.2g].

This works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The instructions of a resolving spell are carried out in the order written, so the tokens will be on the battlefield at that time. Addison may still pay an additional cost for Carrion while casting it for the alternative cost given to it by Sram's Expertise.

entries.question: Alisson casts [Orochi Hatchery] with X = 3. Can Nico counter it with [Thoughtbind]?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Thoughtbind cannot target Orochi Hatchery because with X=3 the spell's mana value is 6, which is greater than 4.
entries.answer:
No. With X = 3, Orochi Hatchery on the stack has mana value 6, so Thoughtbind can't legally target it.

Orochi Hatchery's mana cost is {X}{X}. While it's on the stack, X is the value its controller chose (3), and each {X} symbol counts as that value, so the two X symbols total 6 generic mana — Alisson pays {6}, and Orochi Hatchery's mana value on the stack is 6. (Once it's on the battlefield, X is treated as 0, so its mana value there is 0 — but Thoughtbind cares about the spell on the stack.)

Thoughtbind reads "Counter target spell with mana value 4 or less." A spell with mana value 6 isn't a legal target, so Nico can't even announce Thoughtbind targeting Orochi Hatchery; if the target somehow became illegal later, Thoughtbind would simply not resolve and would go to Nico's graveyard (see [608.2b]). Nico would need X to be 2 or less on Orochi Hatchery (mana value 4 or less) for Thoughtbind to work.

This doesn't change with more than two players — target legality is the same regardless of player count.

Note: the rules excerpts provided here don't include the specific rule text stating that X in a mana cost equals its chosen value while the spell is on the stack; that part is drawn from the card data and standard X-symbol notation given above.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The mana value of a spell is determined by adding together the symbols in the upper right corner of the card. The mana value of Orochi Hatchery on the stack is 6.

entries.question: Alonzo and Nico each control a [Death's Shadow]. Alonzo has 6 life and Nico has 9. Alonzo attacks with their Death's Shadow, and Nico blocks it with theirs. Alonzo casts [Temur Battle Rage] targeting their Death's Shadow. If Nico is dealt as much damage as possible during combat, what is their resulting life total?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Nico ends at 2 life but the reference shows the maximum damage line ends with Nico at 1 life (assigning 6 to the blocker and 1 to Nico in the first strike), so the conclusions conflict.
entries.answer:
Nico ends at 2 life.

Setup: Death's Shadow gets -X/-X where X is its controller's life total, and that applies only on the battlefield. With Alonzo at 6 life, Alonzo's Death's Shadow is a 7/7; with Nico at 9 life, Nico's Death's Shadow is a 4/4 [Death's Shadow ruling #1], [208.1]. Temur Battle Rage gives Alonzo's Death's Shadow double strike, and because Alonzo controls a creature with power 4 or greater (that same 7/7), it also gains trample.

First combat damage step: since an attacking creature has double strike, only it assigns damage in that step [510.4], [702.4b]. Alonzo's Death's Shadow assigns damage equal to its power, 7 [510.1a], [120.2a], [302.4a]. It must assign at least lethal damage to the blocking Nico's Death's Shadow before trampling over; 4 damage is lethal to a 4/4, so 4 goes to Nico's Death's Shadow and 3 to Nico. Nico drops 9 → 6.

Because Nico is now at 6, Nico's Death's Shadow becomes a 7/7 with 4 damage marked on it, so it survives and is still blocking.

Second combat damage step: Alonzo's Death's Shadow assigns again (double strike), and Nico's Death's Shadow assigns its damage here since it never had first or double strike [510.4], [702.4b]. Alonzo's Death's Shadow now needs only 3 more damage to be lethal to the 7/7 that already has 4 damage marked, so it assigns 3 to Nico's Death's Shadow and tramples 4 over to Nico. Nico drops 6 → 2. (Nico's Death's Shadow, now an 11/11 with 7 damage, survives; Alonzo's Death's Shadow takes 7 from it and, being 7/7, is destroyed.)

Total damage to Nico: 3 + 4 = 7, leaving Nico at 2 life.

Caveats: the specific trample assignment rule (assign lethal to blockers, excess to the defending player, counting damage already marked) and the state-based-action rules were not included in the provided context; I've applied trample as granted by Temur Battle Rage's own text. This is a two-player combat; in a multiplayer game the same math applies to whichever single player is the defending player for that attack, and nothing here changes.

entries.answer_gold:
1. In the first combat damage step, Alonzo can assign 6 damage to Nico's Death's Shadow and 1 damage to Nico. Nico's Death's Shadow will die before the second combat damage step, at which point Nico will be dealt another 7 damage.

Assigning any other amount of damage to Death's Shadow in the first combat damage step would result in less total damage dealt to Nico. In particular, assigning any less than 6 damage to Nico's Death's Shadow in the first combat damage step will result in it surviving and being able to block more damage in the second combat damage step.

entries.question: Nathan controls a [Loxodon Line Breaker] enchanted by [Felidar Umbra]. Anne casts [Overwhelming Forces]. How many cards does Anne draw?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly concludes Felidar Umbra's replacement effect prevents Loxodon Line Breaker from being destroyed (the Aura is destroyed instead), so Overwhelming Forces destroys no creature and Anne draws no cards for it.
entries.answer:
Anne draws no cards for Loxodon Line Breaker (so zero cards if it's the only creature Nathan controls; she still draws one for each other creature Overwhelming Forces actually destroys).

Why: Felidar Umbra has umbra armor, which is a replacement effect meaning "If enchanted permanent would be destroyed, instead remove all damage marked on it and destroy this Aura" [702.89a]. When Overwhelming Forces resolves and tries to destroy Loxodon Line Breaker, that destruction event is replaced: Loxodon Line Breaker is never destroyed, and Felidar Umbra is destroyed instead. Since Overwhelming Forces draws "a card for each creature destroyed this way," and Loxodon Line Breaker was not destroyed, it contributes nothing to the count. Felidar Umbra doesn't count either — it's an Aura, not a creature, and it wasn't destroyed by Overwhelming Forces but by the umbra armor effect.

Note on card text vs. general rules: Felidar Umbra's umbra armor overrides the normal outcome of a destruction effect, so the card text wins over the ordinary "destroy all creatures" result. If some other replacement effect also applied to Loxodon Line Breaker being destroyed, Nathan (as its controller) would choose the order in which to apply them [616.1f], [400.6].

Multiplayer note: Overwhelming Forces targets a single opponent, so this works identically in two-player and multiplayer games — only the targeted opponent's creatures are destroyed, and only those actually destroyed are counted.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: None. No creatures were destroyed, only an enchantment.

entries.question: Addison attacks with [Deathbringer Thoctar] and [Jwari Scuttler]. Nasir blocks them each with a [Leatherback Baloth]. What happens with Deathbringer Thoctar's trigger?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude combat damage is simultaneous so both attackers die, Deathbringer Thoctar's ability triggers on Jwari Scuttler's death but does nothing on resolution because Thoctar is already gone.
entries.answer:
Deathbringer Thoctar's ability triggers when Jwari Scuttler dies, but it does nothing when it resolves, because Deathbringer Thoctar has already died too.

Why: in the combat damage step all combat damage is dealt simultaneously (the active player assigns attackers' damage, then the defending player assigns blockers' damage, and it's all dealt at once). Each Leatherback Baloth is blocking exactly one creature, so it assigns all 4 of its damage to the creature it blocks [510.1d], and each blocked attacker assigns all its damage to its single blocker [510.1c]. That means Deathbringer Thoctar (3/3) takes 4 damage and Jwari Scuttler (2/3) takes 4 damage — both are dealt lethal damage simultaneously, and both are put into Addison's graveyard by state-based actions at the same time. Neither Leatherback Baloth (4/5) dies from the 3 and 2 damage it takes.

Deathbringer Thoctar's first ability reads "Whenever another creature dies, you may put a +1/+1 counter on this creature." Jwari Scuttler dying does match that trigger event, so the ability triggers [603.2g]. But per [Deathbringer Thoctar ruling #0], if Deathbringer Thoctar and another creature are dealt lethal damage at the same time, Deathbringer Thoctar hits the graveyard before it could receive any counters — the ability still triggers, but it does nothing on resolution since Deathbringer Thoctar is no longer on the battlefield to receive a counter. (The Leatherback Baloths dying is not at issue here; they survive.)

Timing note: I'm assuming ordinary combat damage with no first strike, no damage prevention, and no pump effects. If something had prevented or reduced the damage to Deathbringer Thoctar so it survived, the trigger would still trigger on Jwari Scuttler's death and you could then actually put a +1/+1 counter on Deathbringer Thoctar; if instead all damage to Jwari Scuttler were prevented, it wouldn't die and the ability wouldn't trigger at all [603.2g], [615.6].

This answer is the same whether it's a two-player game or a multiplayer table — nothing here depends on the number of players (multiplayer variants with limited range of influence [801.7] aren't in play for a simple "another creature dies" trigger controlled by the creature's own controller).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: All combat damage is dealt simultaneously. Deathbringer Thoctar's ability triggers. State-based actions are checked, and Deathbringer Thoctar and Jwari Scuttler die. Then the trigger is put onto the stack. When it resolves, Deathbringer Thoctar is not on the battlefield, so nothing happens.

entries.question: Ayleen casts [Minotaur Warrior]. Nico casts [Frightful Delusion], targeting Minotaur Warrior. Ayleen pays {1}. Do they have to discard a card?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Ayleen must discard a card when Frightful Delusion resolves even if she pays {1} to prevent the counter, matching the reference ruling.
entries.answer:
Yes — Ayleen still discards a card. Minotaur Warrior isn't countered because Ayleen paid the {1} (one generic mana, payable with any color or colorless mana), but Frightful Delusion's discard clause is separate and unconditional: "Counter target spell unless its controller pays {1}. That player discards a card." The official ruling states the player discards a card even if they pay {1} [Frightful Delusion ruling #0].

Mechanically, when Frightful Delusion resolves, Ayleen (the controller of the targeted spell, Minotaur Warrior) follows the instructions in the order written [608.2c]: first the pay-or-counter choice, then the discard. By default Ayleen chooses which card to discard, since Frightful Delusion doesn't specify random or opponent's choice [701.9b]. If Ayleen's hand is empty, nothing is discarded — an effect does as much as possible [609.3].

One timing note: this all happens on resolution of Frightful Delusion, not when it's cast. If Minotaur Warrior had somehow left the stack before Frightful Delusion resolved, Frightful Delusion would have no legal target, wouldn't resolve at all, and no discard would happen [608.2b]. Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games, since only the targeted spell's controller is affected.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Frightful Delusion says to discard a card, so Ayleen must do so.

entries.question: Amber has 2 life and attacks with [Drogskol Reaver] and [Gavony Ironwright]. How much damage will be dealt to Neil in total?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling that Neil takes 8 damage (4 first-strike, then 3 + 1) because Drogskol Reaver is pumped to 4/9 for first strike, lifelink raises Amber to 6, then fateful hour stops and the second strike totals 4 more damage.
entries.answer:
Neil takes 8 damage total, assuming both attackers are unblocked.

Step by step:

1. Amber is at 2 life, so Gavony Ironwright's fateful hour ability is on: "other creatures you control get +1/+4." That pumps Drogskol Reaver from 3/5 to 4/9. Gavony Ironwright does not pump itself ("other creatures"), so it stays 1/4.

2. First-strike combat damage step: Drogskol Reaver has double strike, so it deals damage in this step ([702.4e], and its printed "Double strike" text). It assigns damage equal to its power, 4 ([510.1a], [120.2a], [208.1]). Gavony Ironwright has no first strike, so it deals nothing yet. Neil takes 4.

3. Drogskol Reaver's lifelink makes Amber gain 4 life, putting her at 6. (That life gain also triggers Drogskol Reaver's last ability once — one life-gaining event, one card drawn, per [Drogskol Reaver ruling #1] and [Drogskol Reaver ruling #2].)

4. Amber now has more than 5 life, so Gavony Ironwright's fateful hour ability stops applying. Drogskol Reaver reverts to 3/5.

5. Regular combat damage step: Drogskol Reaver deals 3 (its current power) and Gavony Ironwright deals 1 ([510.1a]). Neil takes 4 more.

Total: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8 damage to Neil. Drogskol Reaver's lifelink gains Amber another 3 life in the second step (a separate life-gain event, so another card is drawn).

Timing note: this assumes nothing else changes Amber's life total in between and that neither attacker is blocked. If Amber's life were somehow kept at 5 or less through the first-strike step (say Neil drains her, or a Drogskol Reaver-triggered draw doesn't matter here), Drogskol Reaver would still be 4/9 in the second step and the total would be 4 + 4 + 1 = 9. If either creature is blocked, its damage goes to the blocking creatures instead, not to Neil ([510.1c]).

Multiplayer: the provided rules here are framed around a single defending player, and the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game as long as Neil is the defending player Drogskol Reaver and Gavony Ironwright are attacking; other opponents take nothing.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 8. Since a creature with double strike is attacking, there are two combat damage steps. In the first one, Drogskol Reaver deals 4 damage to Neil. In the second combat damage step Amber has 6 life, so Drogskol Reaver only deals 3 more damage and Gavony Ironwright deals 1 damage.

entries.question: Nico controls a [Mikaeus, the Unhallowed], [Daunting Defender], [Timber Protector], [Oakgnarl Warrior], [Goblin Outlander], and a 1/1 Vampire creature token. Agustin casts [Day of Judgment]. After everything has resolved, what creatures are on the battlefield?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the same final board state — Oakgnarl Warrior, Timber Protector (returns with a +1/+1 counter), and Goblin Outlander (returns with a +1/+1 counter) remain, while Daunting Defender, Mikaeus, and the token do not.
entries.answer:
Three creatures remain: Oakgnarl Warrior, Timber Protector (returned with a +1/+1 counter), and Goblin Outlander (returned with a +1/+1 counter). Mikaeus, the Unhallowed, Daunting Defender, and the 1/1 Vampire token are gone.

How it plays out, creature by creature, when Day of Judgment resolves and destroys all creatures:

- Oakgnarl Warrior: it's a Treefolk, and Timber Protector gives other Treefolk you control indestructible. Timber Protector is still on the battlefield at the moment Day of Judgment tries to destroy everything, so Oakgnarl Warrior simply isn't destroyed and never leaves the battlefield.
- Timber Protector: its own indestructible grant says "other" Treefolk, so it is destroyed. But it is a non-Human creature Nico controls with no +1/+1 counter, so Mikaeus, the Unhallowed grants it undying. Even though Mikaeus, the Unhallowed dies simultaneously, the undying ability still triggers and returns Timber Protector to the battlefield with a +1/+1 counter (Mikaeus, the Unhallowed ruling #0; see also [603.10a] and [704.8], which use the game state before the simultaneous destruction).
- Goblin Outlander: non-Human, no +1/+1 counter, destroyed, undying from Mikaeus, the Unhallowed returns it with a +1/+1 counter. Its protection from white doesn't help, since Day of Judgment doesn't target or damage it.
- Daunting Defender: it's a Human, so Mikaeus, the Unhallowed never granted it undying. It stays in the graveyard.
- Mikaeus, the Unhallowed: its ability only grants undying to *other* creatures, so it does not return.
- The 1/1 Vampire token: it is non-Human, so undying triggers, but a token that has left the battlefield ceases to exist and there is no card to return, so nothing comes back. (The provided rules don't include the token-ceases-to-exist rule itself, but note that anything returning would be a new object with no memory of its previous existence per [400.7].)

All of these deaths and the two undying triggers happen as one event; the triggers go on the stack the next time a player would receive priority, after state-based actions ([704.3], [610.3d]). Note that when Timber Protector and Goblin Outlander return, they are new objects ([400.7]) and Mikaeus, the Unhallowed is no longer around, so they no longer get its +1/+1 bonus or undying — Timber Protector is a 4/6 with a counter (5/7) and again grants indestructible to other Treefolk, and Goblin Outlander is a 2/2 with a counter (3/3).

This works the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer; [101.4] APNAP ordering would only matter if multiple players had simultaneous choices, which isn't the case here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Timber Protector, Oakgnarl Warrior and Goblin Outlander. Daunting Defender is a Human, regardless of what other creature types is has, so it does not have undying. Oakgnarl Warrior only loses indestructible after Timber Protector has left the battlefield, and all creatures are destroyed at the same time, so Oakgnarl Warrior is not destroyed. Protection does not prevent a permanent from being destroyed, so Goblin Outlander dies. It's not a Human, so it has undying and returns to the battlefield with a +1/+1 counter on it.

entries.question: Alonzo casts [Dance of the Dead], targeting a [Femeref Scouts] in their graveyard. After it resolves, Nico counters the triggered ability with [Disallow]. What happens?
entries.reason: Both conclude the ETB triggered ability was countered so Dance of the Dead remains attached to the Femeref Scouts in the graveyard and nothing else happens.
entries.answer:
Nothing happens: Femeref Scouts stays in Alonzo's graveyard, and Dance of the Dead remains on the battlefield enchanting the Femeref Scouts card in that graveyard.

Why: Dance of the Dead is an Aura with "enchant creature card in a graveyard," so when it resolves it enters the battlefield attached to the targeted Femeref Scouts card in the graveyard [Dance of the Dead ruling #1]. Its enters-the-battlefield ability is a triggered ability that goes on the stack the next time a player would receive priority [603.3], and triggered abilities on the stack are legal targets for effects that specifically counter abilities [113.9]. Disallow says "Counter target spell, activated ability, or triggered ability," so it can counter that trigger.

Because the trigger never resolves, none of its effects occur: Dance of the Dead does not lose "enchant creature card in a graveyard," does not gain "enchant creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura," does not put Femeref Scouts onto the battlefield, and does not reattach. Dance of the Dead is left legally enchanting the Femeref Scouts card in the graveyard, so it isn't put into the graveyard as an illegal Aura. Also, the delayed "When this Aura leaves the battlefield, that creature's controller sacrifices it" trigger and the untap-for-{1}{B} upkeep ability have no creature on the battlefield to matter for — Dance of the Dead just sits there granting +1/+1 and the no-untap clause to a card in a graveyard, which does nothing.

Note the trigger's intervening "if it's on the battlefield" clause is checked on resolution [608.2a], but that's moot here since Disallow removes the ability from the stack before it resolves.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Nico cast Disallow after the Dance of the Dead spell had already resolved and the enters-the-battlefield trigger was on the stack, as stated. If instead Nico had countered the Dance of the Dead spell itself, Dance of the Dead would go to Alonzo's graveyard and no trigger would ever be created.

This works the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer; the number of opponents doesn't change the outcome.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Nothing. The Dance of the Dead remains on the battlefield enchanting the Femeref Scouts in the graveyard.

entries.question: Alex controls [Hurloon Minotaur] that's enchanted with 2 [Soul Link]. Alex attacks, and Nico declares no blockers. How much life does Alex gain?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly concludes that each Soul Link aura triggers independently when Hurloon Minotaur deals 2 damage, giving Alex 2 life from each for a total of 4 life.
entries.answer:
Alex gains 4 life total — 2 life from each of the two Soul Link Auras, as two separate life gain events.

Hurloon Minotaur is a 2/3, so unblocked it deals 2 combat damage to Nico, which causes Nico to lose 2 life ([120.3a], [119.2]). Each Soul Link separately has the triggered ability "Whenever enchanted creature deals damage, you gain that much life," and both are attached to Hurloon Minotaur, so both trigger off that single damage event. Nothing makes multiple Soul Links redundant the way multiple instances of lifelink on one object are redundant ([702.15f]) — Soul Link's triggers are independent abilities on independent Auras, so each one gives Alex 2 life, for 4 life.

These are two distinct life gain events, not one gain of 4, which matters for abilities that trigger "whenever you gain life" (they'd trigger twice), by analogy with the separate-life-gain-events principle in [702.15e] and [119.9]. Alex's life total is adjusted upward by each ([119.3]).

Alex's second Soul Link trigger, "Whenever enchanted creature is dealt damage, you gain that much life," doesn't apply here: Nico declared no blockers, so Hurloon Minotaur isn't dealt any damage.

This works the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer — only the defending player Nico takes the damage, and Alex's life gain is unchanged. (In a Two-Headed Giant game, the gained life would be applied to Alex's team's shared life total, per [810.9] and [810.9a].)

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 4. Each Soul Link gives Hurloon Minotaur a separate triggered ability. They will each trigger and resolve independently.

entries.question: Abby has cast 3 creature spells this turn, then attacks with [Vengevine], which dies in combat. If Abby casts another creature spell, will Vengevine return to the battlefield?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Vengevine only triggers on the second creature spell of the turn (not the fourth), so it will not return after Abby has already cast three creature spells.
entries.answer:
No. Vengevine will not return. Vengevine's ability reads "Whenever you cast a spell, if it's the second creature spell you cast this turn, you may return this card from your graveyard to the battlefield." That's a triggered ability with an intervening "if" clause, which is checked both when the ability would trigger and again when it would resolve (see rule 603.4 as noted in the Intervening "If" Clause entry and rule 608.2a).

Abby has already cast 3 creature spells this turn, so the next creature spell is the fourth one cast this turn. Vengevine's ability triggers only on the second creature spell of the turn, not the third, fourth, or later [Vengevine ruling #0]. It doesn't matter that Vengevine was on the battlefield (not in the graveyard) at the time the earlier creature spells were cast — the ability counts every creature spell cast over the whole turn, regardless of where Vengevine was [Vengevine ruling #1]. So the "second creature spell" moment has already passed while Vengevine was still on the battlefield, and the trigger simply never happens now.

For Vengevine's ability to work, Vengevine must already be in the graveyard as the second creature spell of the turn finishes being cast, and must stay there until the trigger resolves [Vengevine ruling #3]. On a later turn, the count resets: if Vengevine is in Abby's graveyard when she finishes casting her second creature spell of that turn, the ability will trigger and she may return Vengevine to the battlefield.

Nothing here depends on the number of players — the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since the ability only cares about spells Abby herself cast.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Vengevine triggers when the second creature spell of a turn is cast, not the 4th.

entries.question: Ariel attacks with [Frenzied Goblin]. Noe controls [Dromoka Warrior] and [Dune Beetle]. Can they pay {R}{R} to make both of Noe's creatures unable to block?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Frenzied Goblin's single triggered ability can only affect one target and you may pay {R} once as it resolves, so you cannot pay twice to stop both creatures from blocking.
entries.answer:
No. Ariel can't pay {R} twice to stop both Dromoka Warrior and Dune Beetle from blocking. Frenzied Goblin's attack trigger has only one target, and paying {R} multiple times isn't allowed — only the one targeted creature can't block this turn [Frenzied Goblin ruling #0].

So when Frenzied Goblin attacks, the triggered ability goes on the stack targeting exactly one creature — either Dromoka Warrior or Dune Beetle. On resolution, Ariel may pay {R} (one red mana specifically; it is not generic, so it can't be paid with any other color or with colorless). If Ariel pays, that one target gains the restriction "can't block this turn." The other creature is unaffected and may block normally.

A "restriction" is an effect that says a creature can't block (or can't block unless a condition is met); when Noe declares blockers, the defending player checks each creature they control for restrictions, and a declaration that disobeys one is illegal and gets reversed [509.1b] [509.1] [733.1] [Restriction].

The only way to shut off both would be a second instance of the ability (e.g., a second Frenzied Goblin attacking), not a doubled payment.

Multiplayer note: with more than two players, all of Ariel's opponents are defending players, and Frenzied Goblin is attacking one specific defending player (or planeswalker/battle) [802.2a]; that doesn't change the answer — still one target, one {R}.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Frenzied Goblin has a triggered ability, and it only triggers once when it attacks. Ariel chooses whether or not to pay {R} as the trigger resolves.

entries.question: Aurora controls [Summit Prowler]. Nickolas casts [Crippling Chill] targeting Summit Prowler. Before it resolves, Aurora casts [Momentary Blink] targeting the Summit Prowler. What happens to the Summit Prowler? Does Nickolas draw a card?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Momentary Blink resolves first, making Summit Prowler a new object that is no longer a legal target for Crippling Chill, so Crippling Chill doesn’t resolve and Nickolas doesn’t draw.
entries.answer:
Summit Prowler is exiled and returns to the battlefield as a brand-new object, untapped, and Nickolas does NOT draw a card.

Step by step: Momentary Blink was cast later, so it resolves first. It exiles Summit Prowler and returns it to the battlefield under Aurora's control. An object that changes zones becomes a new object with no memory of or relation to its previous existence [400.7k], so the Summit Prowler now on the battlefield is not the same object Crippling Chill targeted — the targeted object left the zone it was in.

When Crippling Chill then tries to resolve, it checks its target's legality. A target that's no longer in the zone it was in when it was targeted is illegal [Illegal Target][608.2b]. Crippling Chill has only one target, so all of its targets are illegal; it doesn't resolve at all and is put into Nickolas's graveyard [608.2b]. Because the spell never resolves, none of its effects happen — Summit Prowler isn't tapped, it isn't prevented from untapping, and the "Draw a card" clause never happens either. That last point matters: the draw is part of the same spell, not a separate ability, so it's lost along with the rest [608.2b].

Timing note: this assumes Momentary Blink resolves before Crippling Chill, which is what happens if Aurora casts it in response while Crippling Chill is still on the stack (last in, first out). If instead Crippling Chill had already resolved before Momentary Blink was cast, Crippling Chill would have tapped Summit Prowler and Nickolas would have drawn — and then Momentary Blink's blink would return Summit Prowler as a new object untapped, with the "doesn't untap" effect no longer applying to it.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The stack resolves from the top down, so the Summit Prowler is exiled and returned to the battlefield first. This causes the Summit Prowler to become a completely new permanent, unrelated to what it was before. It's no longer being targeted by the Crippling Chill, so when Crippling Chill begins to resolve, it will not resolve due to having no legal targets. Nickolas will not draw a card.

entries.question: Ashley controls [Hypersonic Dragon]. In Noah's postcombat main phase, Ashley casts [Relentless Assault]. What happens?
entries.reason: Both conclude Relentless Assault untaps all creatures that attacked and, since it resolves in Noah’s postcombat main phase, creates an additional combat phase (followed by an additional main phase) on Noah’s turn during which he can attack again.
entries.answer:
Relentless Assault works: it untaps all creatures that attacked this turn, and because it resolved during a main phase, it adds an additional combat phase followed by an additional main phase to Noah's turn — after Noah's current postcombat main phase.

Details:

1. Casting timing. Relentless Assault is a sorcery, so normally Ashley could only cast it during her own main phase with an empty stack (117.1a). Hypersonic Dragon says "You may cast sorcery spells as though they had flash," which means for purposes of timing only, treat Relentless Assault as if it had flash — Ashley may cast it any time she could cast an instant, including during Noah's postcombat main phase (609.4a).

2. The extra phases still happen. Relentless Assault ruling #0 says it creates the additional combat and main phase only if it resolves during a main phase. Here it resolves during Noah's postcombat main phase, so that condition is met. Effects that add phases insert them directly after the specified phase (500.8), so Noah gets an extra combat phase and then an extra main phase after his current main phase — on Noah's turn, with Noah as the active player declaring attackers.

3. The added main phase is a postcombat main phase, since only the turn's first main phase is precombat (505.1a). The added combat phase has the usual five steps (506.1).

4. If instead Ashley had cast it during a non-main phase (say Noah's end step or during combat), it would still untap all creatures that attacked this turn, but no extra phases would be created (Relentless Assault ruling #0). I'm assuming here that no other effect makes it resolve outside the main phase.

Multiplayer note: nothing here changes with more than two players — the extra phases belong to the turn's active player (Noah), and if multiple extra phases end up created after the same phase, the most recently created one occurs first (500.8).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: All creatures that attacked this turn are untapped. A new combat phase is created after that main phase, during which Noah can attack again.

entries.question: Nico controls [Grafdigger's Cage]. Amaya controls [Renegade Demon] and has [Golden Hind] in their graveyard. Amaya casts [Living Death]. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Living Death exiles Golden Hind and then returns it from exile while Renegade Demon is sacrificed to the graveyard and not returned, and Grafdigger's Cage doesn't prevent returns from exile.
entries.answer:
Golden Hind comes back; Renegade Demon stays dead. Grafdigger's Cage doesn't stop anything here.

Step by step, as Living Death resolves [Living Death ruling #1]:

1. Each player exiles all creature cards from their graveyard simultaneously. Golden Hind is exiled from Amaya's graveyard. Grafdigger's Cage doesn't prevent this \u2014 Grafdigger's Cage only stops creature cards in graveyards and libraries from *entering the battlefield*, and exiling isn't entering the battlefield.
2. Each player then sacrifices all creatures they control simultaneously. Amaya sacrifices Renegade Demon, which goes to Amaya's graveyard.
3. Each player then puts all cards they exiled this way onto the battlefield. Only cards exiled by the first instruction return [Living Death ruling #0], so Renegade Demon is not returned \u2014 it was never exiled by Living Death and simply sits in Amaya's graveyard.

Golden Hind is put onto the battlefield from the exile zone, not from a graveyard or library, so Grafdigger's Cage's first ability doesn't apply. Exile, graveyard, and library are distinct zones, and Grafdigger's Cage names only the latter two. Grafdigger's Cage's second ability (can't cast spells from graveyards or libraries) is also irrelevant \u2014 Amaya cast Living Death from hand, and Golden Hind isn't being cast at all.

Multiplayer note: Living Death affects each player, so in a game with more than two players every player exiles their graveyard creatures, sacrifices their creatures, and returns the exiled cards, all in the same three simultaneous batches [Living Death ruling #1]. Grafdigger's Cage still wouldn't stop any of those returns, since they all come from exile. If simultaneous choices were required, they'd be made in APNAP order [101.4], but no such choices arise here.

One assumption: Grafdigger's Cage was already on the battlefield before Living Death resolved. If Nico somehow got Grafdigger's Cage onto the battlefield mid-resolution (not normally possible \u2014 nothing can be cast while Living Death is resolving), the outcome would be the same anyway, because the returning cards come from exile.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The Living Death resolves normally. Grafdigger's Cage only prevents creature cards from entering the battlefield from the graveyard or library. Living Death puts them onto the battlefield from exile.

entries.question: Achilles casts and resolves [Approach of the Second Sun]. The game is then restarted with [Karn Liberated]. Achilles casts and resolves Approach of the Second Sun again. Do they win the game?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Karn's restart creates a new game, so the pre-restart cast doesn't count and the post-restart Approach is only the first in the new game, so Achilles doesn't win.
entries.answer:
No. Achilles does not win.

Karn Liberated's −14 restarts the game: the previous game immediately ends (no one wins, loses, or draws it) and all players begin an entirely new game [727.1], [727.1a], [104.6], [Karn Liberated ruling #12]. Nothing that happened in the restarted game carries over into the new game [Karn Liberated ruling #1]. Approach of the Second Sun's win condition asks whether "you've cast another spell named Approach of the Second Sun this game" — "this game" is the new game, in which the pre-restart cast never happened. So the post-restart Approach of the Second Sun is only the first one cast in that game; it instead goes into its owner's library seventh from the top and Achilles gains 7 life. Achilles would need to cast a second Approach of the Second Sun from hand in the new game to win [Approach of the Second Sun ruling #4].

Note also that the physical card is available: all cards from the ended game, wherever they were, are part of the new game and owned by the same players, so the Approach of the Second Sun card starts in Achilles's library (unless Karn Liberated had exiled it, and Approach of the Second Sun is not a permanent card, so it wouldn't be left in exile anyway) [727.2], [Karn Liberated ruling #6]. Recasting the same physical card later does count as "another spell" named Approach of the Second Sun, since a card that changes zones is a new object [Approach of the Second Sun ruling #3], [400.7] — but only casts within the current game count.

Multiplayer: the answer is the same at any player count. A restart involves every player in the game, even under the limited range of influence option [727.7], [801.17], and Achilles becomes the starting player of the new game [727.1a].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The restarted game is a completely new game.

entries.question: Alyson casts [Harm's Way], choosing [Caldera Lake] as the source of damage and Nixon as the target. After it resolves, Alyson taps Caldera Lake for {R}. Is Nixon dealt 1 damage?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Harm's Way redirects the 1 damage Caldera Lake would deal to Alyson to Nixon, so Nixon is dealt 1 damage.
entries.answer:
Yes. Caldera Lake's second mana ability ("{T}: Add {U} or {R}. This land deals 1 damage to you.") makes Caldera Lake deal 1 damage to Alyson, and since Caldera Lake is the source Alyson chose for Harm's Way, that 1 damage is dealt to Nixon instead.

Details:
- Harm's Way is a redirection effect: a replacement effect that causes damage that would be dealt to one recipient to be dealt to another instead [614.9] [Redirection Effect]. Alyson chose Nixon as the target when casting Harm's Way and chose Caldera Lake as the source on resolution [Harm's Way ruling #4]; Alyson never picks the original recipient — the effect applies to whatever Caldera Lake would damage among Alyson and permanents Alyson controls.
- Caldera Lake is the source of the damage because it is the object dealing it [120.1] [120.7], and a permanent is a legal choice of source; the effect then applies to the next damage that permanent deals, whether from combat or from a spell or ability — here, from its mana ability [609.7a].
- Because only 1 of the 2 damage is used, Harm's Way still has a 1-damage "shield" left for later damage from Caldera Lake this turn [Harm's Way ruling #3]. So tapping Caldera Lake a second time for {U} or {R} later in the turn (if it untaps) would also redirect 1 damage to Nixon.
- Note the mode matters: tapping Caldera Lake for {C} deals no damage at all, so nothing would be redirected and the shield wouldn't be used up [609.7b].
- If Nixon has left the game by the time Caldera Lake would deal the damage, the damage isn't redirected and Alyson takes it [Harm's Way ruling #2].

This works identically at a two-player or multiplayer table; Nixon just needs to still be in the game when the damage would be redirected.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The damage is redirected to Nixon. It doesn't matter that it's coming from a source Alyson controls.

entries.question: Aubrey controls [Traveling Philosopher] equipped with [Glaive of the Guildpact] and no Gates. Does it have vigilance and menace?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference — Glaive of the Guildpact grants vigilance and menace regardless of how many Gates you control, with Gates only affecting the power bonus.
entries.answer:
Yes. Traveling Philosopher has both vigilance and menace, even though Aubrey controls no Gates.

Glaive of the Guildpact grants the equipped creature three things in one sentence: "+1/+0 for each Gate you control" and "vigilance and menace." The Gate count only scales the power bonus; it is not a condition on the granted keywords. With zero Gates, Traveling Philosopher gets +0/+0 and is a 2/2, but it still has vigilance (a keyword ability that lets a creature attack without tapping) and menace (it can't be blocked except by two or more creatures). This is confirmed directly by the card's own ruling: "The equipped creature has vigilance and menace even if you control no Gates."

Note that these are genuinely granted abilities, not merely stated qualities — Traveling Philosopher "has" them, so another effect could remove them (rule 113.12). Multiple instances of vigilance would be redundant (rule 702.20c), so a second source of vigilance adds nothing.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table (only the Gate count, which is zero either way, would matter for power).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The only thing that Gates affect is how much Traveling Philosopher's power is increased.

entries.question: Amani casts [Smallpox]. Can Nick discard [Loxodon Smiter] as their card to discard putting it onto the battlefield, then sacrifice it as their creature?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same correct conclusion and explains that Loxodon Smiter's replacement effect puts it onto the battlefield during Smallpox's discard step, so it can be sacrificed in the subsequent sacrifice step.
entries.answer:
Yes. Nick may discard Loxodon Smiter, have it enter the battlefield instead of the graveyard, and then sacrifice that same Loxodon Smiter as their creature for Smallpox.

Why it works:

1. Amani cast Smallpox, so it is a spell an opponent controls that causes Nick to discard. Loxodon Smiter's own text — "If a spell or ability an opponent controls causes you to discard this card, put it onto the battlefield instead of putting it into your graveyard" — is a replacement effect that applies (see rule 614.1c on "instead" replacement effects). Card text like this overrides the normal destination of a discarded card. Nick has still discarded a card, so discard triggers would still fire [Loxodon Smiter ruling #0].

2. Smallpox's steps happen in sequence, not simultaneously: all players lose 1 life, then all players discard simultaneously, and only after that do players choose creatures to sacrifice, starting with the active player and proceeding in turn order [Smallpox ruling #1] (turn order per rule 101.4). Because the discard step fully finishes before the creature-sacrifice choices are made, Loxodon Smiter is already on the battlefield and is a legal — and possibly the only — creature Nick can choose.

3. Nick then still must sacrifice a land in the final step.

Multiplayer note: this is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; the only difference is that the creature (and later land) choices are made by every player in turn order beginning with the active player, each seeing the earlier choices [Smallpox ruling #1] [101.4]. Loxodon Smiter's replacement works for any player who is an opponent of Amani; if Amani themself discarded Loxodon Smiter to their own Smallpox, it would go to the graveyard instead, since the spell would not be controlled by an opponent.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Spells resolve in the order they're written.

entries.question: Ashlyn controls no creatures and casts [Slum Reaper]. Nico controls no creatures. What happens as the trigger resolves?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference conclude Ashlyn must sacrifice Slum Reaper (while Nico, having no creatures, sacrifices nothing), so the final ruling is the same.
entries.answer:
Ashlyn must sacrifice Slum Reaper itself; Nico sacrifices nothing.

Why: Slum Reaper's triggered ability is "When this creature enters, each player sacrifices a creature of their choice." By the time the ability resolves, Slum Reaper is on the battlefield under Ashlyn's control, so Ashlyn does control a creature — Slum Reaper — and Slum Reaper may be the creature its controller sacrifices for its own ability [Slum Reaper ruling #2]. Since it's her only creature, that choice is forced. Nico controls no creatures at all, so Nico simply doesn't sacrifice anything [Slum Reaper ruling #0]; a player can't choose an illegal or impossible option, and there's nothing for Nico to choose [608.2d].

The choices are made during resolution, not when the ability is put on the stack: the active player chooses first, then each other player in turn order, knowing the earlier choices, and then all chosen creatures are sacrificed simultaneously [Slum Reaper ruling #1], [608.2c], [608.2d]. This ability doesn't target anyone, so nothing about it becomes illegal from a lack of creatures [115.10]. After the sacrifice, the ability is removed from the stack and ceases to exist [608.2n].

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming nothing removes Slum Reaper from the battlefield between the trigger going on the stack and its resolution. If Slum Reaper is destroyed, bounced, or exiled in response, then Ashlyn would control no creatures when the ability resolves and would sacrifice nothing either.

Multiplayer: the same reasoning applies to every other player at the table — "each player" includes all of them, and any player with at least one creature must sacrifice one of their choice, in turn order beginning with the active player [Slum Reaper ruling #1].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Ashlyn must sacrifice Slum Reaper.

entries.question: Nico controls [Grafdigger's Cage] and has a [Barbary Apes] in their graveyard. Ariel casts [Ghastly Conscription], targeting Nico. What happens to the Barbary Apes?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Barbary Apes is exiled face down by Ghastly Conscription and then manifested onto the battlefield (Cage doesn't stop it because it comes from exile, not the graveyard).
entries.answer:
Barbary Apes is exiled face down by Ghastly Conscription and then manifested onto the battlefield face down as a 2/2 creature under Ariel's control. Grafdigger's Cage does not stop it.

Why: Grafdigger's Cage says only "Creature cards in graveyards and libraries can't enter the battlefield." Ghastly Conscription first exiles all creature cards from Nico's graveyard in a face-down pile, shuffles that pile, and only then manifests them. By the time the cards enter the battlefield, Barbary Apes is in exile, not in a graveyard or library, so the "can't" effect from Grafdigger's Cage simply doesn't apply — such effects are checked against the permanent as it would exist and the event actually occurring [614.17d]. The Grafdigger's Cage ruling that manifesting is impossible applies specifically to manifesting a card from a graveyard or library [Grafdigger's Cage ruling #1]; Ghastly Conscription manifests from exile instead.

Note also that the exiled pile is shuffled, so neither player knows which face-down 2/2 is Barbary Apes. Ariel controls the manifested permanents, and Nico can turn it face up only if Nico controlled it (they don't). Grafdigger's Cage's second ability (can't cast spells from graveyards or libraries) is irrelevant here — Ghastly Conscription is cast from Ariel's hand.

This works identically at a two-player or multiplayer table; Ghastly Conscription targets one player, and the outcome doesn't depend on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It is exiled face down, then manifested onto the battlefield. Grafdigger's Cage only prevents creature cards entering the battlefield from graveyards or libraries, not from exile.

entries.question: Nico controls [Fathom Feeder] and 3 [Spined Wurm]s. Arthur casts [Alpha Brawl], targeting Fathom Feeder. Which creatures survive?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference: Fathom Feeder and all three Spined Wurms are destroyed.
entries.answer:
None of them survive — Fathom Feeder and all three Spined Wurms are destroyed.

Step by step, with Alpha Brawl targeting Fathom Feeder:

1. Fathom Feeder (a 1/1 with deathtouch) deals damage equal to its power — 1 damage — to each other creature Nico controls, so 1 damage to each of the three Spined Wurms [Alpha Brawl].
2. Then each of those three Spined Wurms deals damage equal to its power — 5 each, 15 total — to Fathom Feeder. This second part happens even though the Spined Wurms have been dealt deathtouch damage, because the two parts happen sequentially and state-based actions are not checked in the middle of a spell's resolution [Alpha Brawl ruling #4], [704.4].
3. Once Alpha Brawl finishes resolving, state-based actions are checked. Each Spined Wurm has toughness greater than 0 and was dealt damage by a source with deathtouch (Fathom Feeder), so all three Spined Wurms are destroyed [704.5h], [702.2b]. Fathom Feeder has 15 damage marked on it against toughness 1, which is lethal damage, so Fathom Feeder is destroyed too [704.5g], [302.7].

Note that the damage itself doesn't destroy anything; the state-based actions do, and they only happen after the spell finishes resolving [120.5], [704.1].

Multiplayer note: this outcome doesn't change with more than two players. Alpha Brawl targets one creature an opponent controls and only affects creatures that same player (Nico) controls, so other players' boards are untouched regardless of table size.

If regeneration or a similar replacement effect were available, it could replace either destruction event [704.5g], [704.5h], but nothing here provides that.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: None of them. Fathom Feeder has deathtouch, and so kills all of the Spined Wurms. The Spined Wurms deal enough damage to the Fathom Feeder that it dies as well.

entries.question: Aubrey controls a [Rotted Hystrix]. They cast [Artful Dodge], targeting the Rotted Hystrix. After it resolves, can they flash it back, again targeting the Rotted Hystrix?
