entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference — Artful Dodge can be flashed back and target Rotted Hystrix again, so the conclusions match.
entries.answer:
Yes. Once Artful Dodge finishes resolving and is in Aubrey's graveyard, Aubrey may immediately cast it again from the graveyard for its flashback cost of {U}, once more targeting Rotted Hystrix.

Why: flashback is a static ability that works while the card is in the graveyard and says "You may cast this card from your graveyard ... by paying [cost] rather than paying its mana cost," plus "if the flashback cost was paid, exile this card instead of putting it anywhere else any time it would leave the stack" [702.34a]. Flashback doesn't change timing permissions, so Artful Dodge, a sorcery, can only be flashed back when Aubrey could normally cast a sorcery — during their own main phase with the stack empty. I'm assuming Aubrey cast the first Artful Dodge in their own main phase; in that case, the moment it resolves the stack is empty and Aubrey receives priority first, so they can flash it back before anyone else acts (see [Artful Dodge ruling #4], which confirms you can cast a flashback card the moment it hits your graveyard on your turn if it's legal to do so). If instead Artful Dodge somehow resolved outside Aubrey's main phase (say, on another player's turn via an effect), Aubrey would have to wait until their own main phase with an empty stack.

Targeting Rotted Hystrix again is legal — Rotted Hystrix is a creature and a legal target — though the effect is redundant, since it already can't be blocked this turn. After the flashback casting resolves, Artful Dodge is exiled rather than returning to the graveyard [702.34a], so there's no third casting.

This works the same whether the game has two players or more; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The only restriction on what Artful Dodge targets is that it must be a creature. It doesn't matter if the spell resolving wouldn't do anything useful.

entries.question: Anabella controls a [Beguiler of Wills] and 2 [Dakmor Scorpion]. They activate it targeting Nicholas's [Southern Elephant]. In response, Nicholas casts [Swat], targeting the Beguiler of Wills. What happens to Beguiler of Wills's ability?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the triggered ability stays on the stack after Beguiler of Wills is destroyed but is removed when it tries to resolve because the target is no longer legal, so it has no effect.
entries.answer:
Beguiler of Wills's ability stays on the stack after Swat destroys Beguiler of Wills, but it then fails to resolve because its target is no longer legal, so Anabella gains control of nothing.

Details:

1. Swat destroys Beguiler of Wills (a 1/1, power 2 or less, a legal target for Swat). Killing the source does not counter the already-activated ability — once activated, an ability exists on the stack independently of its source, and destruction of the source afterward doesn't affect it (rules 113.7a, 602.2a).

2. When Beguiler of Wills's ability tries to resolve, the game rechecks its target (rule 608.2b). The target restriction is "target creature with power less than or equal to the number of creatures you control," and that condition is re-evaluated on resolution. At activation Anabella controlled 3 creatures (Beguiler of Wills plus 2 Dakmor Scorpion), so Southern Elephant's power of 3 was fine. With Beguiler of Wills now in the graveyard, Anabella controls only the 2 Dakmor Scorpion, so Southern Elephant's power 3 exceeds 2 and it is an illegal target.

3. Since the ability's only target is illegal, the ability doesn't resolve; it's removed from the stack and ceases to exist (rules 608.2b, 608.2n). Nicholas keeps Southern Elephant.

If instead Anabella had another creature to keep the count at 3 or more (or Southern Elephant's power dropped to 2 or less), the target would still be legal and the ability would resolve, giving Anabella control of Southern Elephant.

This interaction is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table — nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The ability on the stack is unaffected by the removal of Beguiler of Wills. However when it begins to resolve, the target is no longer legal. (Anabella only controls 2 creatures.) It is removed from the stack and has no effect.

entries.question: Alex has a creature card in their graveyard and activates [Moorland Haunt]. In response, Nasir activates [Crook of Condemnation] to exile all cards in Alex's graveyard. Will Alex create a Spirit token?
entries.reason: Both say yes—the creature was exiled as the activation cost before responses, so Moorland Haunt's ability on the stack still resolves and creates the token.
entries.answer:
Yes — Alex still creates the 1/1 white Spirit creature token with flying.

Exiling a creature card from Alex's graveyard is part of the *activation cost* of Moorland Haunt's ability ({W}{U}, {T}, Exile a creature card from your graveyard), and costs are paid as the ability is activated, before any player gets priority to respond. By the time Nasir activates Crook of Condemnation's "{1}, Exile this artifact: Exile all graveyards" ability, the creature card Alex exiled is already gone from the graveyard, so Crook of Condemnation's effect can't take it back or undo the payment.

Once activated, Moorland Haunt's ability exists on the stack independently of its source and of the card that paid for it (113.7a). It has no targets, so nothing about it can become illegal on resolution (608.2b), and its controller simply follows its instructions and creates the token (608.2c). Note that if Nasir had instead used Crook of Condemnation's first ability, "{1}, {T}: Exile target card from a graveyard," it would have had no legal target among the already-exiled card anyway.

This works the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer; Crook of Condemnation's second ability exiles all graveyards, i.e., every player's, but that still doesn't affect the already-paid cost or the ability on the stack.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The creature card is exiled from Alex's graveyard as a cost to activate Moorland Haunt, and is already in exile when the Crook of Condemnation is activated. The Moorland Haunt's ability will still resolve normally.

entries.question: Ainsley activates [Sorin, Lord of Innistrad]'s third ability, targeting Nathaniel's [Relentless Dead]. What happens to it?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Sorin's ability returns Relentless Dead to Ainsley's control and its self-return death trigger does nothing because the card is no longer in the graveyard.
entries.answer:
Relentless Dead is destroyed by Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's −6 ability, and then that same ability returns the Relentless Dead card from Nathaniel's graveyard to the battlefield under Ainsley's control — Ainsley steals it. Nathaniel remains the card's owner, but Ainsley controls the new Relentless Dead permanent.

Both of Relentless Dead's death triggers still trigger (they trigger on its death, under Nathaniel's control, since Nathaniel controlled it as it died) and they can be ordered on the stack in either order [Relentless Dead ruling #0]. However, the first one — "you may pay {B}. If you do, return it to its owner's hand" — will do nothing, because Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's ability has already returned the Relentless Dead card to the battlefield before that trigger resolves; it's a new object and the trigger can no longer find it in the graveyard. This mirrors Sorin, Lord of Innistrad ruling #2, where an undying trigger fizzles for exactly the same reason. Nathaniel shouldn't bother paying the {B}.

The second trigger still works normally: Nathaniel may pay {X} and return another target Zombie creature card with mana value X from his graveyard to the battlefield under his control.

One caveat: if Relentless Dead were a token copy rather than the real card, Sorin, Lord of Innistrad would destroy it but nothing would return, per Sorin, Lord of Innistrad ruling #0. The question describes the actual card, so the above applies.

This interaction plays out identically in two-player and multiplayer games; the only multiplayer note is that Ainsley must target a creature or other planeswalker, and controlling it afterward means Nathaniel's card is now on Ainsley's side of the table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Sorin, Lord of Innistrad's ability resolves fully before any triggers are put onto the stack. Relentless Dead will enter the battlefield under Ainsley's control. When its trigger resolves, Relentless Dead is no longer in the graveyard, so nothing happens.

entries.question: Atticus controls a [Skinshifter] and activates it to turn it into a 4/4 with trample. After that resolves, can they turn it into a 2/2 with flying?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference correctly conclude Skinshifter can only be activated once each turn, so Atticus cannot activate it again to change it to a 2/2 with flying that turn.
entries.answer:
No. Skinshifter's ability says "Activate only once each turn," so once Atticus has activated it (choosing the Rhino 4/4 trample mode), that same Skinshifter's ability can't be activated again for the rest of the turn — not by Atticus, and not on anyone else's turn until a new turn begins.

Why: text after the colon of an activated ability can be an activation instruction that restricts when the ability can be activated; it isn't part of the effect and functions at all times [602.1b]. A player can't begin to activate an ability that's prohibited from being activated [602.5c]. So the second mode is simply unavailable this turn — Skinshifter remains a 4/4 Rhino with trample until end of turn.

Two notes:
- The restriction is per turn, not per your turn: Skinshifter's ability can be activated during any player's turn, but only once on each turn [Skinshifter ruling #4]. In a multiplayer game that means Atticus could activate it once on each player's turn as the table cycles, choosing a different mode each time; nothing here changes between two players and more.
- Next turn, if Atticus activates it choosing the Bird mode, Skinshifter becomes a 2/2 Bird with flying and stops being a Rhino, since each activation sets its creature type anew [Skinshifter ruling #3].

Also, Skinshifter isn't a loyalty ability, so rules 606.3/113.5 aren't what's stopping the second activation — the card's own text is.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Skinshifter's ability is modal, but it is still one ability. Atticus can't activate that ability more than once per turn, regardless of which mode was chosen.

entries.question: Alvaro casts [Foe-Razer Regent], and chooses to target [Tolarian Scholar] with its triggered ability upon entering the battlefield. Before that ability resolves, Naomi casts [Primal Boost] targeting Tolarian Scholar. Does Foe-Razer Regent die as its ability resolves?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the Regent only dies if Alvaro chooses to have it fight as the triggered ability resolves, and the candidate's detailed explanation matches that ruling.
entries.answer:
Yes — Foe-Razer Regent dies, though technically it dies just after the ability finishes resolving, not during resolution.

Why: Primal Boost gives Tolarian Scholar +4/+4 until end of turn, so it's a 6/7 when Foe-Razer Regent's enter-the-battlefield trigger resolves (the +4/+4 applies in layer 7c on top of its printed 2/3; see rules 613.1g and 613.4b for how power/toughness effects are layered). Tolarian Scholar is still a legal target, so the ability resolves normally (608.2b), and Alvaro chooses whether to fight as it resolves ([Foe-Razer Regent ruling #1]). If Alvaro chooses to fight, Foe-Razer Regent deals 4 damage to Tolarian Scholar (which survives with 7 toughness) and Tolarian Scholar deals 6 damage to Foe-Razer Regent, whose toughness is 5.

State-based actions aren't checked in the middle of a resolution (704.4), so nothing happens until the fight ability finishes resolving. Then, before any player gets priority, 6 damage marked on a 5-toughness Foe-Razer Regent is lethal damage and it's destroyed (120.6).

Alvaro can avoid this: choosing not to fight means no damage is dealt and Foe-Razer Regent survives (its second ability also won't trigger, since no fight occurred). Also note that if Tolarian Scholar somehow became an illegal target first, no fight happens at all and the +1/+1 counter trigger doesn't trigger ([Foe-Razer Regent ruling #0]). Even when the fight does happen, the delayed "two +1/+1 counters at the beginning of the next end step" won't save Foe-Razer Regent — it's already been destroyed long before the end step.

This works the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer; nothing here depends on the number of opponents, only on which creature was targeted.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Only if Alvaro chooses to have it fight. Only the target is chosen when the ability is put onto the stack, the choice of whether to fight is made as the ability resolves.

entries.question: Alondra has 3 [Undead Servant]s in their graveyard and casts another Undead Servant. After it enters the battlefield but before its trigger resolves, Nico activates [Tormod's Crypt] to exile all cards from Alondra's graveyard. When Undead Servant's ability resolves, how many tokens will be created?
entries.reason: Both say the ability counts cards when it resolves and, because Tormod's Crypt exiled Alondra's graveyard before that resolution, there are no Undead Servant cards to count so zero tokens are created.
entries.answer:
Zero tokens. The count is made when Undead Servant's triggered ability resolves, not when it triggered. Because Nico's Tormod's Crypt exiled Alondra's graveyard first, there are no cards named Undead Servant in that graveyard at resolution, so the ability creates no Zombie tokens.

Why: Undead Servant's ruling states you count the number of cards named Undead Servant in your graveyard as the ability resolves ([Undead Servant ruling #0]). Rule 608.2h confirms that when an effect requires information from the game (such as how many cards are in a zone), that information is determined only once, when the effect is applied — i.e., on resolution. Nico's Tormod's Crypt ability ({T}, Sacrifice: Exile target player's graveyard) resolves first, so by the time Undead Servant's trigger resolves the graveyard is empty.

Timing note: I'm assuming Nico's Tormod's Crypt ability actually resolved before Undead Servant's trigger (it was activated in response, so it's above the trigger on the stack and resolves first). If instead Tormod's Crypt were activated only after Undead Servant's trigger had already resolved, Alondra would have gotten 3 tokens (or 4 if a fourth Undead Servant had also reached the graveyard in time), and exiling the graveyard afterward wouldn't remove those tokens.

Player count doesn't matter here: the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since Tormod's Crypt targets one player's graveyard.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 0. The number of tokens to create is determined when the ability resolves, by which point the graveyard has no creatures in it.

entries.question: Aspen has no cards in their library and controls a [Keranos, God of Storms] and [Platinum Angel]. When they begin their draw step, what happens?
entries.reason: Both conclude Aspen fails to draw (so Keranos doesn't trigger) and Platinum Angel prevents the resulting loss, allowing Aspen to continue the turn.
entries.answer:
Aspen attempts to draw from an empty library, doesn't draw a card, and would lose the game — but Platinum Angel stops that, so Aspen keeps playing. Keranos, God of Storms does nothing, because no card was actually drawn or revealed.

Details:

1. Turn-based action at the start of the draw step: the active player draws a card [504.1]. With no cards in the library, Aspen simply fails to draw.
2. Because Aspen attempted to draw from an empty library, the state-based action in [704.5b] (see also [121.4], [104.3c]) would make Aspen lose the game the next time a player would receive priority.
3. Platinum Angel's text — "You can't lose the game and your opponents can't win the game" — overrides that general rule. Its ruling is explicit that it doesn't matter that you're forced to draw with an empty library; you keep playing [Platinum Angel ruling #3]. This is card text beating the general state-based-action rule.
4. Keranos, God of Storms says to reveal the first card you draw on each of your turns. No card was drawn, so there's nothing to reveal, and neither the "reveal a land card" draw trigger nor the "reveal a nonland card" 3-damage trigger happens [Keranos, God of Storms ruling #0 covers only the case where a land actually is revealed]. Note also that Keranos, God of Storms isn't a creature unless your devotion to blue and red is seven or more, but that doesn't change this outcome.
5. If Platinum Angel later leaves the battlefield, Aspen's earlier failed draw is a past event; but any new attempt to draw from the empty library will again put Aspen at risk of losing under [704.5b].

Multiplayer: this works the same with any number of players — Platinum Angel additionally means no opponent can win the game while it's on the battlefield [Platinum Angel ruling #3]. In the Two-Headed Giant variant, an empty-library draw by one player would normally lose the game for the whole team, but a Platinum Angel means neither that player nor their teammate can lose [810.8a].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Aspen can't draw a card, so no card is revealed and none of Keranos, God of Storms's triggered abilities trigger. Aspen will continue with their turn.

entries.question: Amia controls [Sanctuary Cat], and Nico controls [Glacial Chasm] and [Ral Zarek]. Amia attacks Ral Zarek with Sanctuary Cat. Is damage to Ral Zarek prevented?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly concludes that Glacial Chasm only prevents damage to its controller (the player) and does not prevent damage dealt to the planeswalker Ral Zarek, matching the reference.
entries.answer:
No. Sanctuary Cat's 1 combat damage is dealt to Ral Zarek, removing 1 loyalty counter (Ral Zarek goes to 3 loyalty if it was at 4).

Glacial Chasm reads "Prevent all damage that would be dealt to you." That prevention shield protects only Nico, the player — it says nothing about permanents Nico controls, so it does not cover the planeswalker Ral Zarek. A prevention effect is a continuous effect that watches for a damage event and stops the damage from being dealt to whatever it shields [615.1], and Glacial Chasm's shield surrounds Nico alone.

There is also no longer any redirection from planeswalkers to their controller or vice versa: the old rule letting damage aimed at a player be dealt to that player's planeswalker instead has been removed [306.7]. And planeswalkers can be attacked directly [306.6], so Sanctuary Cat's combat damage is dealt to Ral Zarek as its own recipient, never to Nico. Damage to Ral Zarek is therefore not prevented.

If instead Sanctuary Cat had attacked Nico and been unblocked, Glacial Chasm would prevent that 1 damage entirely, and none of it would spill over to Ral Zarek.

This works the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer; Glacial Chasm only ever shields its own controller regardless of the number of players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Ral Zarek is not Nico.

entries.question: Norah controls [Treasure Vault]. Aubrey activates [Pernicious Deed] for X = 0. Will Treasure Vault be destroyed?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Treasure Vault is destroyed because it is an artifact with mana value 0 and Pernicious Deed (X=0) destroys artifacts with mana value 0 or less.
entries.answer:
Yes. Treasure Vault is destroyed.

Pernicious Deed's activated ability reads "{X}, Sacrifice this enchantment: Destroy each artifact, creature, and enchantment with mana value X or less." With X = 0, it destroys every permanent that is an artifact, creature, or enchantment whose mana value is 0 or less.

Treasure Vault is an Artifact Land, so it is an artifact (its land type does not exempt it \u2014 Pernicious Deed doesn't say "noncreature" or exclude lands, it just asks whether the permanent is an artifact). Treasure Vault has no mana cost, and the mana value of an object with no mana cost is 0 (rule 202.3a). 0 is "0 or less," so Treasure Vault meets the condition and is destroyed by the resolving ability, which is a genuine "destroy" effect (rule 701.8b).

A note on X: {X} in Pernicious Deed's activation cost is fixed when the ability is activated (Aubrey chose 0), and a cost of {0} is legal \u2014 Aubrey simply has to acknowledge paying it (rule 118.5a). Aubrey also sacrifices Pernicious Deed as part of the cost, before the ability resolves.

Treasure Vault could survive only if it's regenerated, given indestructible, or otherwise protected in response \u2014 or if Norah sacrifices it first (for instance to its own {X}{X}, {T}, Sacrifice ability), since a permanent put into the graveyard some other way hasn't been "destroyed" (rule 701.8b).

This works identically at a two-player table and in multiplayer: Pernicious Deed destroys qualifying permanents controlled by every player, including Aubrey's own, not just those of a chosen opponent.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Pernicious Deed specifies that it destroys artifacts. It doesn't care if the card has other types as well, only that it has one of the named types. Treasure Vault has mana value 0, and therefore falls under the scope of what Pernicious Deed is destroying.

entries.question: Aylin controls [Stone Haven Outfitter] and [Dromoka Warrior]. Aylin activates [Skullclamp]'s equip ability targeting Dromoka Warrior. What happens when the equip ability resolves?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Skullclamp attaches, Dromoka Warrior gets the equipment-related buffs and does not die when the equip resolves.
entries.answer:
Skullclamp becomes attached to Dromoka Warrior, and Dromoka Warrior survives as a 5/1.

Details:
- The equip ability targets Dromoka Warrior; on resolution it checks the target is still legal (608.2b) and then attaches Skullclamp to Dromoka Warrior (301.5b, 701.3b). Equip can only attach to a creature its controller controls, which Aylin does.
- Once attached, both static buffs apply at the same time, not in sequence: Skullclamp's "Equipped creature gets +1/-1" and Stone Haven Outfitter's "Equipped creatures you control get +1/+1." Dromoka Warrior's base 3/1 becomes 3+1+1 / 1-1+1 = 5/1. Its toughness is never actually 0, so it is not put into the graveyard by state-based actions.
- Stone Haven Outfitter's bonus applies to any creature Aylin controls that has Equipment attached, and it applies only once regardless of how many Equipment are attached (Stone Haven Outfitter ruling #1, Stone Haven Outfitter ruling #2). Note Stone Haven Outfitter itself is not equipped here, so it stays 2/2.
- Nothing is drawn now. If Dromoka Warrior later dies while equipped, Skullclamp's trigger draws two cards and Stone Haven Outfitter's trigger draws one, for three cards total.
- If Skullclamp ever ends up attached to something that isn't a legal creature, a state-based action unattaches it while leaving it on the battlefield (704.5n, 301.5c).

This interaction is identical whether the game has two players or more; the equip ability can only target a creature Aylin controls, so other opponents don't change anything (702.6c).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: After Skullclamp's equip ability resolves, the game checks state-based actions. At that point Dromoka Warrior is getting +1/+1 and does not die.

entries.question: Austin resolves [Duplicant], and uses [Yarok, the Desecrated] to exile [Murasa Brute] then [Grizzly Bears]. Once all the triggers resolve, what is Duplicant's power and toughness?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Yarok causes two separate imprint triggers resolved with Grizzly Bears last, so Duplicant becomes a 2/2.
entries.answer:
Duplicant is a 2/2 (an Artifact Creature — Bear Shapeshifter).

Why: Yarok, the Desecrated makes Duplicant's Imprint trigger an additional time, so there are two separate instances of "When this creature enters, you may exile target nontoken creature." Yarok, the Desecrated doesn't copy the ability — each instance chooses its own target and is resolved separately [Yarok, the Desecrated ruling #2]. Austin resolved them so that Murasa Brute was exiled first and Grizzly Bears second.

Duplicant's static ability says it "has the power, toughness, and creature types of the LAST creature card exiled with it. It's still a Shapeshifter." The last card exiled is Grizzly Bears (2/2 Bear), so Duplicant's base power and toughness are set to 2/2 [Duplicant ruling #0] and its creature types become Bear plus Shapeshifter. Murasa Brute (3/3) is no longer the last exiled card and does nothing further, though it stays exiled. If the triggers had resolved in the other order — Grizzly Bears exiled first, then Murasa Brute — Duplicant would instead be a 3/3 Troll Warrior Shapeshifter; Austin controls both triggers and therefore controls that order.

This is a base-value change in the layer system, so any +1/+1 counters, Auras, or pump effects on Duplicant would still apply on top of the 2/2 [Duplicant ruling #0], and Duplicant's power/toughness would update if Grizzly Bears' printed values somehow changed [Duplicant ruling #3]. None of that is present here.

Player count doesn't matter for this interaction: the number of opponents changes nothing about how many times Imprint triggers or which card counts as last exiled.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Duplicant is a 2/2. Its second ability looks at the last creature card exiled by the first ability, which was Grizzly Bears.

entries.question: Allen controls [Yixlid Jailer] and casts [Ever After] targeting [Dearly Departed] and [Fresh Volunteers]. Will Fresh Volunteers enter with a +1/+1 counter?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same ruling — Fresh Volunteers gets no +1/+1 counter because Yixlid Jailer removes Dearly Departed’s graveyard ability (and even absent Jailer they return simultaneously so the graveyard-trigger wouldn’t apply).
entries.answer:
No — Fresh Volunteers enters with no +1/+1 counter, for two independent reasons.

1) Yixlid Jailer says "Cards in graveyards lose all abilities." Dearly Departed's relevant ability ("As long as this creature is in your graveyard, each Human creature you control enters with an additional +1/+1 counter on it") is an ability that must function while Dearly Departed is in the graveyard. Yixlid Jailer removes it there, so it never applies. The Yixlid Jailer exception in [Yixlid Jailer ruling #3] only covers abilities that will exist on the battlefield (such as "enters with counters" abilities of the card being reanimated); Dearly Departed's ability instead needs to work from the graveyard, so that exception doesn't rescue it.

2) Even without Yixlid Jailer, Ever After returns Dearly Departed and Fresh Volunteers to the battlefield simultaneously. The counter-granting replacement effect is checked as Fresh Volunteers enters, using the continuous effects that already exist and would apply (614.12, 614.12a, 614.1c). Dearly Departed is no longer in a graveyard at that moment — it's entering the battlefield too — so its graveyard-only condition isn't met.

Note Fresh Volunteers is still a Human (Ever After makes it a black Zombie "in addition to its other colors and types"), so type isn't the issue; the enabling ability simply isn't active. Had Ever After returned only Fresh Volunteers with Dearly Departed staying in the graveyard and no Yixlid Jailer on the battlefield, Fresh Volunteers would have entered with one +1/+1 counter (cumulative per Dearly Departed, per [Dearly Departed ruling #0]).

This analysis doesn't depend on player count; it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Dearly Departed has no abilities while in the graveyard.

entries.question: Allan has 3 [Redwood Treefolk] in their graveyard and casts [Izoni, Thousand-Eyed]. After it enters the battlefield but before its trigger resolves, Noelle activates [Scavenger Grounds] to exile all cards from Allan's graveyard. When Izoni, Thousand-Eyed's ability resolves, how many tokens will be created?
entries.reason: The candidate gives the same final ruling that Izoni's ability counts creature cards at resolution and, because Scavenger Grounds exiled Allan's graveyard before resolution, zero tokens are created.
entries.answer:
Zero Insect tokens.

Izoni, Thousand-Eyed's undergrowth trigger counts creature cards in Allan's graveyard when the ability actually resolves, not when it triggered. Under rule 608.2h, if an effect requires information from the game (such as how many creature cards are in a graveyard), that information is determined only once — at the time the effect is applied, i.e., during resolution. Since Noelle's Scavenger Grounds ability resolved first and exiled all graveyards, Allan's three Redwood Treefolk are in exile, not the graveyard, when Izoni, Thousand-Eyed's trigger resolves. The count is 0, so no tokens are created.

Timing note: I'm assuming Scavenger Grounds' ability was activated and fully resolved while the Izoni, Thousand-Eyed trigger was still on the stack (that's what the question describes). If instead Scavenger Grounds' ability were activated but Allan let the Izoni, Thousand-Eyed trigger resolve first — which can't happen if Scavenger Grounds' ability was put on the stack later, since it resolves first — the count would be 3 and Allan would get three Insect tokens. Allan's window to respond is before Scavenger Grounds' ability resolves; note also that Allan can activate Izoni, Thousand-Eyed's {B}{G}, Sacrifice another creature ability in response to increase the count, but only creature cards put into the graveyard and still there at resolution matter (Izoni, Thousand-Eyed ruling #1), and tokens never count (Izoni, Thousand-Eyed ruling #2).

This works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table; Scavenger Grounds exiles all graveyards regardless of the number of players, and the resolution-time counting rule is unchanged.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 0. The number of tokens to create is determined when the ability resolves, by which point the graveyard has no creatures in it.

entries.question: Addisyn controls [Medomai the Ageless] and casts [Savor the Moment]. Can Medomai the Ageless attack during the extra turn?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Medomai the Ageless cannot attack during the extra turn created by Savor the Moment, since "extra turn" means a turn created by a spell or ability and Medomai's text forbids attacking on extra turns.
entries.answer:
No. Medomai the Ageless cannot attack during the extra turn granted by Savor the Moment.

Medomai the Ageless's own printed text says "Medomai can't attack during extra turns." An "extra turn" is any turn created by the effect of a spell or ability [500.7], and Savor the Moment explicitly says "Take an extra turn after this one," so that turn is an extra turn. This card text is a restriction on declaring attackers, so during the declare attackers step Addisyn simply may not choose Medomai the Ageless as an attacker [508.1a] — the card's specific text overrides the general permission to attack with an untapped, non-summoning-sick creature.

Two extra notes:
- It doesn't matter who controls Medomai the Ageless or whose extra turn it is; it can't attack during any extra turn [Medomai the Ageless ruling #1], and "extra turn" means a turn created by a spell or ability, not a tournament additional turn [Medomai the Ageless ruling #0].
- Savor the Moment also makes Addisyn skip the untap step of that extra turn, so if Medomai the Ageless attacked on the previous turn it would still be tapped anyway (and a creature must be untapped to be declared as an attacker) [508.1a].
- Medomai the Ageless could still be put onto the battlefield attacking or be stated to be attacking by some other effect during an extra turn, since such a creature never "attacked" and isn't affected by attack restrictions [508.4c].

This is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; the restriction is on Medomai the Ageless itself, regardless of which opponent or planeswalker it would attack.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. An extra turn is any turn created by a spell or ability. Medomai the Ageless cannot attack during any turn that is not a normal game turn, regardless of the source.

entries.question: Alex activates [Horror of the Dim]'s ability. After that resolves, Nathaniel activates [Detection Tower]. After that resolves, Alex activates Horror of the Dims ability again. After that resolves, can Nathaniel target Horror of the Dim?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Nathaniel can target Horror of the Dim because Detection Tower lets him treat opponents' creatures with hexproof as though they didn't have hexproof.
entries.answer:
Yes. Nathaniel can still target Horror of the Dim.

Detection Tower's ability says "Until end of turn, your opponents and creatures your opponents control with hexproof can be the targets of spells and abilities you control as though they didn't have hexproof." Hexproof means the permanent can't be the target of spells or abilities its controller's opponents control (702.11b). Detection Tower's effect doesn't modify any object's characteristics — it modifies the rules of the game — so under 611.2c and 613.11 the set of things it applies to is not locked in at resolution; it's continuously updated for the rest of the turn. Detection Tower ruling #0 states this directly: creatures that come under your opponents' control later in the turn can be targeted as though they didn't have hexproof.

So it makes no difference that Alex granted hexproof before Detection Tower's ability resolved and then granted it again afterward with a second {U} activation. Any hexproof Horror of the Dim has at the moment Nathaniel chooses targets is simply ignored for Nathaniel's spells and abilities for the remainder of that turn. (If Horror of the Dim instead had shroud — "can't be the target of spells or abilities" at all, from anyone, per 702.18a — Detection Tower would not help, since it only addresses hexproof.)

Multiplayer note: Detection Tower's effect covers "your opponents and creatures your opponents control," so at a table with more than two players it applies to every opponent of Nathaniel's, not just Alex; the answer for Horror of the Dim is the same either way.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Detection Tower doesn't cause Horror of the Dim to lose hexproof, it simply allows Nathaniel to treat creatures that have hexproof as if they did not have hexproof.

entries.question: Alex controls [Gaea's Herald] and casts [Aegis Turtle]. Before that resolves Neil casts [Spell Queller] targeting Aegis Turtle. What happens to Aegis Turtle?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Spell Queller exiles Aegis Turtle so it does not resolve, and that Gaea's Herald's "can't be countered" clause does not prevent Spell Queller from exiling it.
entries.answer:
Aegis Turtle gets exiled and never resolves. Gaea's Herald doesn't help: it only says creature spells can't be countered, and Spell Queller doesn't counter — its enters ability exiles the target spell. A spell that can't be countered can still be exiled by Spell Queller, and it simply won't resolve [Spell Queller ruling #3].

Details:
- Aegis Turtle has mana value 1 (its cost is {U}), so it's a legal target for Spell Queller's "exile target spell with mana value 4 or less."
- Aegis Turtle goes from the stack to exile. It does not enter the battlefield and no creature is created for Alex.
- Later, when Spell Queller leaves the battlefield, its second triggered ability lets the exiled card's owner — Alex — cast Aegis Turtle without paying its mana cost, but only right then, during that ability's resolution; Alex can't hold it to cast later in the turn, though timing permissions based on card type are ignored [Spell Queller ruling #1].
- If Neil's Spell Queller somehow leaves the battlefield before its enters ability resolves, the leaves-the-battlefield trigger resolves first and does nothing, and then Aegis Turtle is exiled permanently [Spell Queller ruling #4].

This works the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer; nothing here depends on the number of players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Aegis Turtle will be exiled and will not resolve. Spell Queller does not "counter" Aegis Turtle so the "can't be countered" clause won't do anything.

entries.question: Adelynn controls [Archetype of Imagination] and [Merfolk of the Pearl Trident]. Nico casts [Sagittars' Volley] targeting Archetype of Imagination. Will Merfolk of the Pearl Trident be dealt damage?
entries.reason: Both conclude Merfolk of the Pearl Trident isn't dealt damage because Sagittars' Volley's destroy instruction removes Archetype of Imagination (ending its continuous flying-grant) before the spell deals damage.
entries.answer:
No — Merfolk of the Pearl Trident is not dealt damage, assuming Archetype of Imagination is actually destroyed.

Why: Sagittars' Volley's instructions are carried out in the order written during its single resolution (608.2c). First it destroys target creature with flying — Archetype of Imagination, which has flying only because of its own first ability granting flying to Adelynn's creatures. The moment Archetype of Imagination is put into the graveyard, its continuous effect ends, so Merfolk of the Pearl Trident no longer has flying. Then, as the second instruction, Sagittars' Volley deals 1 damage to each creature with flying Nico's opponents control. Merfolk of the Pearl Trident isn't a creature with flying at that moment, so it takes nothing.

Exceptions worth noting:
- If Archetype of Imagination is a legal target but isn't destroyed (for example, it has indestructible), it remains on the battlefield, Merfolk of the Pearl Trident still has flying, and both would be dealt 1 damage each [Sagittars' Volley ruling #0].
- If Archetype of Imagination is an illegal target when Sagittars' Volley tries to resolve (it left the battlefield, lost flying, etc.), the spell doesn't resolve at all and no creature is dealt damage [Sagittars' Volley ruling #0, 608.2b].

Multiplayer: the same reasoning applies, but Sagittars' Volley damages each creature with flying controlled by any of Nico's opponents, not just Adelynn's [Sagittars' Volley ruling #1] — other players' fliers that don't depend on Adelynn's Archetype of Imagination for flying would still be dealt 1 damage.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Sagittars' Volley will carry out its instructions in the order written on the card. First, Sagittars' Volley will destroy Archetype of Imagination, then it will deal one damage to each creature with flying that Adelynn controls. At this time, Adelynn controls no creatures with flying as the continuous effect that was granting Merfolk of the Pearl Trident flying is no longer on the battlefield.

entries.question: Aliana controls [Kalakscion, Hunger Tyrant] equipped with [Helm of the Host] and [Mirror Gallery]. When Aliana goes to combat, what will the token look like?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly states the Helm token is a copy of Kalakscion that isn't legendary and that Mirror Gallery doesn't change that (the candidate's added note that the token gains haste is a correct extra Helm effect).
entries.answer:
At the beginning of combat on Aliana's turn, Helm of the Host creates a token that is a copy of Kalakscion, Hunger Tyrant, except the token is not legendary, and it gains haste.

Concretely, the token has all of Kalakscion, Hunger Tyrant's copiable values: the name Kalakscion, Hunger Tyrant, mana cost {1}{B}{B} (black), the type line Creature — Crocodile (with "Legendary" stripped off by Helm of the Host's own exception), power/toughness 7/2, and all of Kalakscion, Hunger Tyrant's rules text and abilities. On top of that it has haste. The token is untapped and not attacking (Helm of the Host doesn't say otherwise), so haste lets it attack the turn it appears.

A few details:
- Helm of the Host's "except the token isn't legendary" is a modification made as part of the copying process, so "non-legendary" becomes part of the token's own copiable values [707.9b].
- Because a spell or ability that creates a copy token sets the token's characteristics from the copied object, its name is Kalakscion, Hunger Tyrant — not "Crocodile Token" or "Kalakscion, Hunger Tyrant Token" [111.4, 707.1].
- Mirror Gallery ("The 'legend rule' doesn't apply") makes no difference here: the token isn't legendary in the first place, so there would be no legend-rule conflict even without Mirror Gallery. Mirror Gallery would only matter if some other effect made the token legendary or if you had two legendary copies.
- The Helm of the Host token is not a copy of the Equipment and does not come equipped; Helm of the Host stays attached to Kalakscion, Hunger Tyrant.
- If Kalakscion, Hunger Tyrant has left the battlefield before Helm of the Host's trigger resolves, or nothing is equipped, no token is created; but if Helm of the Host itself leaves while the trigger is on the stack, you still get a token copying the creature it last equipped, using last known information if needed [Helm of the Host ruling #1].

This works the same at a two-player table or a multiplayer table — nothing about Helm of the Host's trigger depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The token created will be a copy of Kalakscion, Hunger Tyrant except it won't be legendary. Mirror Gallery doesn't impact whether Kalakscion, Hunger Tyrant is legendary or not, it simply allows Aliana to control two or more legendary permanents with the same name without Aliana having to put one in their graveyard.

entries.question: Alonzo controls [Quicksilver, Speedster]. Can Alonzo play [Darksteel Citadel] during an opponent's turn?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion—Quicksilver only lets you cast spells as though they had flash and playing a land (including artifact lands like Darksteel Citadel) is not casting a spell, so you cannot play it during an opponent’s turn.
entries.answer:
No. Alonzo cannot play Darksteel Citadel during an opponent's turn, even with Quicksilver, Speedster tapped.

Why: Quicksilver, Speedster's last ability says "As long as Quicksilver is tapped, you may cast spells as though they had flash." That only affects *casting spells*. Playing a land is not casting a spell — it's a special action that doesn't use the stack, and the land never becomes a spell [305.1] [116.2a] [701.18a]. Darksteel Citadel is an artifact land, and an object that's both a land and another card type can only be played as a land; it can't be cast as a spell [300.2a] [Darksteel Citadel ruling #0]. So the flash permission never applies to it.

The timing restrictions on playing a land still apply in full: the player must have priority, it must be a main phase of *their own* turn, the stack must be empty, and they must not have already played their allowed number of lands [305.1] [701.18a]. A player can't play a land for any reason if it isn't their turn; any effect instructing otherwise is ignored [305.3].

This is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table — the restriction is tied to whose turn it is, not to opponent count. (In the Two-Headed Giant/team variant, each player on a team may play a land during their team's turn [805.4c].) Also note that if some other effect *puts* Darksteel Citadel onto the battlefield, that isn't "playing" it and can happen at times a land play couldn't [305.4].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Quicksilver, Speedster allows Alonzo to cast spells as though they had flash. Playing a land is not the same as casting a spell.

entries.question: Amber is playing commander and on their first turn they cast [Serra Ascendant]. What is its power and toughness?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling that Serra Ascendant is a 6/6 on turn one in Commander (starting life 40), correctly noting the +5/+5 and flying apply while the player is at 30+ life.
entries.answer:
6/6 (a 6/6 with flying and lifelink), assuming Amber's life total is at the Commander starting total of 40 and hasn't dropped below 30.

Serra Ascendant is printed as a 1/1. Its static ability, "As long as you have 30 or more life, this creature gets +5/+5 and has flying," is a continuous effect that applies whenever the condition is true. Power and toughness are determined by starting with the printed numbers and then applying applicable continuous effects [302.4c], and this +5/+5 is applied on top of the printed 1/1, giving 6/6, plus flying alongside its lifelink.

One honesty note: the rules excerpts provided here don't include the rule that states the Commander starting life total (the only starting-life rule given is [904.5], which is for Archenemy: 40 for the archenemy, 20 for everyone else). I'm relying on Amber being at 40 life on turn one. If Amber's life total were below 30 at the moment you check, Serra Ascendant would simply be a 1/1 with lifelink; the ability turns on and off dynamically as the life total crosses 30.

Multiplayer: Commander is usually played with more than two players, but that changes nothing here — the ability only looks at your own life total, not opponents'. The one variant that does differ is Two-Headed Giant, where the check uses your team's shared life total [810.9a], [Serra Ascendant ruling #1].

Also worth knowing for combat: if Serra Ascendant is dealt damage at the same moment you gain life that pushes you to 30 or more, the +5/+5 is applied before checking whether the damage is lethal [Serra Ascendant ruling #0].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 6/6. The starting life total in commander is 40.

entries.question: Antonio controls [Festering Thicket], two [Island]s, [Snow-Covered Mountain], and [Wastes]. They cast [Exotic Disease]. What is the value of X?
entries.reason: Both conclude X = 4, counting the four distinct basic land types present (Swamp, Forest, Island, Mountain) and noting Snow-Covered Mountain counts as Mountain while Wastes provides no basic land type.
entries.answer:
X = 4. Exotic Disease's domain ability counts the number of basic land types among lands Antonio controls. The five basic land types are Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest.

Counting Antonio's lands:
- Festering Thicket is a Swamp Forest, so it supplies both Swamp and Forest. Even though Festering Thicket isn't a basic land, it genuinely has those two basic land types ([Festering Thicket ruling #0]).
- The two Islands supply Island (duplicates don't count twice).
- Snow-Covered Mountain supplies Mountain; being snow doesn't matter for domain.
- Wastes is a basic land but has no basic land type at all, so it contributes nothing.

That's Swamp, Forest, Island, Mountain = 4 distinct basic land types; only Plains is missing. So the target player loses 4 life and Antonio gains 4 life.

Note that this X is defined by Exotic Disease's own text, so Antonio does not choose it; it's determined on resolution rather than announced during casting ([107.3], [107.3a]). Also note Exotic Disease's mana cost is {4}{B} — the {4} is generic and the {B} must be black mana ([107.4b], [202.1a]); that X in the text is unrelated to the cost. This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games; in multiplayer, Antonio simply chooses which single player Exotic Disease targets.

entries.question: Nicholas controls [Meddling Mage], naming "[Ogre Resister]". Can Ariel cast [Sakashima the Impostor], copying an Ogre Resister on the battlefield?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling and reasoning: Meddling Mage only stops casting spells with the chosen name, and Sakashima is cast as "Sakashima the Impostor" and only becomes a copy on entering the battlefield.
entries.answer:
Yes. Ariel can cast Sakashima the Impostor for {2}{U}{U} and have it enter as a copy of Ogre Resister.

Meddling Mage's ability says "Spells with the chosen name can't be cast" — it's a casting restriction that looks at the name of the spell as it's being cast [601.3a]. When Ariel casts Sakashima the Impostor, the object on the stack is a spell named "Sakashima the Impostor," with all the characteristics of that card [601.2a]; "Ogre Resister" is not its name, so Meddling Mage's prohibition never applies.

The copy effect happens later and doesn't change this. Sakashima the Impostor's own text is a replacement effect applied as it enters the battlefield, and it explicitly says "except its name is Sakashima the Impostor." So even after copying Ogre Resister on the battlefield, the permanent is named Sakashima the Impostor, and in any case a permanent on the battlefield is not a spell, so Meddling Mage's "spells ... can't be cast" clause is irrelevant to it [109.2b]. Note also that the copy choice is made as part of the event that puts Sakashima the Impostor onto the battlefield, so the Ogre Resister being copied must already be on the battlefield at that time [Sakashima the Impostor ruling #2].

This works the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer; Meddling Mage's restriction applies to every player's spells regardless of player count, and nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. Sakashima the Impostor is named "Sakashima the Impostor" as it's cast, so Meddling Mage doesn't affect it. It only becomes a copy of Ogre Resister as it enters the battlefield. That isn't casting a spell, so Meddling Mage doesn't affect that either.

entries.question: Ari has controlled [Willow Elf] enchanted with [Nyxborn Hydra] since their last turn. Nathan casts [Nocturnal Hunger] targeting Willow Elf. After Nocturnal Hunger resolves and Willow Elf is put into Ari's graveyard, can Ari attack with Nyxborn Hydra?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Nyxborn Hydra simply ceases to be a bestowed Aura and remains on the battlefield as a creature without changing zones, so Ari — having controlled it continuously since their turn began — may attack with it.
entries.answer:
Yes. Once Willow Elf is destroyed by Nocturnal Hunger and put into Ari's graveyard, Nyxborn Hydra becomes unattached, stops being an Aura, and stays on the battlefield as an Enchantment Creature — Hydra, and Ari can attack with it (assuming it's Ari's turn and the destruction happened before or during Ari's declare attackers step).

Why: normally an Aura attached to an illegal object or attached to nothing is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action [704.5m], but bestow is an explicit exception — a bestowed Aura that becomes unattached simply ceases to be bestowed [702.103f]. Nyxborn Hydra's bestow reminder text ("It becomes a creature again if it's not attached") overrides the general Aura rule. It loses enchant creature, the Aura-making effect ends, and it remains on the battlefield as an enchantment creature keeping its +1/+1 counters, reach, and trample [Nyxborn Hydra ruling #4].

Summoning sickness isn't a problem: Nyxborn Hydra can attack the turn it becomes unattached because it has been under Ari's control continuously — even while it was an Aura — since Ari's most recent turn began, which the question states [Nyxborn Hydra ruling #4].

Note it never changed zones, so it is not a new object [400.7].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Nathan cast Nocturnal Hunger during Ari's turn at a point before attackers are declared. If instead Nocturnal Hunger resolved after attackers were declared, Nyxborn Hydra simply wasn't declared as an attacker that combat (it was an Aura at that time); if it resolved on Nathan's turn, Ari attacks with Nyxborn Hydra on their following turn as normal.

Player count doesn't matter here: the provided rules give no different outcome for two players versus a multiplayer table, other than Ari choosing which opponent or planeswalker/battle to attack in multiplayer.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. Ari has controlled Nyxborn Hydra continuously since their most recent turn began, so it can attack.

entries.question: Anders casts [Shining Shoal] with X=1, choosing [Sulfurous Springs] as the source of damage and Noa as the target. Anders taps Sulfurous Springs for {R}. Is Noa dealt 1 damage?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion that Shining Shoal redirects the 1 damage from Sulfurous Springs to Noa, so Noa is dealt 1 damage.
entries.answer:
Yes — Noa is dealt 1 damage, assuming Anders controls Sulfurous Springs and Shining Shoal had already resolved before Sulfurous Springs was tapped (that's the order given in the question).

Why: Shining Shoal reads "The next X damage that a source of your choice would deal to you and/or creatures you control this turn is dealt to any target instead." With X=1, the chosen source is Sulfurous Springs and the chosen target is Noa. Sulfurous Springs is a permanent, so it's a legal choice of damage source, and a source doesn't need to be capable of dealing damage to be chosen — though here it plainly is [609.7a] [120.7]. When Anders activates "{T}: Add {B} or {R}. This land deals 1 damage to you," Sulfurous Springs deals 1 damage to Anders. That's exactly the event Shining Shoal's shield is watching for, so the 1 damage is redirected and dealt to Noa instead; the shield is then used up [615.1] [614.1].

The shield rechecks the source's properties when the damage would be dealt; since Shining Shoal names a specific source rather than a property like a color, Sulfurous Springs still matches and the replacement applies [609.7b] [615.9].

Timing caveat: if Anders had tapped Sulfurous Springs for {R} first (for example, to help pay {X}{W}{W}), that 1 damage would already have been dealt to Anders before Shining Shoal resolved, and Shining Shoal would sit waiting for a later damage event from Sulfurous Springs instead. Note also Shining Shoal has an alternative cost — exiling a white card with mana value X (here, 1) from hand rather than paying its mana cost — which avoids needing red mana at all.

Multiplayer: no difference. Noa is simply the chosen target, whether the table has two players or more; nothing here depends on a defending player or on turn order.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. The damage is redirected to Noa. It doesn't matter that it's coming from a source Anders controls.

entries.question: Adrien controls 5 artifacts and activates [Tezzeret, Master of the Bridge]'s +2 ability. Noemi casts [Petty Theft] in response, sending one of Adrien's artifacts back to their hand. How much life does Adrien gain?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion that Adrien gains 4 life, correctly noting X is determined on resolution after Petty Theft returns one artifact.
entries.answer:
Adrien gains 4 life (and Tezzeret, Master of the Bridge deals 4 damage to each opponent).

Tezzeret, Master of the Bridge's +2 ability reads "Tezzeret deals X damage to each opponent, where X is the number of artifacts you control. You gain X life." X isn't locked in when the ability is activated; the ability checks the game for information only once, as it resolves (rule 608.2h; see also 611.2d for variables in resolving spells/abilities). Petty Theft resolves first, returning one of Adrien's five artifacts to their hand, so when Tezzeret, Master of the Bridge's ability finally resolves Adrien controls 4 artifacts. X = 4 for both the damage and the life gain 
ot 5 for one and 4 for the other.

Multiplayer note: the +2 hits each opponent, so with more than two players every opponent is dealt 4 damage, but Adrien still gains only 4 life once — the life gain doesn't scale with the number of opponents. (Two-Headed Giant is the exception noted on the card's ruling: the opposing team loses twice X life while Adrien still gains X.)

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Petty Theft fully resolves before the +2 ability resolves, which is how "in response" works. If instead the artifact were bounced after the +2 ability had already resolved, X would have been 5 and Adrien would have gained 5 life.

entries.answer_gold: Adrien will gain 4 life when Tezzeret's ability resolves, because the ability counts the number of artifacts they control on resolution, not on activation.

entries.question: Aspen controls [Pyromancer Ascension] and has [Thirst for Meaning] in their graveyard. Aspen casts a second Thirst for Meaning from their hand. At Nathalie's first opportunity, they activate [Lantern of the Lost] to exile Aspen's graveyard. Will Pyromancer Ascension get a quest counter?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Pyromancer Ascension's ability triggers when the second Thirst for Meaning is cast and still allows putting a quest counter on resolution even if the graveyard was exiled afterward.
entries.answer:
Yes — Pyromancer Ascension still gets a quest counter.

Pyromancer Ascension's first ability triggers on casting an instant or sorcery that has the same name as a card in your graveyard. That condition is checked at the moment Aspen casts the second Thirst for Meaning, while the first Thirst for Meaning is still in Aspen's graveyard, so the ability triggers and goes on the stack above the spell.

Nathalie's Lantern of the Lost activation happens after that trigger is already on the stack. Exiling all cards from all graveyards removes the first Thirst for Meaning, but Pyromancer Ascension's first ability is not an intervening-"if" ability, so nothing rechecks the graveyard condition on resolution (compare 608.2a, which only rechecks for intervening-"if" triggers). The ruling is explicit: if Pyromancer Ascension's first ability triggers, you put a quest counter on it even if the card in your graveyard leaves your graveyard by the time the ability resolves, or even if the spell you cast is countered (Pyromancer Ascension ruling #4). Note the counter is a "may" — Aspen chooses on resolution whether to put it on (603.5).

Ordering note: this assumes Nathalie activates Lantern of the Lost in response, i.e., after Aspen's cast. If instead Nathalie had somehow exiled the graveyard before Aspen cast the second Thirst for Meaning, the ability would never have triggered at all and no counter would be put on Pyromancer Ascension.

Also note Pyromancer Ascension's second ability is unaffected here in a different way: it only triggers if Pyromancer Ascension already had two or more quest counters when the spell was cast (Pyromancer Ascension ruling #2). This answer is the same at any player count; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Pyromancer Ascension triggers when Thirst for Meaning is cast. The trigger doesn't check to see if the trigger state is still true upon resolution.

entries.question: Nico controls [Meng Huo's Horde] and Alondra controls no creatures. Alondra casts [Loxodon Convert]. In response to Loxodon Convert, Nico casts [Unified Will] targeting Loxodon Convert. When Unified Will resolves, will Loxodon Convert be countered?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Loxodon Convert is countered because a spell on the stack isn't a creature and Unified Will compares creatures on the battlefield, so Nico's one creature versus Alondra's zero meets the condition.
entries.answer:
Yes — Loxodon Convert is countered.

The check happens only when Unified Will resolves (Unified Will ruling #0). At that moment Nico controls Meng Huo's Horde, one creature on the battlefield. Alondra controls zero creatures: Loxodon Convert is still a creature spell on the stack, and it only becomes a creature permanent Alondra controls when it resolves and is put onto the battlefield (302.2). A spell on the stack isn't on the battlefield, and Unified Will's comparison of creatures controlled looks at the battlefield (403.2). So 1 > 0, the condition is met, and Loxodon Convert is countered.

Timing note: I'm assuming Unified Will was cast in response to Loxodon Convert (as stated), so Loxodon Convert never resolved. If instead Loxodon Convert had already resolved and were on the battlefield, it wouldn't be a spell at all and couldn't be targeted by Unified Will. Also, if between casting and resolution Alondra gained creatures (or Meng Huo's Horde left the battlefield) so that Nico no longer controlled more, Unified Will would resolve and simply do nothing.

Multiplayer: nothing changes. Unified Will only compares Nico's creature count to that of the targeted spell's controller (Alondra); other players' creatures are irrelevant.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. Loxodon Convert on the stack is not a creature, it's a creature spell. It is not counted towards Unified Will.

entries.question: Avery controls [Mindlock Orb]. Nora casts [Assassin's Trophy] targeting Mindlock Orb. Can Avery search for a land?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Assassin's Trophy destroys Mindlock Orb first, removing its search-preventing effect, so Avery may search for a land.
entries.answer:
Yes — Avery can search. Assassin's Trophy destroys Mindlock Orb first, and only then does the rest of the spell's effect ("Its controller may search their library for a basic land card, put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle") happen. Since Mindlock Orb has already left the battlefield by that point, its "Players can't search libraries" effect no longer exists, so Avery may search their library for a basic land card, put it onto the battlefield, and shuffle. Searching means looking at all cards in the stated zone and possibly finding one matching the description [Search / 701.23].

Because the search is optional and for a card of a stated quality in a hidden zone, Avery isn't required to find a basic land even if one is there [701.23b, 701.23g]; if Avery declines or finds nothing, they still shuffle.

Two variations worth noting:
- If Mindlock Orb is an illegal target when Assassin's Trophy tries to resolve, the spell doesn't resolve at all and no player searches [Assassin's Trophy ruling #3].
- If Mindlock Orb is a legal target but isn't destroyed (for example, it has indestructible), the ruling says its controller may still search [Assassin's Trophy ruling #1] — but with Mindlock Orb still on the battlefield, its own text "Players can't search libraries" applies and stops Avery from actually searching. Card text overrides the general permission here; Avery would simply shuffle.

This works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table: only the destroyed permanent's controller (Avery) gets the search, and Mindlock Orb's effect, while it exists, applies to every player.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The text on Assassin's Trophy resolves in the order that it is printed. In this case it means that Mindlock Orb is destroyed, and then Avery searches for a land, because at this point the continuous effect generated by Mindlock Orb is no longer in existence preventing the search.

entries.question: Amari casts [Solitary Confinement]. After that resolves, they cast [Command the Dreadhorde] targeting [Draco] and [Reaper King]. Do they enter the battlefield, and does Amari lose any life?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: both creature cards enter the battlefield and Solitary Confinement prevents the damage so Amari loses no life.
entries.answer:
Yes — Draco and Reaper King both enter the battlefield under Amari's control, and Amari loses no life at all.

Why: Command the Dreadhorde deals damage to its controller equal to the total mana value of the chosen cards. Draco's mana value is 16 and Reaper King's is 10 (its monocolored hybrid symbols each count as 2), so the spell would deal 26 damage to Amari. But Solitary Confinement says "Prevent all damage that would be dealt to you," and that prevention isn't limited to combat damage [Solitary Confinement ruling #1]. All 26 damage is prevented, so Amari's life total doesn't change.

Damage and entry order: Command the Dreadhorde deals the damage before Draco and Reaper King are put onto the battlefield [Command the Dreadhorde ruling #1]; that ordering just doesn't matter here since no damage is actually dealt. Both cards are then put onto the battlefield under Amari's control, and Reaper King's own "Whenever another Scarecrow you control enters" trigger doesn't trigger off Draco (a Dragon).

Solitary Confinement's shroud clause is irrelevant here: Command the Dreadhorde targets creature and/or planeswalker cards in graveyards, not a player, so Amari having shroud doesn't stop them from casting or resolving their own spell. Note also that the targets are checked on resolution — if Draco or Reaper King somehow left its graveyard first, it would be an illegal target and wouldn't be put onto the battlefield (608.2b).

Player count doesn't change anything: Command the Dreadhorde only damages its own controller, so the result is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: They enter the battlefield and Amari loses 0 life. Solitary Confinement prevents the damage that Command the Dreadhorde would deal, but the rest of the spell's instructions are still carried out.

entries.question: Alex controls [Grave Pact] and three [Bogstomper]s. Nico controls three [Ogre Resister]s and casts [Dread Cacodemon]. After that resolves how many creatures will Nico have to sacrifice?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion: Dread Cacodemon destroying Alex’s three Bogstompers triggers Grave Pact three times, so Nico must sacrifice three creatures.
entries.answer:
Nico will have to sacrifice three creatures — one for each of the three Grave Pact triggers.

Why: Dread Cacodemon's enters trigger (assuming Nico cast it from hand, as its intervening-if clause requires) destroys all creatures Nico's opponents control — that's Alex's three Bogstompers — then taps all other creatures Nico controls. The three Bogstompers all die at once, and Alex's Grave Pact triggers separately for each creature Alex controlled that died, so three triggered abilities go on the stack [Grave Pact ruling #3].

Each Grave Pact ability resolves one at a time, and on each resolution every other player sacrifices a creature of their choice. So Nico sacrifices one creature three times, for a total of three. Nico's own three Ogre Resisters plus Dread Cacodemon are four creatures, so Nico can choose which three to lose (Dread Cacodemon is a legal choice); after all three triggers Nico is left with exactly one creature.

Important: Nico's sacrifices do not re-trigger Alex's Grave Pact — it only triggers when a creature Alex controls dies. A chain reaction would only occur if Nico also controlled a Grave Pact [Grave Pact ruling #2].

Multiplayer note: with more than two players, each opponent of Alex — not just Nico — sacrifices a creature on each of the three resolutions. On each resolution the active player chooses first (if it isn't Alex's turn), then each other player in turn order, and all chosen creatures are sacrificed simultaneously [Grave Pact ruling #4], [101.4]. Nico's own total is still three either way.

Timing assumption: I'm treating all three Bogstompers as being destroyed simultaneously by Dread Cacodemon's ability, which is what the card says. If instead they somehow died one at a time, the count would be unchanged (still three triggers, three sacrifices) — only the order of choices would differ.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Three. When Dread Cacodemon resolves, it will cause Grave Pact to trigger three times. Even though it was a single event that caused Alex's creatures to die, Grave Pact sees each instance of a creature dying as a separate trigger event.

entries.question: Abram casts [Lightning Bolt] targeting Nola. As it resolves, can Abram choose to deal the damage to Nola's [Vivien Reid]?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude you cannot redirect Lightning Bolt's damage from the targeted player to their planeswalker on resolution — the spell deals 3 damage to the chosen target (the player) unless a replacement/redirection effect specifically moves it.
entries.answer:
No. Abram must target Vivien Reid at the time Lightning Bolt is cast if he wants to damage it; he can't decide on resolution to move the damage from Nola to Nola's Vivien Reid.

Why: Lightning Bolt says "Lightning Bolt deals 3 damage to any target," and "any target" means a single creature, player, planeswalker, or battle chosen when the spell is cast [115.4]. Once Nola is the chosen target, Lightning Bolt deals its 3 damage to Nola.

The old planeswalker damage-redirection rule — which used to let a player choose to have noncombat damage aimed at an opponent hit a planeswalker that opponent controlled instead — has been removed from the rules [306.7]. Damage can still be redirected, but only by an actual redirection effect: a replacement effect from some other card or ability that says damage dealt to one creature, planeswalker, or player is dealt to another instead [614.9] [Redirection Effect] [614.1]. Neither Abram nor Nola gets a free choice to do that here; without such an effect in play, all 3 damage from Lightning Bolt hits Nola, and Vivien Reid keeps its 5 loyalty.

If Abram wanted the damage on Vivien Reid, he needed to name Vivien Reid as the target when casting Lightning Bolt [115.4]. Also note that targets can only be changed by an effect that specifically says so, and such an effect is applied by its own controller, not chosen freely on resolution [115.7b].

This answer is the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer — nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Lightning Bolt deals damage to its target, Nola. There is no rule that allows damage dealt to a player to be redirected to a planeswalker.

entries.question: Nico controls [Fugitive Wizard] and [Falkenrath Reaver]. Alexander casts [Massacre Girl]. In response to Massacre Girl's trigger Nico casts [Village Rites], choosing to sacrifice Fugitive Wizard. After everything has resolved, what does the battlefield look like?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Falkenrath Reaver dies (the death trigger fired before the ETB resolved), whereas the reference correctly states the delayed death trigger isn’t created until the ETB ability resolves, so Reaver survives.
entries.answer:
End result: Alexander controls Massacre Girl (a 4/4 with menace, undamaged). Nico controls no creatures at all — Fugitive Wizard was sacrificed to Village Rites, and Falkenrath Reaver ends up 0/0 and is put into Nico's graveyard as a state-based action. Nico has drawn two cards.

Step by step:

1. Massacre Girl enters and its enters-the-battlefield trigger ("each other creature gets -1/-1 until end of turn") goes on the stack.
2. Nico responds by casting Village Rites, sacrificing Fugitive Wizard as an additional cost during casting. Fugitive Wizard is in Nico's graveyard immediately; it never gets hit by anything else.
3. That sacrifice is a creature dying, so Massacre Girl's second ability ("Whenever a creature dies this turn, each creature other than Massacre Girl gets -1/-1 until end of turn") triggers and goes on the stack above Village Rites. Note this is a leaves-the-battlefield-style death trigger, which the game "looks back in time" for (CR 603.10a), so it does trigger even though Fugitive Wizard is already gone.
4. The death trigger resolves first: Falkenrath Reaver becomes 1/1 until end of turn.
5. Village Rites resolves: Nico draws two cards, and Village Rites goes to Nico's graveyard (CR 608.2n).
6. The original enters trigger resolves last: each creature other than Massacre Girl gets -1/-1. Applying both -1/-1 effects in layer 7c in timestamp order, Falkenrath Reaver is 2/2 → 1/1 → 0/0.
7. Falkenrath Reaver has 0 toughness and dies. That death triggers Massacre Girl's second ability once more, but when it resolves there are no creatures other than Massacre Girl left, so it does nothing.

Massacre Girl is never affected by either of its own effects ("each other creature" / "other than Massacre Girl"), so it survives at 4/4.

Timing assumption: I assumed Village Rites was cast while Massacre Girl's enters trigger was still on the stack, as stated. If instead Nico had let the enters trigger resolve first, Falkenrath Reaver would already be 1/1, then sacrificing Fugitive Wizard would trigger the death ability and shrink Falkenrath Reaver to 0/0 — same final board.

Multiplayer note: nothing here depends on the player count. If other players controlled creatures, their creatures would also take both -1/-1 effects, and each additional creature that died would trigger Massacre Girl's death ability again, potentially cascading further.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Falkenrath Reaver and Massacre Girl are still alive. When Massacre Girl's trigger resolves, Falkenrath Reaver will get -1/-1 and won't die.

Massacre Girl's triggered ability consists of two parts: a trigger that gives all creatures -1/-1 when it enters, and a text that sets up a delayed trigger that will cause a -1/-1 trigger to be put onto the stack every time something dies. At the time Fugitive Wizard dies, Massacre Girl's triggered ability hasn't resolved yet, and hasn't set up the delayed trigger, therefore nothing new will be added to the stack.

entries.question: Does [Gemini Engine]'s token enter the battlefield tapped?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the Twin token enters untapped because Gemini Engine's ability only creates it "attacking" and does not cause it to enter tapped.
entries.answer:
No. The Twin token created by Gemini Engine enters the battlefield untapped, and attacking. Gemini Engine's ability says only that the token is created "attacking"; it never says tapped, and permanents enter untapped, unflipped, face up, and phased in unless a spell or ability says otherwise [110.5b]. This is confirmed directly by the card's own ruling: "The Twin token enters as an untapped attacking creature. It's not subject to any costs to attack or restrictions on attacking" [Gemini Engine ruling #3].

A couple of related points:

- Being put onto the battlefield attacking is not the same as being tapped. Creatures normally tap when declared as attackers, but the Twin token was never declared as an attacker " it is simply created in an attacking state as the triggered ability resolves [701.7a], so no tapping event occurs.
- The token has no characteristics beyond those the ability defines [111.3], so it has no "enters tapped" static ability of its own (such abilities are replacement effects that apply as the permanent enters, not triggered abilities) [614.1c, 603.6d]. If some other permanent on the battlefield had an effect like "Permanents enter tapped," that outside replacement effect would still apply and the Twin token would enter tapped " but nothing on Gemini Engine itself does that.
- Its power and toughness are locked in as Gemini Engine's power and toughness at the time it's created, then other continuous effects like anthems apply on top [Gemini Engine ruling #1, Gemini Engine ruling #0].

This answer is the same whether you're playing a two-player game or a multiplayer game; in multiplayer, the token is simply attacking whichever player or planeswalker Gemini Engine is attacking.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No.

entries.question: Abdullah controls [Arcane Adaptation] naming "Zombie" and casts [Embalmed Brawler]. Can they reveal [Seven-Tail Mentor] from their hand for amplify?
entries.reason: Both conclude Arcane Adaptation makes creature cards in your hand the chosen type, so Seven-Tail Mentor can be revealed to satisfy Embalmed Brawler's amplify.
entries.answer:
Yes. Seven-Tail Mentor can be revealed for Embalmed Brawler's amplify.

Why: Arcane Adaptation says "Creatures you control are the chosen type in addition to their other types. The same is true for creature spells you control and creature cards you own that aren't on the battlefield." With "Zombie" chosen, Seven-Tail Mentor sitting in Abdullah's hand is a Zombie Fox Samurai in addition to its other types [205.1b], since Arcane Adaptation's static ability applies continuously wherever the card is [611.3a].

Amplify 1 on Embalmed Brawler means "As this creature enters, reveal any number of cards from your hand that share a creature type with it. This permanent enters with 1 +1/+1 counter on it for each card revealed this way. You can't reveal this card or any other cards entering the battlefield at the same time" [702.38a]. Embalmed Brawler is a Zombie both natively and via Arcane Adaptation, and Seven-Tail Mentor is now also a Zombie, so they share a creature type. Revealing it gives Embalmed Brawler one +1/+1 counter (a 3/3), plus one more for each other qualifying card revealed.

Ordering note: Arcane Adaptation's type-changing effect is applied first, and replacement effects that care about creature types (like amplify) then see the modified types [Arcane Adaptation ruling #0].

Remember Embalmed Brawler's other ability: whenever it attacks or blocks, Abdullah loses 1 life for each +1/+1 counter on it.

Nothing here depends on player count; the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. While normally continuous effects don't apply to cards not on the battlefield, Arcane Adaptation specifically states that it applies to cards that aren't on the battlefield, such as in your hand or library.

entries.question: Addison controls three [Lavabelly Sliver]s. They cast and resolve the fourth Lavabelly Sliver. How much damage can they deal to Nico?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the entering Lavabelly Sliver generates four separate ETB triggers (three granted by the existing Slivers plus its own), allowing four 1-damage instances to be assigned to Nico.
entries.answer:
Addison can deal 4 damage to Nico (and gains 4 life), assuming every trigger targets Nico.

Each Lavabelly Sliver grants "Sliver creatures you control have 'When this creature enters, it deals 1 damage to target player or planeswalker and you gain 1 life.'" That grant applies to all Slivers Addison controls, including the granting Lavabelly Sliver itself. So when the fourth Lavabelly Sliver enters the battlefield, it has four separate instances of that enters ability: one from each of the three Lavabelly Slivers already on the battlefield, plus one from its own static ability.
