Each instance is a distinct triggered ability and triggers separately for the single entry event (603.2c; the ability-word rules such as 702.108b, 702.112c, and 702.116b confirm the general principle that multiple instances of the same triggered ability each trigger on their own). That's four triggers on the stack, each targeting a player or planeswalker independently — Addison may point all four at Nico for 4 total damage, or split them among Nico, other opponents, and planeswalkers. Addison gains 1 life per trigger regardless, for 4 life.

The three Lavabelly Slivers already on the battlefield do not trigger; they aren't entering. In a two-player game all four triggers can only hit Nico or a planeswalker; at a multiplayer table each trigger chooses its own target, so Addison could spread the damage across several opponents instead.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 4 damage. As soon as Lavabelly Sliver enters the battlefield, it has four instances of "When this creature enters the battlefield, it deals 1 damage to target player or planeswalker and you gain 1 life". The game then checks to see if any abilities triggered, which four did.

entries.question: Ahmad is on their second mulligan, down to five cards. When Ahmad goes to put cards on the bottom of their library, how many cards will they be putting on the bottom and in what order?
entries.reason: The candidate states Ahmad will put two cards on the bottom and may choose their order, matching the reference ruling.
entries.answer:
In a two-player (non-Brawl) game, Ahmad puts 2 cards on the bottom of their library, in any order Ahmad chooses. After taking a second mulligan Ahmad shuffles their hand into their library, draws a fresh 7 (their starting hand size), then puts a number of cards equal to the number of mulligans they've taken — two — on the bottom, leaving the five-card opening hand [103.5].

Order: Ahmad chooses the order freely; the two cards go to the bottom in any order Ahmad likes, and Ahmad does not reveal that order [103.5], [401.4].

Timing/format caveat: this assumes a regular two-player game. In a multiplayer game (or any Brawl game), the first mulligan a player takes doesn't count toward either the number of cards bottomed or the number of mulligans allowed, so a "second mulligan" there would have Ahmad draw 7 and bottom only 1, keeping six cards — Ahmad would need a third mulligan to be down to five [800.6], [903.12g], [103.5c]. Also note mulligan declarations are made in turn order (starting player first, then each other player, or by team in shared-team-turns games), but all mulligans are then taken simultaneously, so Ahmad bottoms their cards at the same time as anyone else who mulliganed [103.5], [103.5d].
entries.answer_gold: Ahmad will be putting two cards on the bottom of their library, and they will choose the order.

entries.question: Adonis casts [Assassin's Trophy] targeting [Nihil Spellbomb]. Nico searches for a [Snow-Covered Swamp] and wants to tap it to pay for the triggered ability of Nihil Spellbomb. Can they do this?
entries.reason: Both conclude the land will be available to produce {B} when the Nihil Spellbomb trigger resolves (Assassin's Trophy resolves first), so Nico can tap the Snow-Covered Swamp to pay.
entries.answer:
Yes. Nico can tap the Snow-Covered Swamp for {B} to pay for Nihil Spellbomb's second triggered ability and draw a card.

Why: the summoning-sickness restriction only applies to creatures. Rules 302.6, 107.5 and 602.5a all say that a *creature's* activated ability with {T} in its cost can't be activated unless that creature has been under its controller's control continuously since their most recent turn began. Snow-Covered Swamp is a land, not a creature, so it can be tapped for mana the moment it enters the battlefield.

Sequence assumed: Assassin's Trophy resolves, destroying Nihil Spellbomb; as part of that same resolution Nico searches and puts Snow-Covered Swamp onto the battlefield untapped. Nihil Spellbomb's ability ("When this artifact is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, you may pay {B}. If you do, draw a card.") triggered on the destruction and goes on the stack afterward, so the land is already on the battlefield and available. Note the cost is {B} — one black mana specifically, not generic — and Snow-Covered Swamp's mana ability adds {B}, so it works.

The {B} payment is a cost paid on resolution of the trigger (118.12), and Nico may activate the land's mana ability at that time (605.1, 605.3c). Snow being a supertype doesn't matter here; snow isn't a type of mana and nothing about the payment requires {S} (Snow-Covered Swamp ruling #3).

Timing caveat: if instead the Snow-Covered Swamp were somehow already tapped, it couldn't be tapped again to pay (107.5, 118.3) and the trigger would simply do nothing. Also, if Nihil Spellbomb had already left the battlefield (making it an illegal target), Assassin's Trophy wouldn't resolve at all and no one would search (Assassin's Trophy ruling #3). None of this changes between two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Assassin's Trophy will resolve completely before Nihil Spellbomb's trigger is placed onto the stack ([603.3],[117.2a]). The payment of {B} is made as the trigger resolves.

entries.question: Noemi controls [Stranglehold]. Axl sacrifices [Arid Mesa] just to shuffle their library. Afterwards Noemi would like to cast [Archive Trap] for its alternative cost. Can they do this?
entries.reason: Both conclude Axl didn't search their library due to Stranglehold, and a mere shuffle doesn't satisfy Archive Trap's "opponent searched" condition.
entries.answer:
No — Noemi can't use Archive Trap's alternative cost, because Axl never actually searched a library.

Stranglehold flatly says "Your opponents can't search libraries." That card text overrides the normal functioning of the search instruction: when Arid Mesa's ability resolves, Axl simply skips the search (and therefore finds and puts nothing onto the battlefield), then carries out the remaining instruction and shuffles their library. Axl can still legally activate Arid Mesa's ability — {T}, pay 1 life, sacrifice it — since Stranglehold restricts searching, not activation; the shuffle still happens even though nothing was found.

Archive Trap's alternative cost reads "If an opponent searched their library this turn, you may pay {0} rather than pay this spell's mana cost." Archive Trap checks whether an opponent searched, not whether they found anything [Archive Trap ruling #1] — but here no search occurred at all, only a shuffle. Shuffling is not searching, so the condition is unmet.

Noemi may still cast Archive Trap by paying its normal mana cost of {3}{U}{U} (three generic plus two blue) [Archive Trap ruling #2]; the alternative cost never changes the card's mana cost or mana value anyway [Archive Trap ruling #3].

Multiplayer note: Stranglehold and Archive Trap both key off "opponents," so the analysis is the same at any table size — if some other opponent of Noemi's did search a library this turn, that would satisfy Archive Trap's condition even though Axl's Arid Mesa activation didn't.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Axl did not actually search their library, and therefore the condition for paying Archive Trap's alternative cost has not been met.

entries.question: Addison casts [Touch of the Void] targeting Nova's [Orzhov Racketeers]. Does Nova still get spirit tokens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion and correct reasoning: Touch of the Void exiles the creature instead of it dying, so Afterlife's "when this creature dies" trigger does not occur.
entries.answer:
No — Nova gets no Spirit tokens. Touch of the Void's replacement effect says that if a creature dealt damage this way would die this turn, exile it instead. Orzhov Racketeers therefore never dies (it's never put into a graveyard from the battlefield); it's exiled instead, so its afterlife 2 trigger, which triggers only "when this creature dies," never triggers at all.

I'm assuming Touch of the Void resolves and deals its 3 damage to Orzhov Racketeers (a 3/2, so lethal). Note that per [Touch of the Void ruling #4], the exile replacement applies for the rest of the turn even if Orzhov Racketeers would die later for some other reason (another damage source, a destroy effect, -X/-X lethality, etc.) — in every such case it's exiled and afterlife still doesn't trigger.

Afterlife is a leaves-the-battlefield-style dies trigger, and such triggers use the "look back in time" rule [603.10a] to check the game state just before the event — but that only matters if a dies event happens. Here the event is a move to exile, not to the graveyard, so there is nothing to trigger on. Once Orzhov Racketeers is in exile it is a new object with no relation to its prior existence [400.7].

This answer is the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer; nothing here depends on the number of opponents. Card text ("exile it instead") overrides the ordinary result of lethal damage destroying the creature.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. A creature is considered to have "died" if it moves from the battlefield to the graveyard.. Touch of the Void replaces the creature moving to the graveyard with moving the creature to exile instead, which doesn't qualify as the creature dying, and therefore doesn't cause the afterlife. Trigger to go onto the stack. ([702.135a])

entries.question: Alonso controls [Blood Moon] and a [Gemstone Mine] with zero mining counters. Nylah then casts [Disenchant] targeting Blood Moon. After that resolves, will Alonso have to sacrifice Gemstone Mine?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Gemstone Mine only sacrifices as part of its activated ability resolving and since that ability can't be activated while Blood Moon was in effect (or the counters were removed by other means), Alonso will not have to sacrifice it.
entries.answer:
No. Alonso does not sacrifice Gemstone Mine.

Why: Gemstone Mine's sacrifice clause is not a state-based action and not a triggered ability — it is part of the effect of activating "{T}, Remove a mining counter from this land: Add one mana of any color. If there are no mining counters on this land, sacrifice it." It only ever happens as part of resolving that activated ability. While Blood Moon was on the battlefield, Gemstone Mine was a Mountain and lost that ability entirely (setting a land's subtype to a basic land type makes it lose the abilities generated by its rules text and gain only the basic land mana ability, per [305.7]), so the counters must have come off some other way — and per [Gemstone Mine ruling #0], if the last mining counter is removed in some way other than activating its ability, Gemstone Mine won't be sacrificed.

Once Nylah's Disenchant destroys Blood Moon, Gemstone Mine goes back to having its printed text with zero mining counters. Nothing checks "no mining counters" on its own: state-based actions only cover the listed conditions [704.1], and there is no state-based action for a land with no counters (the counter-based state-based action in the provided rules is the battle/defense-counter one, [122.1g], [310.7]). State-based actions are checked whenever a player would get priority [704.3], [117.5], and none of them apply here. Alonso simply has a Gemstone Mine whose ability can no longer be activated, because he can't pay the "Remove a mining counter" cost.

Timing note: I'm assuming the counters were already gone before Disenchant resolved, as stated. If instead Alonso had activated Gemstone Mine's ability for its last counter at a moment when Blood Moon was not applying, that activation's resolution would sacrifice it — the sacrifice rides along with the ability, not with the land's current counter count.

Player count doesn't matter here: nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Gemstone Mine only checks if there are no mining counters on it as the activated ability resolves. Since there are no mining counters on Gemstone Mine Alonso will never be able to activate it, and therefore it will never check how many mining counters are on it.

entries.question: Ariel casts [Scapeshift] sacrificing seven lands. Ariel finds six [Mountain]s and one [Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle]. Ariel would like to have the first trigger deal three damage to Neymar's [Unsettled Mariner], and the rest to deal damage to Neymar. After the first trigger resolves, will Ariel still have to pay for the Unsettled Mariner triggers?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that all Valakut triggers target (producing six Unsettled Mariner triggers) and those Mariner triggers go on and resolve before the Valakut triggers, so Ariel must pay for them (killing Mariner first won't prevent them).
entries.answer:
Yes — and worse than that: Ariel ends up facing six separate Unsettled Mariner triggers, all of which must be paid (or the Valakut triggers get countered) *before* any of the damage happens, so killing Unsettled Mariner first isn't possible.

Why:

1. All seven lands (six Mountains and Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle) enter the battlefield simultaneously during Scapeshift's resolution. Each of the six Mountains causes Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle's second ability to trigger, and the intervening "if" clause is satisfied because for each Mountain there are five other Mountains ([Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle ruling #3]).

2. Nothing happens at the moment abilities trigger; the six Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle triggers all wait and are put on the stack together the next time a player would receive priority, i.e., after Scapeshift finishes resolving (117.2a, 603.3d). Targets are chosen at that time, as part of putting each trigger on the stack (603.3d, referencing 601.2c). So Ariel must declare all six targets right then — one at Neymar's Unsettled Mariner and five at Neymar — before any of them resolve.

3. Unsettled Mariner's ability triggers "whenever you or a permanent you control becomes the target of a spell or ability an opponent controls." Targeting Neymar personally counts just as much as targeting Unsettled Mariner. Since the six Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle triggers each target once, Unsettled Mariner triggers six times — one per targeting event (603.2c; [Unsettled Mariner ruling #0] and [Unsettled Mariner ruling #1] confirm the trigger counts per distinct target within one spell/ability, and here each Valakut trigger is a separate ability anyway).

4. Those six Unsettled Mariner triggers are put on the stack above the six Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle triggers the next time priority would be received, so they all resolve first. Ariel must pay {1} each time (six generic mana total, {6}, payable with any colors or colorless) or the corresponding Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle trigger is countered. Unsettled Mariner is still on the battlefield the whole time this is decided.

5. Only after all that does the first Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle trigger resolve and deal 3 damage to Unsettled Mariner. Killing it then is too late — the remaining Valakut triggers and the already-created Unsettled Mariner triggers exist on the stack independently of their source (113.7a).

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Ariel picks all targets when the triggers go on the stack, which the rules require — there is no legal way to resolve one Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle trigger and then choose targets for the others. If instead some Valakut triggers came from a later, separate batch of Mountains entering after Unsettled Mariner had already died, those would produce no Unsettled Mariner triggers at all.

Multiplayer note: with more than two players, the same analysis holds; the only change is that all players' triggers that have triggered are put on the stack in APNAP order by their controllers (603.3d, 117.2a), and Unsettled Mariner only triggers off targets its controller owns/controls.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes, Ariel chooses targets for Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle's ability as they go on the stack. After Ariel has chosen all the targets for Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle's abilities, Neymar will put an Unsettled Mariner trigger onto the stack for each time they or Unsettled Mariner was targeted. Unsettled Mariner dying won't affect the triggers that are already on the stack, and all of the Unsettled Mariner triggers will resolve before any of the Valakut, the Molten Pinnacle triggers do anyway.

entries.question: Ashley casts [Cauldron's Gift] spending three black mana while their graveyard has no cards in it. As it resolves, [Ironroot Treefolk] is put into the graveyard from the library. Can Ashley choose to return it to the battlefield with Cauldron's Gift?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling — the four-card mill happens on resolution and Ashley may choose the freshly milled Ironroot Treefolk to return to the battlefield.
entries.answer:
Yes. Ashley can return Ironroot Treefolk to the battlefield with a +1/+1 counter on it.

Because at least three black mana was spent, Cauldron's Gift's adamant ability mills four cards, and that milling happens first as the spell's controller follows the instructions in the order written [608.2c]. Only after that does Ashley make the choice of a creature card in the graveyard. Since Cauldron's Gift does not target the card it returns, the choice is made on resolution with the graveyard as it then exists — so Ironroot Treefolk, which was just milled from the library, is a legal choice [Cauldron's Gift ruling #0], [115.10]. No player may act between the mill, the choice, and the return [Cauldron's Gift ruling #2].

The fact that the graveyard was empty when Cauldron's Gift was cast is irrelevant, precisely because there was no target to choose at announcement. Ironroot Treefolk returns as a 3/5 Treefolk with an additional +1/+1 counter, making it 4/6.

This works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. As spells and abilities resolve, the instructions are carried out in the order they are printed on the card. Ashley first takes the top four cards of their library and puts them into their graveyard, then chooses which creature they would like to return. The choice of which creature to return is made upon resolution.

entries.question: Adonis controls [Tocatli Honor Guard] and [Selvala, Heart of the Wilds]. Adonis casts [Catacomb Slug]. When it enters the battlefield, will Selvala, Heart of the Wilds's ability trigger?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Tocatli Honor Guard's static ability prevents Selvala's triggered ability from triggering when Catacomb Slug enters the battlefield.
entries.answer:
No. Selvala, Heart of the Wilds's triggered ability won't trigger at all, because Tocatli Honor Guard says "Creatures entering don't cause abilities to trigger." Catacomb Slug is a creature, so its entering the battlefield simply doesn't cause any triggered ability to trigger, including Selvala, Heart of the Wilds's "Whenever another creature enters" ability ([Tocatli Honor Guard ruling #1], [Tocatli Honor Guard ruling #3]).

Details:
- Normally, when a permanent enters the battlefield, all permanents on the battlefield (including the newcomer) are checked for enters-the-battlefield triggers matching that event (603.6a). Tocatli Honor Guard's static ability shuts that check off for creatures entering, and this is card text that overrides the general result.
- Note the trigger condition is separate from the "may draw" check: even without Tocatli Honor Guard, Selvala, Heart of the Wilds's ability would trigger on Catacomb Slug entering, but on resolution Adonis would draw only if Catacomb Slug's power (2) were greater than each other creature's power — and Selvala, Heart of the Wilds is itself 2/3, so 2 is not greater than 2 and no card would be drawn. With Tocatli Honor Guard out, the ability never even goes on the stack.
- Selvala, Heart of the Wilds's mana ability ({G}, {T}: Add X mana) is unaffected; it's a mana ability that doesn't use the stack ([Selvala, Heart of the Wilds ruling #0]).

This answer doesn't change with the number of players: Tocatli Honor Guard's ability applies to all creatures entering, regardless of who controls them, so the same result holds in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The text on Tocatli Honor Guard prevents any 'enter the battlefield' abilities from triggering, even if the permanent that is triggering them is not the permanent that has the ability.

entries.question: Alonso casts [Piracy] and would like to tap all of Nico's lands but not cast any spells. Can Alonso do this?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion: Piracy lets Alonso tap Nico's lands and produce restricted mana but does not force him to cast spells or spend that mana.
entries.answer:
Yes. Piracy says "Until end of turn, you may tap lands you don't control for mana," so while Piracy's effect is active Alonso may activate the mana abilities of Nico's lands, and nothing requires him to actually cast a spell. He just needs a time when he can activate a mana ability — any moment he has priority, or a moment when a cost includes a mana payment (rule 118.2) or a resolving spell/ability gives him the option to pay mana (rules 117.2e, 608.2g).

A few practical points:

- Tapping a land for mana is a mana ability, not a spell; it doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to (rule 605.5b makes clear a spell is never a mana ability, and mana abilities resolve immediately). So Nico can't stop the lands from being tapped once Piracy has resolved.
- The mana Alonso produces is restricted: Piracy's own text says "Spend this mana only to cast spells." If Alonso casts nothing, that mana simply goes unused and empties from his mana pool when the step or phase ends. Card text like this overrides the general freedom to spend mana on anything.
- So the tapping is legal, but its only real value is denying Nico untapped lands; Alonso gains nothing else from the floating mana.
- Note Alonso can't do this during the untap step, since no player receives priority then (rule 502.4).

Multiplayer: Piracy refers to "lands you don't control," not to a single opponent, so with more than two players Alonso may tap any player's lands he doesn't control, not just Nico's. The answer is otherwise identical in two-player and multiplayer games.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Piracy has already resolved. Before it resolves, Alonso has no permission to tap Nico's lands at all.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Piracy creates a restriction on what Alonso must spend the mana on, but does not prevent them from not spending the mana.

entries.question: Asa controls [Bloom Tender] and [Old Man of the Sea]. Then, Asa resolves Old Man of the Sea's ability to gain control of Nova's [Dune Beetle]. When Asa activates Bloom Tender's ability, how much mana is produced?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference — Bloom Tender produces three mana ({U}{B}{G}) because Asa controls Old Man of the Sea and, via its control effect, Dune Beetle.
entries.answer:
Asa's Bloom Tender produces three mana: {U}{B}{G} — one blue, one black, and one green.

Why: Bloom Tender's Vivid ability checks, for each of the five colors, whether you control a permanent of that color, and adds one mana of each such color; the same permanent can count for multiple colors, and it never makes more than one of any color (max {W}{U}{B}{R}{G}) [Bloom Tender ruling #2] [Bloom Tender ruling #3]. Asa controls Bloom Tender (green), Old Man of the Sea (blue), and — because Old Man of the Sea's ability resolved and gave Asa control of Dune Beetle for as long as Old Man of the Sea remains tapped and its power stays high enough — Dune Beetle (black). Control, not ownership, is what matters, so Nova's Dune Beetle counts for Asa while the control effect lasts.

Notes and assumptions: (1) I'm assuming Asa controls no other colored permanents (e.g., no white or red permanents, and any lands present are colorless), which would each add their color. Bloom Tender can't add colorless mana even if Asa controls colorless permanents such as basic lands [Bloom Tender ruling #1]. (2) Old Man of the Sea being tapped doesn't matter for counting colors — it's still a permanent Asa controls, and an ability remains a mana ability regardless of game state [605.2]. (3) I'm assuming Bloom Tender has been under Asa's control since Asa's most recent turn began, or has haste; otherwise its {T} ability can't be activated at all [602.5a] [702.10c]. (4) Bloom Tender's ability is an activated mana ability — no target, and it could add mana [605.1a] — so it doesn't use the stack and resolves immediately, with Asa retaining priority [405.6c].

If at that moment Old Man of the Sea were to become untapped (or its power dropped below Dune Beetle's), control of Dune Beetle would revert to Nova and Bloom Tender would only make {U}{G}.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players; it works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table, since only permanents Asa controls are counted.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Three - one of each of the three colors among creatures Asa controls. 

While Nova still owns Dune Beetle, Old Man of the Sea's ability creates a control-changing effect which gives control of Dune Beetle to Asa. When Bloom Tender's ability resolves, it does not care that Nova is the owner Dune Beetle - just that Asa is the controller.

entries.question: Aaron controls [Endrek Sahr, Master Breeder] and [Pontiff of Blight]. They cast [Primeval Shambler]. What is the maximum number of extort triggers they can pay for?
entries.reason: Both conclude two extort triggers — only Pontiff and Endrek have extort when Primeval Shambler is cast, and the thrull tokens are created too late to trigger.
entries.answer:
Two. Aaron can pay {W/B} at most twice, for a total of 2 extort triggers.

Why: extort is a triggered ability that reads "Whenever you cast a spell, you may pay {W/B}. If you do, each opponent loses 1 life and you gain life equal to the total life lost this way" [702.101a]. When Primeval Shambler is cast, the only permanents Aaron controls that have extort are Pontiff of Blight (its own printed extort) and Endrek Sahr, Master Breeder (which has extort because Pontiff of Blight grants it to "other creatures you control"). That's two separate instances, and each instance triggers separately [702.101b]. For each extort trigger you may pay {W/B} a maximum of one time, and you decide when that trigger resolves [Pontiff of Blight ruling #2].

The Thrull tokens do not add triggers. Endrek Sahr, Master Breeder's ability also triggers on casting Primeval Shambler and creates five 1/1 Thrulls (Primeval Shambler's mana value is 5), but those tokens only exist after that trigger resolves — long after Primeval Shambler was cast — so the extort they gain from Pontiff of Blight has no cast event to trigger on. Likewise Primeval Shambler itself is still a spell on the stack, not a creature you control, when it is cast [601.2a].

Cost note: each payment is exactly one {W/B} hybrid symbol, payable with one white or one black mana — not generic mana.

Multiplayer difference: the number of extort triggers (2) is the same regardless of player count; only the effect scales, since each opponent loses 1 life and Aaron gains life equal to the total life lost that way [702.101a]. With one opponent that's 1 life per trigger (2 total); with three opponents it's 3 life per trigger (6 total). Life gained tracks actual life lost, so an opponent whose life total can't change contributes nothing [Pontiff of Blight ruling #0].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Two. Even though tokens with extort are created before Primeval Shambler resolves, they are created only after Primeval Shambler has already been cast. They are therefore not on the battlefield in time for their extort abilities to trigger. ([702.101a])

entries.question: Azalea casts [Eject] targeting Nico's [Narset, Parter of Veils]. When it resolves, does Azalea draw?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Eject resolves in order so Narset is returned before the draw, removing its draw restriction and allowing Azalea to draw.
entries.answer:
Yes — Azalea draws a card. Eject's effects happen in order during its single resolution: first Nico's Narset, Parter of Veils is returned to Nico's hand, and only then does Azalea draw. Narset, Parter of Veils's static ability ("Each opponent can't draw more than one card each turn") only functions while Narset, Parter of Veils is on the battlefield, so by the time the draw instruction is carried out that restriction no longer exists — even if Azalea had already drawn a card earlier in the turn (for example, in Azalea's draw step). Note that Narset, Parter of Veils never retroactively undoes draws already made, and it only affects draws while it's in play (see [Narset, Parter of Veils ruling #3], which confirms cards drawn before Narset, Parter of Veils entered are unaffected).

The one way Azalea wouldn't draw: if Narset, Parter of Veils has become an illegal target by the time Eject tries to resolve (for example, it left the battlefield or gained protection/hexproof from Azalea in response). Then Eject doesn't resolve at all and none of its effects happen, including the draw — [Eject ruling #0]. Note also that Eject can't be countered, so a counterspell won't stop it, but making the target illegal still will.

Azalea is the controller of Eject because Azalea cast it ([405.4], [112.2]), so "draw a card" refers to Azalea ([109.5]).

This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table: Narset, Parter of Veils restricts each of Nico's opponents individually, and removing it from the battlefield lifts the restriction for all of them equally.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The spell's instructions are performed sequentially in the order written, so Narset, Parter of Veils is not on the battlefield anymore to prevent Azalea from drawing.

entries.question: Ainsley controls [Spellweaver Volute] that's enchanting [Cruel Truths] in their graveyard. What zone is Spellweaver Volute in?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference — Spellweaver Volute is on the battlefield even though it enchants Cruel Truths in a graveyard.
entries.answer:
Spellweaver Volute is on the battlefield. It is an enchantment permanent like any other Aura, and it stays on the battlefield even though the object it enchants — Cruel Truths — is a card in a graveyard, not a permanent [Spellweaver Volute ruling #2] [Spellweaver Volute ruling #4].

Details:
- An Aura enters the battlefield attached to an object or player; the thing it's attached to is "enchanted" [303.4b]. Spellweaver Volute's enchant ability reads "Enchant instant card in a graveyard," so its legal attachment is a card in the graveyard rather than a permanent — this card text governs over the usual expectation that Auras enchant permanents [Spellweaver Volute ruling #4].
- So the Aura (Spellweaver Volute) is on the battlefield; the enchanted card (Cruel Truths) is in Ainsley's graveyard; Spellweaver Volute itself is not in the graveyard [Spellweaver Volute ruling #2].
- It only leaves the battlefield if it stops being legally attached: if Cruel Truths changes zones (cast, exiled, etc.), Spellweaver Volute "falls off" and is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action [Spellweaver Volute ruling #5] [704.5m] [704.1]. Same thing if its own ability exiles the enchanted card and no other instant card in a graveyard can be chosen [Spellweaver Volute ruling #0].

This is the same in two-player and multiplayer games, except that in multiplayer an Aura can't enchant an object outside its controller's range of influence, and would be put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action if it were [801.8].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Spellweaver Volute is on the battlefield. The game doesn't require an Aura to be in the same zone as the object it's attached to.

entries.question: Nathan activates their [Grim Lavamancer] targeting Amaris. In response Amaris gains control of Grim Lavamancer with [Caught Red-Handed]. When Grim Lavamancer's ability resolves, who decides whether to redirect the damage to Amaris's [Mordenkainen]?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the damage is dealt to Amaris with no choice or redirection to Mordenkainen, so the candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference.
entries.answer:
Nobody gets that choice — the damage is dealt to Amaris. Grim Lavamancer's ability was activated targeting Amaris, and that target is locked in; no effect in play changes it. The rules provided contain no mechanism by which damage from a spell or ability targeting a player may be redirected to a planeswalker that player controls, so Mordenkainen simply isn't involved. Redirection only happens if some effect actually creates a redirection effect (rule 614.9), and Caught Red-Handed does not create one.

If you're asking who would make decisions for the ability generally: Nathan does. The controller of an activated ability on the stack is the player who activated it (rule 113.8), and Amaris gaining control of Grim Lavamancer with Caught Red-Handed does not transfer control of the already-activated ability — the ability exists independently of its source on the stack. So Nathan would make any choices the ability calls for on resolution, and only an effect that explicitly says so could let a player change or choose new targets (rules 115.7, 115.7d).

Assumption on timing: I'm reading it as Caught Red-Handed resolving while Grim Lavamancer's ability is still on the stack. If instead Caught Red-Handed had resolved before Nathan activated the ability, Nathan couldn't have activated it at all, since Amaris would control Grim Lavamancer and only its controller can use its {R}, {T} ability.

This analysis is the same whether the game has two players or more; the only multiplayer wrinkle in the provided rules concerns what happens to a controlled permanent if the control effect ends after a player leaves the game (rule 800.4c), which doesn't apply here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Neither player has a choice, the damage must be dealt to Amaris. Grim Lavamancer targeted Amaris. There is no rule that allows that damage to be redirected anywhere.

entries.question: Aubrey controls [Heliod, Sun-Crowned] and casts [Shamble Back]. Can they choose to put Heliod, Sun-Crowned's +1/+1 counter on one of the tokens created by Shamble Back?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the token is created before the life gain and Heliod's triggered ability is put on the stack afterward, so Aubrey can target one of the tokens.
entries.answer:
Yes. The Zombie token is created before the life gain happens, so by the time Heliod, Sun-Crowned's triggered ability is put on the stack and targets are chosen, the 2/2 black Zombie token already exists on the battlefield and is a legal target ("target creature or enchantment you control").

Why: Shamble Back's effects happen in printed order as it resolves — exile the creature card from a graveyard, then create the 2/2 black Zombie creature token, then "You gain 2 life." Heliod, Sun-Crowned's ability ("Whenever you gain life, put a +1/+1 counter on target creature or enchantment you control") triggers on that life gain, but it isn't put on the stack until Shamble Back has finished resolving and a player would next receive priority. At that moment Aubrey chooses the target, and the Zombie token is available. Aubrey could instead target Heliod, Sun-Crowned itself if desired ([Heliod, Sun-Crowned ruling #0]).

Note on Shamble Back: if the targeted creature card in the graveyard has become an illegal target, Shamble Back doesn't resolve at all — no token, no life gain, and Heliod, Sun-Crowned never triggers ([Shamble Back ruling #0]).

This works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table; the only targeting restriction is that the creature or enchantment be one Aubrey controls.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Aubrey creates the tokens, then gains life as part of the resolution of Shamble Back. After Shamble Back has resolved, Heliod, Sun-Crowned's trigger will be put on the stack. At that point Aubrey can choose a token as their target.

entries.question: Ariel casts [Evil's Thrall] targeting Nasir's [Trained Armodon]. At the beginning of their end step, they choose to exile Trained Armodon with their [Conjurer's Closet]. Whose control will Trained Armodon enter the battlefield under?
entries.reason: Both conclude Conjurer's Closet returns Trained Armodon to the battlefield under Ariel's control, so the candidate reaches the same ruling.
entries.answer:
Trained Armodon returns to the battlefield under Ariel's control — and stays there indefinitely, even after Evil's Thrall's duration would have expired.

Why: Conjurer's Closet reads "exile target creature you control, then return that card to the battlefield under your control." At the time the ability triggers and resolves, Ariel controls Trained Armodon thanks to Evil's Thrall, so it's a legal target. When an effect instructs a player to put an object onto the battlefield, it enters under that player's control unless stated otherwise, and here the Closet explicitly states "under your control" — Ariel's ([110.2a]). The returning card is a new object with no memory of Evil's Thrall's temporary control effect, and the Conjurer's Closet ruling confirms that a creature returned "under your control" is controlled indefinitely afterward ([Conjurer's Closet ruling #0]).

Nasir remains the owner of the Trained Armodon card ([110.2], [400.3]) — control changed, ownership never did. So if Trained Armodon later goes to a graveyard, hand, or library, it goes to Nasir's.

Multiplayer note: in a game with more than two players, if Ariel later leaves the game, Trained Armodon is exiled rather than reverting to Nasir, per the Conjurer's Closet ruling and [800.4c] (this applies because the control here comes from the Closet's one-shot "enters under your control," and the default controller, Ariel, has left). In a two-player game that scenario simply ends the game.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming the Closet's end-step trigger resolves while Ariel still controls Trained Armodon via Evil's Thrall. If instead Evil's Thrall's control effect had already ended before the trigger resolved, Trained Armodon would no longer be a "creature you control," the target would be illegal, and the ability would do nothing — leaving Trained Armodon under Nasir's control.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It returns under Ariel's control, because Conjurer's Closet says it does.

entries.question: Ariel casts [Thoughtseize] targeting Nehemiah. In response, Nehemiah casts their last card, and when Thoughtseize resolves, Nehemiah has zero cards in hand. Does Ariel lose 2 life?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Thoughtseize still causes Ariel to lose 2 life even if the targeted player has no cards to reveal or discard, so they reach the same ruling.
entries.answer:
Yes — Ariel loses 2 life.

Thoughtseize reads "Target player reveals their hand. You choose a nonland card from it. That player discards that card. You lose 2 life." Nehemiah is still a legal target (Nehemiah is still in the game and hasn't gained an effect making them illegal), so Thoughtseize resolves [608.2b]. Ariel's controller follows the instructions in order [608.2c]: Nehemiah reveals an empty hand, there is no nonland card to choose, so no card is chosen and nothing is discarded — but the final instruction, "You lose 2 life," is not conditional on a card being discarded. Ariel loses 2 life regardless [Thoughtseize ruling #0]. Thoughtseize is then put into Ariel's graveyard [307.2], [608.2n].

This is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game: Thoughtseize affects only the single targeted player, Nehemiah, and only Ariel loses life.

(Timing note: I'm assuming Nehemiah emptied their hand before Thoughtseize resolved, as stated. If Nehemiah had instead still held a nonland card at resolution, Ariel would choose it, Nehemiah would discard it, and Ariel would still lose the 2 life.)

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes. 

Although there are no cards to choose from, Nehemiah is still a legal target for Thoughtseize and it will do as much as is possible.

entries.question: Alijah controls [Clockwork Beast] which has one +1/+0 counter on it. They want to activate its ability with X = 8. Can they?
entries.reason: Both answers agree Alijah may announce and pay for X = 8, but the ability can only place enough counters to bring Clockwork Beast to seven total (so with one already on it, only six of the eight will be placed).
entries.answer:
Yes — Alijah may announce X = 8, provided they can pay {8} in full. Nothing in Clockwork Beast's ability caps the value of X; the cap applies only to the effect when the ability resolves.

Details:

1. Announcing X: Clockwork Beast's ability is "{X}, {T}: Put up to X +1/+0 counters on this creature." Because X isn't defined by the ability's text, Alijah chooses and announces its value as part of activating the ability [107.3a]. X = 8 is a legal choice.

2. Paying: The activation cost becomes {8} (eight generic mana, payable with any colors or with colorless mana) plus tapping Clockwork Beast [107.4b, 602.1]. Alijah must be able to pay all of it — partial payments aren't allowed and a player can't pay a cost without the resources to pay it fully [118.3]. Clockwork Beast must be untapped to pay {T}. If Alijah starts the activation and can't complete payment, the activation is illegal and is reversed [733.1]. Also note the timing restriction on the ability: it can be activated only during Alijah's upkeep.

3. What it accomplishes: On resolution, Alijah puts up to X (up to 8) counters on Clockwork Beast, but the ability can't cause the total number of +1/+0 counters on Clockwork Beast to exceed seven [Clockwork Beast ruling #3]. With one counter already there, only six counters actually go on; the extra two mana are wasted. Alijah may also choose to put on fewer [Clockwork Beast ruling #4].

So it's legal but inefficient — X = 6 achieves exactly the same result for two less mana. (Other effects could still push Clockwork Beast above seven counters, per [Clockwork Beast ruling #2], but this ability can't.)

Player count doesn't matter here; this works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes, but when it resolves Alijah can't choose to put the full 8 +1/+0 counters on it; only up to 6.

entries.question: Ariel would like to choose colorless for [Uncharted Haven]. Can they?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Ariel cannot choose "colorless" because "choose a color" requires one of the five colors (white, blue, black, red, or green), so the candidate reaches the same ruling as the reference.
entries.answer:
No. When Uncharted Haven instructs Ariel to "choose a color" as it enters, Ariel must pick one of the five colors: white, blue, black, red, or green [105.1]. Colorless is explicitly not a color, and neither is "multicolored" [105.4], [Colorless]. So "colorless" is not a legal choice for Uncharted Haven.

Key terms: a "color" in Magic means one of exactly those five [105.1]; an object with no color is colorless, but that's the absence of color, not a sixth color [Colorless]. Note also that colorless mana ({C}) is a type of mana, but that doesn't make it a color for the purposes of a "choose a color" instruction [Colorless].

Because Ariel must choose one of the five colors, Uncharted Haven's ability "{T}: Add one mana of the chosen color" will always produce one mana of that chosen color. The only way Uncharted Haven ends up with no chosen color is if it somehow arrives on the battlefield without the choice being made (for example, it isn't actually entering as itself), in which case its mana ability produces no mana at all [Uncharted Haven ruling #0], [106.5].

This answer is the same regardless of the number of players at the table; nothing here depends on two-player versus multiplayer.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Colorless is not a color.

entries.question: Aleah controls [Amorphous Axe] attached to [Ich-Tekik, Salvage Splicer]. How many counters does Ich-Tekik, Salvage Splicer get when an artifact is put into the graveyard from the battlefield?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling that Ich-Tekik gets two +1/+1 counters because it counts as both Ich-Tekik and a Golem while Amorphous Axe is attached.
entries.answer:
Ich-Tekik, Salvage Splicer gets two +1/+1 counters, not one.

Amorphous Axe makes the equipped creature "every creature type," so while Amorphous Axe is attached to Ich-Tekik, Salvage Splicer, Ich-Tekik, Salvage Splicer is itself a Golem (as well as a Phyrexian Human Artificer). Ich-Tekik, Salvage Splicer's triggered ability reads "put a +1/+1 counter on Ich-Tekik and a +1/+1 counter on each Golem you control." Those are two separate instructions in one resolution, and Ich-Tekik, Salvage Splicer satisfies both — it is Ich-Tekik, and it is a Golem you control — so it receives one counter from each instruction, for two total. Each other Golem you control (such as the token from Ich-Tekik, Salvage Splicer's enters ability) still gets exactly one counter.

The ability triggers only once per artifact put into a graveyard from the battlefield (rule 603.2c: an ability triggers once each time its trigger event occurs, though a single event containing multiple occurrences — such as a wrath destroying several artifacts — triggers it once per artifact). Note also that if the artifact that hit the graveyard was Amorphous Axe itself, the game does not look back in time for this kind of trigger, and by the time the ability resolves Ich-Tekik, Salvage Splicer is no longer equipped and therefore no longer a Golem, so it would get only the single counter from the "put a +1/+1 counter on Ich-Tekik" clause (compare rule 603.10a, which lists the limited set of abilities that do look back in time).

Also, per [Ich-Tekik, Salvage Splicer ruling #2], if Ich-Tekik, Salvage Splicer leaves the battlefield before the ability resolves, you still put a +1/+1 counter on each Golem you control.

This works identically in two-player and multiplayer games — the ability triggers on any artifact put into a graveyard from the battlefield, regardless of whose it was, and only counts Golems you control.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 2, as it is also a Golem.

entries.question: If Andre casts [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces] to copy [Maelstrom Wanderer], does Andre cascade?
entries.reason: Both conclude Andre does not cascade because Sakashima isn't a copy of Maelstrom Wanderer while it's being cast, so no cascade trigger exists.
entries.answer:
No. Andre does not cascade.

Cascade is a triggered ability that functions only while the spell with cascade is on the stack; it triggers "when you cast this spell" ([702.85a]). Andre cast Sakashima of a Thousand Faces, which is a {3}{U} spell (mana value 4) with no cascade ability of its own. When a spell is cast, it goes on the stack with the characteristics of the card ([601.2a]), so on the stack it is just Sakashima of a Thousand Faces — nothing about Maelstrom Wanderer is involved yet, and there is no cascade trigger.

Sakashima of a Thousand Faces' copy effect says "You may have Sakashima enter as a copy of another creature you control." An object that enters the battlefield "as a copy" becomes a copy as it enters, not after ([707.5]) — and that happens on the battlefield, long after the casting event that cascade cares about has passed. So the Sakashima of a Thousand Faces permanent will be a copy of Maelstrom Wanderer (with Sakashima of a Thousand Faces' own other abilities added, per [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces ruling #1]), meaning it has two cascade abilities printed on it, but those abilities only do something when you cast a spell that has them — they do nothing from the battlefield.

What Andre does get: the copy has Maelstrom Wanderer's "Creatures you control have haste," and any enters-the-battlefield triggers of the copied creature would trigger ([707.5], [Sakashima of a Thousand Faces ruling #8]); Maelstrom Wanderer has none, since cascade is a cast trigger, not an ETB trigger.

One timing note: if instead the question were about Maelstrom Wanderer itself being cast, both cascade instances would trigger separately ([702.85c], [Maelstrom Wanderer ruling #2]). Also, if some other effect let Andre cast a copy of Maelstrom Wanderer as a spell, that cast would trigger cascade ([707.12]) — but Sakashima of a Thousand Faces copying on the battlefield is not that.

Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No, cascade is a cast trigger and Sakashima of a Thousand Faces isn't a copy of Maelstrom Wanderer until it's on the battlefield.

entries.question: If Agustin uses [Kiki-Jiki, Mirror Breaker] to make a token of [Sea Gate Banneret], then uses [Brudiclad, Telchor Engineer] to turn the token Sea Gate Banneret into a different token, does Agustin have to sacrifice it still?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Kiki-Jiki’s delayed “sacrifice it” applies to the original token object and isn’t undone by Brudiclad turning that same token into a copy, so it is still sacrificed.
entries.answer:
Yes. Agustin still sacrifices that token at the beginning of the next end step.

Kiki-Jiki, Mirror Breaker's ability creates the token and sets up a delayed trigger that says "Sacrifice it." That "it" tracks the specific token object Kiki-Jiki, Mirror Breaker created, not its name or characteristics. Brudiclad, Telchor Engineer's triggered ability makes that token become a copy of another token — a copy effect that changes the token's copiable values, but it doesn't create a new object, doesn't move it to another zone, and doesn't destroy the delayed sacrifice instruction. Brudiclad, Telchor Engineer ruling #3 confirms the copy only replaces defined copiable values; it isn't making a fresh token. So the same permanent is still the thing Kiki-Jiki, Mirror Breaker told Agustin to sacrifice, and it goes to the graveyard at the beginning of the next end step, now with whatever characteristics it copied from the chosen token.

Contrast with Kiki-Jiki, Mirror Breaker ruling #0: if some *other* creature becomes a copy of (or enters as a copy of) the Kiki-Jiki token, that other creature is a different object and is not sacrificed. That's the reverse of Agustin's case — here the original token itself is the one that changed, so it's still on the hook.

Also note (Kiki-Jiki, Mirror Breaker ruling #4) that if a replacement effect had made multiple tokens, every one of them would be sacrificed.

This works identically at a two-player table and in multiplayer; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Brudiclad, Telchor Engineer's beginning-of-combat trigger resolves during the same turn, before the end step. If instead the token were somehow gone or the copy happened after the delayed trigger already resolved, there'd be nothing left to sacrifice — but a mid-turn copy change never saves it.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes, Kiki-Jiki, Mirror Breaker asks Agustin to sacrifice the token it creates, it doesn't give the token an ability that makes Agustin sacrifice it, so turning into something else does nothing.

entries.question: Alex controls [Angel of Jubilation] and casts [Dash Hopes]. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Dash Hopes functions normally and that players may pay life to counter it because Angel of Jubilation only prevents paying life as part of casting spells or activating abilities, not the optional payment made by Dash Hopes' resolution.
entries.answer:
Dash Hopes works normally: when Alex casts Dash Hopes, its "when you cast" trigger goes on the stack, and any player — including Alex — may pay 5 life to counter Dash Hopes. Angel of Jubilation does not stop that payment.

Why: Angel of Jubilation's last ability reads "Players can't pay life or sacrifice creatures to cast spells or activate abilities." It only shuts off paying life as part of casting a spell or activating an ability (i.e., as a cost paid during rules 601.2b/601.2f cost payment, such as an alternative or additional cost — see 118.8d, 118.9, 118.9b). The 5 life for Dash Hopes is not a cost of casting anything; it's an optional payment made during the resolution of Dash Hopes' triggered ability, after Dash Hopes has already been cast and paid for (its cost is just {B}{B}). Angel of Jubilation's ruling confirms the ability looks at the action being taken, not at wording on other cards, and the action here isn't "paying life to cast a spell or activate an ability."

So Alex pays {B}{B}, the trigger resolves, and each player in turn order gets the chance to pay 5 life; if any does, Dash Hopes is countered and never counters its target. If no one pays, Dash Hopes resolves and counters the target spell.

Multiplayer note: the wording "any player" means every player at the table (not just one opponent) can pay in a game with more than two players, so with more opponents it's likelier someone pays. In a two-player game only Alex and the single opponent may pay. Also note Angel of Jubilation's ability applies to all players, so no player — including opponents — could pay life as part of casting a spell, but again that restriction never touches the Dash Hopes trigger.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Dash Hopes resolves as normal. Players may pay life to counter it because the payment is not to activate an ability or cast a spell.

entries.question: Aleah attacks with a [Cloak and Dagger, Entwined] enchanted with [Lifelink]. How much life will Aleah gain?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Aleah gains 2 life because multiple instances of lifelink are redundant and lifelink causes the creature's controller to gain life equal to the damage dealt.
entries.answer:
Aleah gains 2 life (assuming Cloak and Dagger, Entwined is unblocked and deals its full 2 combat damage), and it's a single life-gain event, not two.

Why: Cloak and Dagger, Entwined already has lifelink printed on it, and the Aura Lifelink grants the enchanted creature lifelink as well. Multiple instances of lifelink on the same object are redundant [702.15f], so the second instance does nothing extra. Damage dealt by a source with lifelink causes that source's controller to gain that much life in addition to the damage's other results [702.15b, 120.3f] — so 2 damage dealt means 2 life gained, once. Note also that the life goes to the controller of the enchanted creature, Aleah, not to the controller of the Aura Lifelink if those were different players [Lifelink ruling #0].

Caveats on the amount: the life gained tracks damage actually dealt. If Cloak and Dagger, Entwined is blocked, it still gains Aleah 2 life for damage dealt to the blocking creature (lifelink applies to damage dealt to permanents too) [120.3f]; if the damage is prevented or reduced, Aleah gains only as much life as damage is actually dealt, and if 0 damage is dealt there is no life-gain event at all [119.9]. Deathtouch doesn't change the amount of damage dealt or life gained.

Multiplayer: this is unchanged with more than two players — whichever player or planeswalker/battle Cloak and Dagger, Entwined is attacking, the damage it deals gains Aleah that much life. (Two-Headed Giant is the exception in that life gain applies to a team's shared life total [810.9].)

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Aleah will gain 2 life. Additional occurrences of lifelink are redundant.

entries.question: Abraham controls a tapped [Pack Mastiff] enchanted with Nathalia's [Sleeping Potion]. What happens when Abraham activates Pack Mastiff's activated ability?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Pack Mastiff's ability can be activated while it's tapped and it doesn't target, so Nathalia's Sleeping Potion does not trigger or get sacrificed.
entries.answer:
Abraham can activate Pack Mastiff's ability normally, and Nathalia's Sleeping Potion is NOT sacrificed.

Why: Pack Mastiff's ability costs {1}{R} (one generic mana plus one red mana) — there is no tap symbol {T} or untap symbol {Q} in the cost. The restrictions that a creature's activated ability can't be activated while the creature is tapped-for-cost or while it's "summoning sick" apply only to abilities with {T} or {Q} in their activation cost [107.5, 107.6, 302.6, 602.5a]. So Pack Mastiff being tapped is irrelevant; a tapped permanent can still activate abilities that don't require tapping. Abraham may activate it any time he has priority [113.3b].

As for Nathalia's Sleeping Potion: its sacrifice trigger reads "When enchanted creature becomes the target of a spell or ability, sacrifice this Aura." Pack Mastiff's ability says "Each creature you control named Pack Mastiff gets +1/+0 until end of turn" — it uses no word "target," so nothing is targeted and Nathalia's Sleeping Potion's trigger does not trigger. It stays on the battlefield, and Pack Mastiff still won't untap during Abraham's untap step.

Result: each creature Abraham controls named Pack Mastiff, including the tapped enchanted one, gets +1/+0 until end of turn (the enchanted Pack Mastiff becomes 3/2), and it remains tapped and enchanted.

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players — it works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Nothing, other than the normal resolution of Pack Mastiff's ability. Pack Mastiff's ability doesn't use the word "target" and so while it has an effect on itself, it won't cause Sleeping Potion's ability to trigger.

entries.question: Ariel attacks with [Survivor of Korlis]. Nevaeh blocks with [Trained Caracal]. What happens after the declare blockers step?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Survivor of Korlis deals first-strike damage killing Trained Caracal before it can deal damage, so Nevaeh gains no life.
entries.answer:
Because Survivor of Korlis has first strike, the combat phase gets two combat damage steps, and Trained Caracal dies before it ever deals damage.

Step by step:

1. First combat damage step: since at least one creature in combat (Survivor of Korlis) has first strike as the step begins, only creatures with first strike or double strike assign combat damage in that step [510.4, 702.7b, 506.1]. Ariel, as active player, announces that the blocked Survivor of Korlis assigns its damage to the creature blocking it, Trained Caracal — all of it, since Trained Caracal is the only blocker [510.1, 510.1a, 510.1c]. Trained Caracal, having neither first strike nor double strike, assigns nothing this step. The damage is then dealt simultaneously as a turn-based action, with no priority in between [510.2, 703.4m]. Survivor of Korlis is a 1/1, so Trained Caracal (a 1/1) is dealt 1 damage, which is lethal.
2. State-based actions then see Trained Caracal with lethal damage and it is put into the graveyard, before players get priority.
3. Second combat damage step: only the remaining attackers and blockers that lacked first strike/double strike in the first step, plus any creature that currently has double strike, assign damage [510.4, 702.4b]. Trained Caracal is no longer on the battlefield, so it assigns no damage and its lifelink gains Nevaeh no life. Survivor of Korlis does not assign damage again (it has first strike, not double strike). Survivor of Korlis survives untouched, and since it was blocked, Nevaeh takes no damage [510.1c].

Then the phase proceeds to the end of combat step.

Assumption: nothing else happens in the declare blockers step (no pump, removal, or first-strike granting to Trained Caracal). If Nevaeh had, for example, given Trained Caracal first strike or extra toughness before damage, Trained Caracal could survive or trade and its lifelink would gain Nevaeh 1 life.

Multiplayer note: this works the same regardless of the number of players, since only Ariel (the active player) and Nevaeh (the defending player) are involved in the assignment [510.1]. Under the shared-team-turns variant, the active team announces attacker damage assignment and then the defending team announces blocker damage assignment [805.10f].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: There is a first combat damage step during which Survivor of Korlis deals one (lethal) damage to Trained Caracal. Trained Caracal is destroyed when state-based actions are checked, before having the opportunity to deal damage during the second damage step. Nevaeh therefore does not gain life.

entries.question: Autumn cast [Scholar of the Ages]. In their graveyard are [Slip On the Ring], [Fortifying Draught], and 2 copies of [Poison the Well]. What are their options when it comes to returning cards?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling that Autumn may return zero, one, or any combination of two of those instant/sorcery cards from their graveyard.
entries.answer:
Autumn's Scholar of the Ages trigger lets them choose up to two targets total from among the instant and/or sorcery cards in their graveyard — so zero, one, or two of Slip On the Ring, Fortifying Draught, and the two copies of Poison the Well, in any mix.

All four cards qualify: Slip On the Ring and Fortifying Draught are instants, and both copies of Poison the Well are sorceries, and the ability says "instant and/or sorcery cards." Legal choices include Slip On the Ring + Fortifying Draught, Slip On the Ring + one Poison the Well, both copies of Poison the Well, any single card, or nothing at all. What Autumn cannot do is return two instants plus two sorceries — the cap is two cards total, not two of each type [Scholar of the Ages ruling #0].

A couple of practical notes: the targets are chosen when the enters-the-battlefield trigger is put on the stack, and the returned cards go from the graveyard to Autumn's hand. Nothing here depends on the number of players — the ability only looks at Autumn's own graveyard, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game. Also, these are simply cast-from-hand cards afterward; none of the graveyard-casting keywords such as flashback [702.34a] or jump-start [702.133a] are involved.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: They can either return no cards, one card of their choosing, or any combination of two.

entries.question: Alexis casts [Mind Games], paying the additional cost for buyback. They then cast [Fork] targetting Mind Games. Will Fork return to Alexis's hand upon resolution?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Fork itself has no buyback and goes to the graveyard, while only the original Mind Games (for which buyback was paid) returns to Alexis's hand.
entries.answer:
No. Fork goes to its owner's graveyard when it resolves — buyback is an ability of Mind Games, not of Fork, and copying a spell doesn't give Fork that spell's abilities.

Details:

1. Buyback means "You may pay an additional [cost] as you cast this spell" and "If the buyback cost was paid, put this spell into its owner's hand instead of into that player's graveyard as it resolves" [702.27a]. That static ability functions only on the Mind Games spell while it is on the stack; Fork is a separate spell with its own text and no buyback.
2. When Fork resolves, it puts a copy of Mind Games on the stack and Fork itself is put into the graveyard, leaving the copy behind with no card representing it [Fork ruling #11], [707.10], [405.1], [608.1].
3. The copy of Mind Games does copy all decisions made for the original, including additional costs paid — so the copy "has buyback paid" [707.10]. But there is no card associated with the copy, so nothing goes to Alexis's hand from it; the copy simply ceases to exist as a state-based action once it leaves the stack [704.5e], [Fork ruling #0], [112.1a].
4. The original Mind Games card, for which Alexis actually paid the buyback cost of {2}{U} in addition to its mana cost of {U}, does return to Alexis's hand as it resolves [702.27a], [601.2b], [601.2f].

So the net result: Fork → graveyard; the Mind Games copy → ceases to exist after resolving (it still taps its target); the real Mind Games card → Alexis's hand.

Assumption on timing: Alexis cast Fork while Mind Games was still on the stack (the only legal window, since Fork needs a spell to target). Nothing here depends on player count — the answer is the same at a two-player or multiplayer table, though with more players remember Fork's copy is controlled by whoever cast Fork [707.10], [112.2a].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. When Fork resolves, it will create a copy of Mind Games on the stack, but does not itself become a copy of Mind Games. Therefore, it will simply be put into Alexis's graveyard as the final step of resolving.

entries.question: Ayleen cast [Sazh Katzroy] and choose not to search their library. Noe would like to cast [Archive Trap] for its alternative cost. Can they?
entries.reason: Both conclude Noe cannot cast Archive Trap for {0} because Ayleen declined to search her library, so the alternative-cost condition was not met.
entries.answer:
No. Since Ayleen declined the optional search, no library search happened, so Archive Trap's alternative cost condition ("If an opponent searched their library this turn") isn't met and Noe can't pay {0}.

Why: Sazh Katzroy's enters trigger reads "you may search your library for a Bird or basic land card..." — it's optional. Declining means Ayleen never searched. Archive Trap ruling #1 only waives the requirement that the searching player *found* something; it still requires that a search actually occurred. Archive Trap ruling #0 likewise stresses that a search happens only when an effect actually says "search" and is carried out. Had Ayleen chosen to search but found nothing (which is allowed — a player searching a hidden zone for cards with a stated quality need not find them, per [701.23b], and may choose to search even when the follow-up actions are impossible, per [701.23g]), the condition would be met and Noe could cast Archive Trap for {0}.

Noe's other option: Archive Trap can always simply be cast for its normal mana cost of {3}{U}{U} (three generic plus two blue), per Archive Trap ruling #2. Note also that paying the alternative cost never changes Archive Trap's mana cost or mana value of 5 (Archive Trap ruling #3, and [118.9c]); alternative costs are optional replacements for the mana cost ([118.9b]).

Multiplayer note: the condition is about "an opponent" of Noe. In a two-player game that's just Ayleen. At a table of three or more, if any other opponent of Noe searched their library this turn, the alternative cost would be available regardless of Ayleen's choice.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Ayleen didn't actually search their library, so the qualifications for Archive Trap's alternative cost haven't been met.

entries.question: Asia activates the second ability of [Sensei's Divining Top] and would like to sacrifice it to [Throne of Geth] before putting it on top of their library. Can they do this?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Asia may sacrifice Sensei's Divining Top to Throne of Geth in response to Top's activated ability, causing Throne's ability to resolve first and Top's ability to still let Asia draw a card but not return the Top to the library since it's in the graveyard.
entries.answer:
Yes. Asia activates Sensei's Divining Top's second ability ({T}: Draw a card, then put this artifact on top of its owner's library), and while that ability is on the stack they can activate Throne of Geth's ability, paying its cost by tapping Throne of Geth and sacrificing Sensei's Divining Top as the artifact. Sacrificing Sensei's Divining Top is legal even though it's already tapped from paying its own activation cost — sacrificing just means its controller moves it from the battlefield to its owner's graveyard [701.21a], and the cost is paid as part of activating Throne of Geth's ability [601.2h].

Sensei's Divining Top's ability exists independently on the stack once activated, so it still resolves. When it does, Asia draws a card, and because Sensei's Divining Top is no longer on the battlefield, it is not moved to the top of the library — it stays in the graveyard [Sensei's Divining Top ruling #1]. Throne of Geth's proliferate ability resolves first (it was activated later and is above on the stack), then Sensei's Divining Top's ability resolves for the draw.

Note also that Throne of Geth can sacrifice itself for its own ability [Throne of Geth ruling #0], but here Sensei's Divining Top is the artifact being sacrificed. Nothing here depends on player count, so the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Asia can activate the second ability of Sensei's Divining Top and then sacrifice it to Throne of Geth in response. When it resolves, Asia will just draw a card.

entries.question: Andy casts [Abrupt Decay] targeting Nancy's 5/5 Horse creature token, then responds by targeting it with [Arcane Denial]. What happens?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference conclude that Arcane Denial can't counter Abrupt Decay but its delayed draw effects still occur and Abrupt Decay then resolves, destroying the token.
entries.answer:
Arcane Denial resolves first and fails to counter Abrupt Decay, but its other effects still happen; then Abrupt Decay resolves and destroys the 5/5 Horse token.

Details:

1. Arcane Denial was cast in response, so it's on top of the stack and resolves first [117.7], [608.1].
2. Abrupt Decay is still a legal target for Arcane Denial — a spell that counters spells may target it — so Arcane Denial resolves rather than being removed for an illegal target [608.3b is for permanent spells; here the relevant point is targeting legality], and per Abrupt Decay's own text "This spell can't be countered," the counter effect simply does nothing. Card text overrides the general counter rule [701.6a], which would otherwise remove Abrupt Decay from the stack and put it in Andy's graveyard.
3. Arcane Denial's remaining instructions still apply as written [608.2c], [Abrupt Decay ruling #1]: at the beginning of the next turn's upkeep, Abrupt Decay's controller (Andy) may draw up to two cards, and Arcane Denial's controller draws a card. Those are delayed triggers that happen on the next upkeep, not immediately.
4. Because Abrupt Decay was never actually countered, no "whenever a spell is countered" trigger would see it either [603.10e].
5. Abrupt Decay then resolves. A creature token has a mana value of 0, so Nancy's 5/5 Horse token is a legal target (nonland permanent, mana value 3 or less) and is destroyed. As a token that leaves the battlefield, it ceases to exist.

Assumption on timing/who cast what: I read the question as Nancy responding with Arcane Denial, targeting Abrupt Decay on the stack. If instead Andy cast Arcane Denial himself, the outcome is identical except Andy is both the drawer of the single card and the player who may draw up to two. Nothing here changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer table — only the two players involved are affected.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Arcane Denial resolves but can't counter Abrupt Decay. During Nancy's upkeep, Andy draws one to three cards, based on their choice.

entries.question: Alexander has a [Gigapede] in their graveyard and one in their hand. How many times can Alexander trigger [Hashaton, Scarab's Fist]?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Hashaton will trigger only once at the beginning of Alexander’s upkeep because only one Gigapede’s graveyard-triggered discard occurs, producing a single discard event.
entries.answer:
Once per turn — at the beginning of each of Alexander's upkeeps — assuming no other discard outlets.

How it loops: the Gigapede in the graveyard has "At the beginning of your upkeep, if this card is in your graveyard, you may discard a card. If you do, return this card to your hand." Alexander discards the Gigapede that's in hand, and the graveyard Gigapede returns to hand. Because a creature card (the second Gigapede) was discarded, Hashaton, Scarab's Fist's ability "Whenever you discard a creature card, you may pay {2}{U}..." triggers. That's one trigger; a triggered ability triggers only once per occurrence of its trigger event (603.2c), and one discard is one event.

After that, the positions have simply swapped: the discarded Gigapede is now the one in the graveyard, and the returned Gigapede is in hand. So the same loop is available again next upkeep — one Hashaton, Scarab's Fist trigger per turn cycle, not repeatedly within a turn, since only one Gigapede is ever in the graveyard at a time and each Gigapede's upkeep ability is a separate instance that only functions from the graveyard (113.2c). If Alexander somehow had both Gigapede cards in the graveyard at once, each would trigger separately and each discard would trigger Hashaton, Scarab's Fist.

Paying {2}{U} is optional and is made on resolution; if paid, Alexander creates a tapped token copy of Gigapede that's a 4/4 black Zombie. Note the cost is two generic plus one blue specifically.

This works identically in two-player and multiplayer games, since the trigger is on Alexander's own upkeep and only cares about Alexander's discards.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Once. Gigapede's triggered ability will go on the stack at the beginning of Alexander's upkeep, and once Alexander discards their second Gigapede it will no longer be the beginning of Alexander's upkeep. The second copy's ability won't trigger.

entries.question: Angie controls [Joiner Adept] and three [Lumbering Falls]. They play a [Mystic Sanctuary] as their land for turn. Will it enter the battlefield untapped and trigger?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Joiner Adept only grants a mana ability (not the Island basic land type), so Mystic Sanctuary won't meet the "other Islands" condition, enters tapped, and its enter-untapped trigger won't occur.
entries.answer:
No. Mystic Sanctuary enters the battlefield tapped, and its "enters untapped" trigger does not trigger.

Why: Mystic Sanctuary's own text is "This land enters tapped unless you control three or more other Islands." That is a replacement effect that modifies how Mystic Sanctuary enters the battlefield, checked as Mystic Sanctuary enters, based on the permanents already on the battlefield [614.1c] [614.12] [Mystic Sanctuary ruling #1]. The check is specifically for the land type Island — a subtype — not for lands that can produce {U}.

Lumbering Falls is just "Land" with no basic land type; it isn't an Island. Joiner Adept only grants Angie's lands the ability "{T}: Add one mana of any color" [Joiner Adept ruling #0]; it grants a mana ability, not the Island subtype. So the three Lumbering Falls are not "other Islands," Angie controls zero other Islands, and the "unless" condition fails.

Because Mystic Sanctuary enters tapped, its triggered ability — "When this land enters untapped, you may put target instant or sorcery card from your graveyard on top of your library" — never has its trigger event occur, so nothing goes on the stack [603.6a] [603.1]. Note also that even later animating a Lumbering Falls with {2}{G}{U} wouldn't help: that's a type change on a permanent already on the battlefield, and it still wouldn't be an Island [Lumbering Falls ruling #3].

This answer doesn't depend on player count — the check is only about permanents Angie controls, so it's the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Also note: if some other effect had put Mystic Sanctuary onto the battlefield tapped, it would enter tapped regardless of Islands [Mystic Sanctuary ruling #0]; here it's played as a land for turn, so only its own replacement effect applies.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No, while Joiner Adept's static ability gives lands the additional ability to tap for mana of any color, it does not grant basic land types, which Mystic Sanctuary requires in order to enter untapped or to trigger.

entries.question: Noel controls [Judith, the Scourge Diva] and [Ogre Warrior]. Aria attacks with [Obsidian Giant]. Noel blocks Obsidian Giant with Ogre Warrior. At their first opportunity, Aria casts [Recalibrate] to return Judith, the Scourge Diva to Noel's hand. Will Obsidian Giant die?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Judith's static boost is gone before combat damage is dealt, leaving Ogre Warrior as a 3/3 and Obsidian Giant surviving, so the candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference.
entries.answer:
No — Obsidian Giant survives. With Judith, the Scourge Diva gone from the battlefield before the combat damage step, Ogre Warrior loses the +1/+0 from Judith, the Scourge Diva's static ability and is a 3/3. Obsidian Giant is a 4/4, so 3 damage isn't lethal to it.

Assumed timing: Aria casts Recalibrate in the declare blockers step, after blockers are declared but before combat damage is dealt (that's "first opportunity" after the block). Under that timing:

- Obsidian Giant is still a blocked creature. Removing Judith, the Scourge Diva from the battlefield doesn't change that, and even removing a blocker wouldn't unblock it [509.1h].
- In the combat damage step, Obsidian Giant is blocked by exactly one creature, Ogre Warrior, so it assigns all 4 of its damage to Ogre Warrior [510.1c]. Ogre Warrior, blocking exactly one creature, assigns its 3 damage to Obsidian Giant [510.1d].
- Result: Ogre Warrior (3 toughness) dies; Obsidian Giant (4 toughness, 3 damage marked) lives.
- Judith, the Scourge Diva's death trigger doesn't help either: it isn't on the battlefield when Ogre Warrior dies, so nothing triggers, and its ability wouldn't have finished off Obsidian Giant anyway.

If instead Aria had waited until after combat damage was already dealt, Ogre Warrior would have been a 4/3 when damage was assigned, dealing 4 damage to Obsidian Giant and killing it, and Judith, the Scourge Diva's ability would have triggered on Ogre Warrior's death (a nontoken creature dying) for 1 damage to any target.
