This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it works the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game, since only Aria (the attacking player) and Noel (the defending player) are involved in this combat.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Judith, the Scourge Diva's effect is a continuous effect that only applies while its on the battlefield. Aria has returned Judith, the Scourge Diva to Noel's hand after blockers have been declared but before damage has been dealt, so its ability will not be taken into account when calculating how much damage Ogre Warrior will deal.

entries.question: Nico controls [Kargan Warleader] and [Garenbrig Carver]. Amina attacks with their [Horned Turtle]. Nico blocks Horned Turtle with Garenbrig Carver. Amina casts [Consign to Dream] to return Kargan Warleader to Nico's hand. Will Horned Turtle die?
entries.reason: Both conclude Horned Turtle survives because Kargan Warleader's buff no longer applies if it's removed before combat damage is dealt, so the blocking Garenbrig Carver deals only 3 damage.
entries.answer:
No — Horned Turtle survives, assuming Consign to Dream resolves before combat damage is dealt.

Garenbrig Carver is a 3/2 Human Warrior. While Kargan Warleader is on the battlefield, its static ability ("Other Warriors you control get +1/+1") makes Garenbrig Carver a 4/3. Once Amina's Consign to Dream removes Kargan Warleader from the battlefield (and because Kargan Warleader is red-and-white, it goes on top of Nico's library rather than to hand), Garenbrig Carver immediately reverts to 3/2.

In the combat damage step, Garenbrig Carver is a blocking creature blocking exactly one creature, so it assigns all of its combat damage — now 3 — to Horned Turtle (rule 510.1d). Horned Turtle is a 1/4, so 3 damage is not lethal and it survives. Horned Turtle, blocked by Garenbrig Carver, assigns its 1 damage to Garenbrig Carver (rule 510.1c), which is not lethal to a 3/2 either. Both creatures live.

Note that Kargan Warleader leaving the battlefield does not remove Garenbrig Carver from combat — only Kargan Warleader itself left, and it wasn't in combat (rule 506.4). Garenbrig Carver remains a blocking creature.

Timing caveat: if instead Consign to Dream is cast and resolves after combat damage has already been dealt, Horned Turtle would already have been dealt 4 damage by the then-4/3 Garenbrig Carver and would have died as a state-based action at that time; removing Kargan Warleader afterward changes nothing for it. The related ruling on Kargan Warleader (that damage stays marked, so nonlethal damage can become lethal when Kargan Warleader leaves) works the other way — it can kill your own damaged Warriors, e.g. if Garenbrig Carver had 2 damage marked while it was a 4/3, losing Kargan Warleader would make that damage lethal.

This analysis doesn't depend on the player count — it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since only Amina is the defending player's opponent here and no other player is involved in this combat.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Kargan Warleader's effect is a continuous effect that only applies while it's on the battlefield. Amina has returned Kargan Warleader to Nico's hand after blockers have been declared but before damage has been dealt, so its ability will not be taken into account when calculating how much damage Garenbrig Carver will deal.

entries.question: Avery targets their [Trained Armodon] with [Goldenhide Ox]. Neil controls two 1/1 Human Soldier tokens. How many creatures will Neil have to block with?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Neil is only required to block Trained Armodon with at least one creature (he may choose which and isn't forced to block with both).
entries.answer:
Neil must block Trained Armodon with at least one creature — a single 1/1 Human Soldier token satisfies the requirement. He may choose to block with both tokens if he wants, but he isn't forced to.

Why: Goldenhide Ox's constellation ability creates a blocking *requirement* on Trained Armodon ("must be blocked this turn if able"). Per [Goldenhide Ox ruling #3], the defending player must assign at least one blocker to the targeted creature if they control any creature that could block it, and per [Goldenhide Ox ruling #1] the ability doesn't force any particular creature to be the one that blocks. Neil chooses which of his two tokens blocks. When Neil declares blockers, he checks his creatures against requirements and must obey the maximum number of requirements possible without violating restrictions ([509.1c], [509.1a]); one requirement here is satisfied by one blocker.

Assumption: only Trained Armodon is attacking (or at least, it's the only attacker carrying a must-be-blocked requirement). If Avery also attacked with Goldenhide Ox or another creature that separately had to be blocked, Neil would have to spread his blockers so that each such attacker gets at least one blocker — with two such attackers and two tokens, one token on each ([Goldenhide Ox ruling #0]). Also, if Trained Armodon had an evasion restriction such as menace, Neil would need two blockers on it.

Multiplayer note: if more than one player is being attacked, each defending player declares blockers in APNAP order and legality is judged ignoring other players' creatures and attackers aimed elsewhere ([802.4b], [802.2a], [101.4]); Neil's obligation still only concerns creatures attacking him, his planeswalkers, or battles he protects ([509.1a]).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: One. Goldenhide Ox just states that Trained Armodon must be blocked, but Neil can choose how many and which creatures end up blocking it.

entries.question: Avery controls [Solemnity] and suspends [Duskrider Peregrine]. Is Avery able to put time counters on Duskrider Peregrine?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Solemnity only stops counters on permanents on the battlefield, so suspended cards in exile can receive time counters.
entries.answer:
Yes. Solemnity does not stop time counters from being put on Duskrider Peregrine while Duskrider Peregrine is a suspended card in exile.

Why: Solemnity reads "Players can't get counters. Counters can't be put on artifacts, creatures, enchantments, or lands." Those object types refer to permanents on the battlefield; a card in the exile zone isn't one of them. The Solemnity ruling is explicit: counters can be put on cards that aren't on the battlefield, and notably suspended cards will still get time counters [Solemnity ruling #4].

So the initial exiling works normally: taking the suspend special action on Duskrider Peregrine exiles it from Avery's hand with three time counters on it, paying {1}{W} [702.62a] [116.2f]. Duskrider Peregrine is then "suspended" because it has suspend, is in exile, and has one or more time counters on it [702.62b] [Duskrider Peregrine ruling #4]. Any later effect that adds time counters — for example time travel, which lets you put a time counter on or remove one from suspended cards you own in exile — can also add counters to Duskrider Peregrine despite Solemnity [701.56a].

Contrast: once Duskrider Peregrine is actually cast and enters the battlefield as a creature, Solemnity would then prevent counters from being put on it, including as it enters [Solemnity ruling #8].

This doesn't depend on player count — Solemnity's restriction and suspend work identically in two-player and multiplayer games, and Solemnity affects all players' ability to get counters, not just Avery's.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Solemnity only affects artifacts, creatures, enchantments and lands on the battlefield.

entries.question: Natalee controls [Alquist Proft, Master Sleuth]. Alex targets it with [Weigh Down], and Natalee targets it with [On Alert] at their earliest opportunity. What happens to Alquist Proft, Master Sleuth?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude On Alert resolves first (+2/+2) then Weigh Down applies (-3/-3), leaving Alquist Proft as a 2/2 until end of turn and not dying.
entries.answer:
Alquist Proft, Master Sleuth survives as a 2/2 (and is untapped).

Sequence: Alex casts Weigh Down targeting Alquist Proft, Master Sleuth; it goes on the stack. Natalee responds with On Alert (the Adventure half of Silverflame Squire // On Alert, an instant) targeting Alquist Proft, Master Sleuth. Because the stack resolves last-in-first-out, On Alert resolves first.

1. On Alert resolves. Alquist Proft, Master Sleuth is still on the battlefield and still a legal target, so the spell resolves normally (608.2b): it gets +2/+2 until end of turn, becoming 5/5, and is untapped (relevant only if Natalee had tapped it for its {X}{W}{U}{U}, {T}, Sacrifice a Clue ability — note that Alquist Proft, Master Sleuth also has vigilance, so attacking wouldn't have tapped it). Silverflame Squire // On Alert is then exiled per the Adventure text, and Natalee may cast Silverflame Squire from exile later.
2. Weigh Down resolves. Alquist Proft, Master Sleuth is still a legal target, so it gets -3/-3. Combined with the +2/+2, it is 3+2-3 = 2, so a 2/2 until end of turn. Its toughness is above 0, so it is not put into the graveyard.

If instead Natalee had somehow let Weigh Down resolve first, Alquist Proft, Master Sleuth would be 0/0 and die immediately as a state-based action, and On Alert would then have no legal target and wouldn't resolve (608.2b). That's why casting On Alert "at the earliest opportunity" — in response, while Weigh Down is still on the stack — saves it. Also note Weigh Down's additional cost (exile a creature card from Alex's graveyard) was already paid on casting and isn't refunded.

This works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table; no player count matters here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
When each player casts their spell, it's put onto the top of the stack. The top object on the stack resolves first, so On Alert resolves first, giving Alquist Proft, Master Sleuth +2/+2. Then Weigh Down resolves, giving it -3/-3. It ends up as a 2/2.

As the turn ends, both effects simultaneously Cease applying, and it goes back to being a 3/3.

entries.question: Abdiel controls [Virtue of Knowledge] and [Omnath, Locus of Creation] and plays a land. After all triggers have resolved, how much life will they have gained, and will they have any mana in their mana pool?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference — Abdiel gains 4 life and ends with one each of white, blue, red, and green mana in their mana pool.
entries.answer:
Abdiel gains 4 life and ends up with {R}{G}{W}{U} in their mana pool.

Why: the land entering causes Omnath, Locus of Creation's landfall triggered ability to trigger. Virtue of Knowledge says that if a permanent entering causes a triggered ability of a permanent you control to trigger, that ability triggers an additional time — so Omnath, Locus of Creation's landfall ability triggers twice, not once, and Virtue of Knowledge does not copy it; each instance is a separate trigger put on the stack ([Virtue of Knowledge // Vantress Visions ruling #1], [Virtue of Knowledge // Vantress Visions ruling #27]).

Omnath, Locus of Creation's ability checks how many times it has resolved this turn:
- First resolution: gain 4 life.
- Second resolution: add {R}{G}{W}{U} (one red, one green, one white, and one blue mana — no generic mana).

There is no third resolution, so no 4 damage to opponents or planeswalkers. Assuming this is the first land Abdiel has played this turn and no other landfall triggers have already resolved; if Omnath, Locus of Creation's ability had already resolved once earlier this turn, the two new resolutions would instead be the mana and then the 4 damage to each opponent and each planeswalker you don't control, with no life gain.

About the mana: Omnath, Locus of Creation's landfall ability is not a mana ability — it uses the stack and can be responded to, because its trigger event is a land entering, not a mana ability ([Omnath, Locus of Creation ruling #0]; contrast rule 605.4a, where true triggered mana abilities never use the stack). So the {R}{G}{W}{U} appears only when that second trigger resolves, and it will empty from the mana pool at the end of the current step or phase if unused.

Multiplayer: the answer is identical with two players or more — nothing here depends on opponent count, since the damage clause (which hits each opponent) never happens with only two resolutions.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Abdiel will have gained 4 life and have {W}{U}{R}{G} in their mana pool. Virtue of Knowledge makes Omnath, Locus of Creation's trigger trigger twice, just like if two lands had entered the battlefield at the same time.

entries.question: Can Amina activate [Planebound Accomplice] to put the back face of [Kytheon, Hero of Akros] onto the battlefield?
entries.reason: Both conclude "no" — in hand Kytheon is a creature (front face only), so it's not a planeswalker card and cannot be put onto the battlefield by Planebound Accomplice.
entries.answer:
No. Planebound Accomplice's ability says "You may put a planeswalker card from your hand onto the battlefield," and while it's in Amina's hand the card Kytheon, Hero of Akros // Gideon, Battle-Forged is a legendary creature card, not a planeswalker card — in any zone other than the stack/battlefield, a nonmodal double-faced card has only its front face's characteristics. So it isn't a legal choice for Planebound Accomplice at all.

Even setting that aside, a double-faced card put onto the battlefield from a zone other than the stack enters with its front face up by default [712.14a]; only an effect that explicitly says "transformed" (or "converted") would make it enter with the Gideon, Battle-Forged face up [712.14a], and Planebound Accomplice's ability says no such thing. Nor can the back face be cast [Kytheon, Hero of Akros // Gideon, Battle-Forged ruling #10].

The normal way to get Gideon, Battle-Forged is Kytheon, Hero of Akros's own triggered ability, which exiles Kytheon, Hero of Akros and returns him to the battlefield transformed — that instruction is what makes the back face come up [712.14a].

This answer doesn't depend on player count; it works the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

entries.answer_gold: No. In Amina's hand Kytheon, Hero of Akros is not a planeswalker card.

entries.question: Can [Myriad Landscape]'s last ability find two [Wastes]?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion: Myriad Landscape cannot find two Wastes because Wastes has no land type (though you may find one).
entries.answer:
No — Myriad Landscape's last ability can't find two Wastes, but it can find one.

Myriad Landscape's ability reads "Search your library for up to two basic land cards that share a land type." Wastes is a basic land (it has the "basic" supertype, so it qualifies as a basic land card per [305.8]), but Wastes has no land type at all — its type line is just "Basic Land" with no subtype after a dash ([305.5], [205.3i]), and [Wastes ruling #0] confirms Wastes is not a land type. Two cards with no land type cannot "share a land type," so a pair of Wastes fails the ability's requirement. (Land types are the subtypes listed in [205.3i]; the five basic land types are Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, and Forest per [305.6].)

You may, however, find a single Wastes: [Myriad Landscape ruling #0] states you can choose to find just one basic land card with Myriad Landscape's last ability, and with only one card there's no second card for it to share a type with. It enters the battlefield tapped, as Myriad Landscape specifies.

Also note that even when you do find two lands, the search is optional in scope — a hidden-zone search never forces you to find cards you don't want ([701.23b]) — though Myriad Landscape's "up to two" wording already covers this.

None of this changes between a two-player game and a multiplayer game; the ability only searches your own library.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Wastes has no basic land types, so it can't share a basic land type with anything.

entries.question: Nico controls [Ancient of the Equinox]. Alvin casts [Evil Twin]. Can they have it enter the battlefield as a copy of Ancient of the Equinox?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Evil Twin can enter as a copy of Ancient of the Equinox because choosing a creature to copy isn't targeting, so hexproof doesn't prevent the copy.
entries.answer:
Yes. Alvin may have Evil Twin enter the battlefield as a copy of Nico's Ancient of the Equinox, even though Ancient of the Equinox has hexproof — choosing a permanent to copy is not targeting, and Evil Twin's own text ("You may have this creature enter as a copy of any creature on the battlefield") simply requires that the creature be on the battlefield.

What Alvin's Evil Twin becomes: it copies the copiable values printed on the face that is currently up, i.e. Ancient of the Equinox — a 4/4 Treefolk creature with trample and hexproof, green by its color indicator (rule 707.2 lists color indicator, name, types, rules text, and power/toughness among copiable values; rule 204.1 covers the color indicator). Per the exception in Evil Twin's text, it also has "{U}{B}, {T}: Destroy target creature with the same name as this creature" — that granted ability is part of its copiable values (rules 707.9a, 707.9b). Since both permanents are now named Ancient of the Equinox, Alvin can pay {U}{B} (one blue and one black mana) and tap to try to destroy Nico's — but Nico's Ancient of the Equinox has hexproof, so it can't be targeted by that ability; the ability could only target another same-named creature that Alvin can legally target.

Things that aren't copied: Nico's permanent's status (tapped/untapped, face up/face down, etc.), counters, Auras, and any non-copy effects are not copied (rules 707.2, 110.5, Evil Twin ruling #7). Enters-the-battlefield and "as this enters" abilities of the copied creature would apply and trigger (rule 707.5, Evil Twin ruling #6), but Ancient of the Equinox has none.

Assumption on timing: this assumes Nico's Autumnal Gloom has already transformed and Ancient of the Equinox is on the battlefield as a creature when Evil Twin's copy choice is made. If it were still an untransformed Autumnal Gloom (a noncreature enchantment), Evil Twin couldn't copy it at all, and if it somehow entered simultaneously with Evil Twin it also couldn't be chosen (Evil Twin ruling #5). Alvin may also decline to copy anything, in which case Evil Twin is a 0/0 and dies (Evil Twin ruling #4).

The provided rules contain no multiplayer-specific wrinkle here: the answer is the same whether the table has two players or more, since the choice is made solely by Evil Twin's controller.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Hexproof prevents Ancient of the Equinox from being the target of an opponent's spell or ability, but Evil Twin doesn't target anything.

entries.question: Ashley attacks with [Dual-Sun Adepts] while Nico controls [Archetype of Courage]. Will Dual-Sun Adepts deal combat damage twice?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Archetype of Courage only strips first strike (not double strike), so Dual-Sun Adepts retains double strike and deals damage in both combat damage steps.
entries.answer:
Yes. Dual-Sun Adepts still deals combat damage in both combat damage steps. Archetype of Courage says creatures your opponents control "lose first strike and can't have or gain first strike" — it says nothing about double strike, and double strike is a separate keyword ability. Since Nico's Archetype of Courage doesn't remove double strike from Ashley's Dual-Sun Adepts, Dual-Sun Adepts keeps it.

Because at least one attacking or blocking creature has first strike or double strike as the combat damage step begins, there are two combat damage steps. Dual-Sun Adepts assigns damage in the first step (it has double strike) and again in the second step, since the second step includes attackers and blockers that currently have double strike [510.4] [702.4b] [702.7b]. Damage assigned in each step is dealt simultaneously as a turn-based action that doesn't use the stack [510.2] [703.4m], and Dual-Sun Adepts deals damage equal to its power (2, unless pumped) each time [120.2a].

Note that Nico's Archetype of Courage does grant first strike to Nico's own creatures, so any of Nico's blockers will deal their damage in the first combat damage step alongside Dual-Sun Adepts. If Dual-Sun Adepts is destroyed by that first-strike damage, it won't be around to assign damage in the second step.

This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games: Archetype of Courage affects creatures each opponent controls, but it only strips first strike, never double strike, no matter how many opponents are at the table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. While similar to first strike, double strike is a different ability and Archetype of Courage will have not remove it from Dual-Sun Adepts.

entries.question: Alyson declares [Godsire] as an attacker. After blockers are declared, they activate Godsire's ability, tapping it. Does this remove it from combat?
entries.reason: Both conclude that tapping Godsire after it has been declared as an attacker does not remove it from combat (and thus doesn't stop its combat damage).
entries.answer:
No. Tapping Godsire after it has already been declared as an attacker does not remove Godsire from combat, and it does not prevent Godsire's combat damage. Rule 506.4b states explicitly that tapping or untapping a creature that's already been declared as an attacker or blocker doesn't remove it from combat and doesn't prevent its combat damage.

Godsire has vigilance, so it didn't tap when it attacked (508.1f notes attacking simply causes creatures to become tapped — vigilance skips that), leaving it available to pay the {T} cost of "{T}: Create an 8/8 Beast creature token that's red, green, and white." Paying that cost is a tap, not an effect that removes Godsire from combat. Removal from combat happens only for the listed events in 506.4/506.4b — leaving the battlefield, changing controller, phasing out, an effect that specifically removes it from combat, regenerating, or ceasing to be a creature — and none of those apply here. Godsire remains an attacking (and, if it was blocked, blocked) creature and will deal its 8 combat damage in the combat damage step.

The 8/8 Beast token created this way is not attacking: it wasn't declared as an attacker, and nothing puts it onto the battlefield attacking (compare 508.4d, which covers creatures explicitly put onto the battlefield attacking). It simply enters as an untapped, non-combat creature.

This answer is the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer; nothing about removal from combat here depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No, tapping a creature that's already been declared as an attacker will not remove it from combat.

entries.question: Aspen controls [Frogtosser Banneret]. Will it affect the cost of [Notorious Throng]?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Notorious Throng is a Rogue and that Frogtosser Banneret reduces its casting cost (including when cast for its prowl cost).
entries.answer:
Yes. Frogtosser Banneret reduces the cost of Notorious Throng either way, because Notorious Throng is a Rogue spell (it's a Kindred Sorcery — Rogue).

- Cast normally: mana cost {3}{U} becomes a total cost of {2}{U}. Only the generic portion shrinks; the {U} is untouched [118.7a].
- Cast for its prowl cost of {5}{U} (an alternative cost, available if Aspen dealt combat damage to a player this turn with a Rogue): the total cost becomes {4}{U}. Cost reductions apply to an alternative cost just as they do to a mana cost [118.9d], [601.2f], and Frogtosser Banneret's own ruling confirms exactly this case [Frogtosser Banneret ruling #1].

Note that the reduction doesn't change Notorious Throng's printed mana cost or mana value — only what Aspen actually pays [118.9c]. Paying the reduced prowl cost still counts as paying the prowl cost [118.7], so the extra-turn clause still applies.

The total cost is locked in once determined; a Frogtosser Banneret that arrives after Notorious Throng is already on the stack won't help [602.4], [601.2f].

This works identically in two-player and multiplayer games; the only multiplayer wrinkle is in Notorious Throng's own text (damage dealt to your opponents, plural) and in whether a Rogue connected with some player for prowl — not in the cost reduction itself.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Notorious Throng is a Rogue.

entries.question: Autumn casts [Ojutai Interceptor] for its morph cost. If Nicole wants to counter it with [Spell Burst], what is the mana value of the Ojutai Interceptor on the stack?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly states that the face-down morphed Ojutai Interceptor spell has no mana cost and thus mana value 0, matching the reference ruling.
entries.answer:
The face-down Ojutai Interceptor spell has a mana value of 0, so Nicole must choose X = 0 for Spell Burst (paying {U}, plus {3} more if she wants buyback).

Why: casting Ojutai Interceptor for its megamorph cost means it's cast as a 2/2 face-down creature spell with no name, no text, no subtypes, and no mana cost, paying {3} instead of its mana cost [702.37a, 702.37b, 702.37c]. Those face-down characteristics are what's on the stack, and effects that care about a spell's characteristics see only them [708.4]. An object with no mana cost has mana value 0 [202.3a] (Ojutai Interceptor is not a double-faced or melded card, so no exception applies). Its printed {3}{U} / MV 4 is irrelevant while it's face down.

Spell Burst counters a spell with mana value X, and for spells with {X} the chosen value determines the mana value of Spell Burst itself [202.3e, Spell Burst ruling #0]. So Nicole announces X = 0 and pays {U} (Spell Burst's own mana value on the stack will be 1).

Timing note: this assumes Spell Burst is cast while the face-down Ojutai Interceptor spell is still on the stack. If Autumn's face-down permanent has already resolved and been turned face up for its megamorph cost {3}{U}, it is no longer a spell at all and Spell Burst can't target it.

Player count doesn't matter here; the provided rules on mana value and morph are the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 0. A morphed spell is a 2/2 creature with no mana cost. Since the spell has no mana cost, its mana value is 0.

entries.question: Addison controls [The Sentry, Golden Guardian], which has lethal damage marked on it. Natalie casts [Scar], placing a -1/-1 counter on The Sentry, Golden Guardian. Will The Sentry, Golden Guardian die?
entries.reason: Both conclude it doesn't die — indestructible prevents destruction from lethal damage and the -1/-1 counter doesn't reduce its toughness to 0.
entries.answer:
No — The Sentry, Golden Guardian survives. Scar's -1/-1 counter makes The Sentry, Golden Guardian a 4/4, so the damage marked on it is still lethal (greater than or equal to its toughness), and the state-based action in rule 704.5g would destroy it — but The Sentry, Golden Guardian has indestructible, so that destruction simply doesn't happen. Indestructible means the permanent can't be destroyed by lethal damage or by "destroy" effects.

The only way a -1/-1 counter could kill The Sentry, Golden Guardian is by reducing its toughness to 0, which is a different state-based action (a creature with 0 or less toughness is put into the graveyard, and indestructible doesn't stop that). One counter takes a 5/5 to 4/4, nowhere near 0, so it stays on the battlefield.

Note that damage never destroys anything by itself; it's only marked, and state-based actions check it (120.5, 120.6, 302.7). Those checks happen automatically before any player would next receive priority (117.5, 704.1), including right after Scar finishes resolving (608.1). All damage marked on The Sentry, Golden Guardian is removed during the cleanup step anyway (514.2), while the -1/-1 counter stays permanently.

Timing doesn't change the result here: whether the damage was marked before or after Scar resolved, the check is the same and indestructible applies either way. This answer is unaffected by player count — nothing here depends on there being exactly two players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Since The Sentry, Golden Guardian has indestructible, it won't die due to having lethal damage marked on it. Having damage marked on it does not change a creature's toughness, so the -1/-1 counter will not cause it to die due to having 0 toughness, as its toughness is still greater than 0.

entries.question: [Rionya, Fire Dancer] creates a copy of [Humble Defector], which Arlo activates, giving to Nico. Does the token get exiled at the end of the turn?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the token copy is exiled at the beginning of the next end step regardless of who controls it.
entries.answer:
Yes — the token is exiled at the beginning of the next end step, even though Nico now controls it.

Why: Rionya, Fire Dancer's ability creates a delayed triggered ability, "Exile them at the beginning of the next end step." A delayed triggered ability keeps track of the specific objects it refers to; it still affects an object even if that object's characteristics (or here, its controller) change, so long as the object is still in the zone the ability expects — the battlefield [603.7c]. The token copy of Humble Defector never left the battlefield when Arlo activated its ability; only control changed, which doesn't make it a new object [400.7 applies only to zone changes]. So the delayed trigger finds it and exiles it. Once the token is in exile, it ceases to exist the next time state-based actions are checked [111.7], [704.1].

Note also that Rionya, Fire Dancer's delayed trigger is controlled by Arlo (Rionya's controller), not by Nico, so Nico gaining control of the token copy of Humble Defector doesn't change who controls the exile trigger.

Multiplayer wrinkle (Humble Defector requires a "target opponent," so this is at least a two-player situation and often a multiplayer one): if Arlo leaves the game before the end step, the delayed triggered ability that would be controlled by Arlo isn't put onto the stack at all, so the token is never exiled by it [800.4d]. Separately, if Nico (the current controller) leaves the game, the control effect ends and the token would revert to the last player still in the game who controlled it [Humble Defector ruling #3]; if the token's owner Arlo leaves the game, the token — an object owned by Arlo — leaves the game with him [800.4a], [111.2], and a token that has left the battlefield can't come back [111.8].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Arlo activates the token's ability during his own turn (as Humble Defector's ability requires) and before the end step, i.e., before the exile trigger goes on the stack. If instead the trigger has already resolved and exiled the token, activating it is moot — the token is gone and ceases to exist [111.7].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Rionya, Fire Dancer just says "Exile them at the beginning of the next end step." It doesn't care who controls the token at that time.

entries.question: Aubrey casts [Rescue the Foal] targeting their [Hazezon Tamar] in response to its enters-the-battlefield ability. What happens at the beginning of Aubrey's next upkeep?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that two delayed triggers are created and that Aubrey will make two separate batches of Sand Warrior tokens equal to their land count (producing 2X total if the land count is the same).
entries.answer:
At the beginning of Aubrey's next upkeep, two separate delayed triggered abilities go on the stack, and Aubrey creates two batches of X 1/1 red-green-white Sand Warrior tokens (X counted separately for each, equal to the number of lands Aubrey controls at that time) — so 2X tokens total if the land count is the same.

Why:

1. Hazezon Tamar's enters-the-battlefield ability is already on the stack when Rescue the Foal is cast. Rescue the Foal resolves first: it exiles Hazezon Tamar and returns that card to the battlefield. The returned permanent is a brand-new object with no connection to the exiled card (400.7; Pegasus Guardian // Rescue the Foal ruling #4) — any counters cease to exist, Auras go to their owners' graveyards, Equipment unattaches.
2. Because Hazezon Tamar left the battlefield, its second ability, "When Hazezon leaves the battlefield, exile all Sand Warriors," triggers. It only affects Sand Warriors actually on the battlefield when it resolves (Hazezon Tamar ruling #1), so at this point it typically exiles nothing.
3. The new Hazezon Tamar entering the battlefield triggers a fresh copy of its enters ability.
4. The original enters ability (still on the stack) then resolves and creates its delayed triggered ability. A delayed triggered ability is created only on resolution, and it doesn't matter whether Hazezon Tamar is still on the battlefield or who controls it afterward — the player who put it onto the battlefield gets the tokens (603.7a, 603.7c; Hazezon Tamar ruling #0). The new Hazezon Tamar's trigger likewise resolves and creates a second delayed triggered ability.

Both delayed abilities say "at the beginning of your next upkeep," and both were created this turn, so both trigger at Aubrey's next upkeep. Aubrey (the active player) puts both on the stack in the order they choose and resolves them one at a time; each independently counts lands as it resolves.

Timing note: this assumes Rescue the Foal was cast and resolved while the first enters trigger was still on the stack, as stated. If instead Rescue the Foal were cast after that trigger had already resolved, you'd still end up with two delayed abilities (the original one plus the new Hazezon Tamar's), so the upkeep result is the same; only if the exile happened before Hazezon Tamar's ability ever triggered would there be just one.

Multiplayer: no difference. The tokens go to Aubrey either way; the only multiplayer wrinkle is APNAP ordering if several players' triggers wait at the same time (101.4).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Aubrey creates twice as many tokens as the number of lands they control. Hazezon Tamar's enters-the-battlefield ability has resolved twice, creating two instances of the delayed trigger ability creating tokens. One instance of Hazezon Tamar's leaves-the-battlefield ability has resolved, but did not do anything since at that time Aubrey did not control any Sand Warriors.

entries.question: Aubrey controls [Urza's Saga] and it has two lore counters on it. Can they activate Urza's Saga to tap for {C}?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Urza's Saga's chapter I grants it the permanent "{T}: Add {C}" ability, so with two lore counters it can tap for {C}.
entries.answer:
Yes. Urza's Saga can tap for {C}, assuming its chapter I ability already resolved (which it will have, since Urza's Saga entered with one lore counter and now has two).

Why: Urza's Saga's chapter I ability reads "This Saga gains '{T}: Add {C}.'" That's a triggered ability that triggered and resolved when the first lore counter was put on Urza's Saga (rule 107.15/714.2b: "{rN}—[Effect]" means "When one or more lore counters are put onto this Saga, if the number of lore counters on it was less than N and became at least N, [effect]"). The granted ability is not limited to that turn — per Urza's Saga ruling #5, Urza's Saga keeps the abilities granted by chapters I and II for as long as it's on the battlefield. So with two lore counters, Urza's Saga has both "{T}: Add {C}" and the {2}, {T} Construct-token ability.

Practical notes:
- "{T}: Add {C}" produces one colorless mana specifically; it cannot be used as, or replaced by, colored mana, though {C} can of course pay generic costs.
- This is a mana ability, so it doesn't use the stack and can't be responded to.
- Urza's Saga must be untapped and (being a land that entered this turn) is still fine to tap — lands aren't affected by summoning sickness unless they're also creatures.
- Urza's Saga is still a Saga: when the third lore counter arrives and the chapter III ability leaves the stack, the state-based action in 704.5s/714.4 makes Aubrey sacrifice it, so use the mana ability while it's still around.

None of this changes between a two-player and a multiplayer game; lore counters are added during Aubrey's own precombat main phase (rules 505.4, 714.3c, 703.4f) regardless of player count.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. The first chapter ability causes Urza's Saga to gain the ability "{T}: Add {C}.", and nothing is causing it to lose that ability.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Omnath, Locus of Creation] and [Yarok, the Desecrated]. Autumn plays a land. What happens?
entries.reason: Both conclude Yarok causes Omnath's landfall to trigger twice, resulting in Autumn gaining 4 life and adding {R}{G}{W}{U}.
entries.answer:
Playing one land triggers Omnath, Locus of Creation's landfall ability twice, and the two instances resolve as the "first time" and "second time" for the turn: Autumn gains 4 life on the first resolution, and adds {R}{G}{W}{U} on the second.

Why: Yarok, the Desecrated says "If a permanent entering causes a triggered ability of a permanent you control to trigger, that ability triggers an additional time." A land entering is a permanent entering, and Omnath, Locus of Creation's landfall ability is a triggered ability of a permanent Autumn controls, so it triggers twice rather than once [Yarok, the Desecrated ruling #4]. Yarok, the Desecrated doesn't copy the ability — each instance is a separate trigger, with choices made separately [Yarok, the Desecrated ruling #2]. Both instances go on the stack (Autumn chooses the order, though here they're identical) and resolve one at a time [Omnath, Locus of Creation ruling #5].

Omnath, Locus of Creation counts resolutions, not triggers, so the first to resolve gives 4 life and the second adds {R}{G}{W}{U} (one red, one green, one white, and one blue mana — no generic and no {C}). Both instances use the stack and can be responded to; the mana-producing instance is still not a mana ability, because the trigger event (a land entering) isn't a mana ability [Omnath, Locus of Creation ruling #0], so players get priority before it resolves.

If Autumn plays or otherwise puts a second land onto the battlefield that same turn, that also triggers twice; those would be the third and fourth resolutions — the third makes Omnath, Locus of Creation deal 4 damage to each opponent and each planeswalker Autumn doesn't control, and the fourth does nothing [Omnath, Locus of Creation ruling #1]. A landfall trigger happens for any land entering under Autumn's control, not just land drops [Omnath, Locus of Creation ruling #3].

Multiplayer difference: nothing changes for the life gain or the mana. Only the third resolution differs — it hits each opponent for 4 (so every opponent at a multiplayer table, not just one), plus each planeswalker Autumn doesn't control. In Two-Headed Giant, that third resolution makes the opposing team lose 8 life, and every other player's planeswalkers, including a teammate's, are dealt 4 [Omnath, Locus of Creation ruling #2].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yarok, the Desecrated will cause Omnath, Locus of Creation to trigger twice, so Autumn will gain 4 life and add {R}{G}{W}{U}.

entries.question: Aspen controls [Imoti, Celebrant of Bounty] and casts [Apex Devastator]. How many cascade triggers happen?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude there are five separate cascade triggers (four printed on Apex Devastator plus one granted by Imoti), so the candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference.
entries.answer:
Five cascade triggers.

Apex Devastator has four printed instances of cascade, and because its mana value is 10 (6 or greater), Imoti, Celebrant of Bounty gives it a fifth instance of cascade. Each instance triggers separately [702.85c], so casting Apex Devastator puts five separate cascade triggers on the stack.

Each of those five triggers checks against Apex Devastator's own mana value of 10, so each exiles cards from the top of Aspen's library until a nonland card with mana value less than 10 is exiled, and Aspen may cast it without paying its mana cost if the resulting spell's mana value is also less than 10 [702.85a]. Any cascade abilities on the spells cast this way refer to the mana value of the spell that caused them to trigger, not Apex Devastator's [Apex Devastator ruling #0].

Resolution order: the triggers resolve one at a time. The spell cast from the first cascade goes on the stack above the remaining cascade triggers and resolves before Aspen exiles cards for the second, and so on [Apex Devastator ruling #1].

Note also that once Apex Devastator has been cast, removing Imoti, Celebrant of Bounty won't take away that fifth cascade trigger [Imoti, Celebrant of Bounty ruling #0]; only losing control of Imoti, Celebrant of Bounty during the process of casting would stop the spell from gaining cascade [Imoti, Celebrant of Bounty ruling #1].

This count is the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer — cascade only involves Aspen's own library.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 5. Apex Devastator has four plus one granted by Imoti, Celebrant of Bounty. Multiple instances of cascade are not redundant.

entries.question: Nikolas controls [Mindcrank]. Amelia casts [Cruel Tutor]. Will the card Amelia put on top of their library get milled?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Cruel Tutor's life loss happens after the tutored card is placed and Mindcrank triggers after the spell resolves, milling the tutored card.
entries.answer:
Yes — the card Amelia searched up will be milled (along with the next card down).

Why: Cruel Tutor is a single resolving spell. It has Amelia search their library, shuffle, put the found card on top, and then lose 2 life — all during that one resolution [608.1]. Because the shuffle and the "put that card on top" instruction happen together, the result is a randomized library except that the tutored card is in the specified position, on top [701.24g]. The life loss happens after that, so by the time Mindcrank's ability triggers, the tutored card is already sitting on top.

Mindcrank's ability ("Whenever an opponent loses life, that player mills that many cards") is a triggered ability. It doesn't resolve in the middle of Cruel Tutor; it goes on the stack after Cruel Tutor finishes resolving and resolves separately [608.1]. When it resolves, Amelia mills 2 cards from the top of their library — the first of which is the card Cruel Tutor put there. Nikolas may then see it, since a milled card can be found in the public zone it moved to (Amelia's graveyard) [701.17c].

Assumption on timing: I'm reading the sequence as written on Cruel Tutor (search/shuffle/put on top, then lose life). That order is fixed by the card's text, so there's no alternate ordering here — the tutored card can't dodge the mill unless Amelia does something in response to the Mindcrank trigger (for example, drawing the card) before the trigger resolves.

Multiplayer note: this works the same at any table size. Mindcrank triggers on life loss by an opponent of Nikolas, so if a third player also lost life, Mindcrank would trigger separately for each of them; a player losing life who is not Nikolas's opponent (i.e., Nikolas himself) wouldn't trigger it.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Mindcrank triggers during the resolution of Cruel Tutor and will be put onto the stack after Cruel Tutor finishes resolving. (Amelia can cast an instant before the trigger resolves.)

entries.question: Alessandro attacks with [Territorial Kavu]. There are no cards in any player's graveyard. Can Alessandro choose to use the second mode of Territorial Kavu's triggered ability?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Alessandro may choose the second mode and legally choose zero targets ("up to one") so the ability can be put on the stack even with all graveyards empty.
entries.answer:
Yes. Alessandro can choose the second mode of Territorial Kavu's attack trigger even with all graveyards empty.

That mode reads "Exile up to one target card from a graveyard." Because it says "up to one" target, choosing zero targets is a legal choice, so the mode isn't illegal for lack of targets. The controller of a modal triggered ability chooses the mode as the ability is put on the stack, and a mode can't be chosen only if it would be illegal — for example, if it required a target and no legal target existed [603.3c] [700.2b] [700.2a]. Targets are announced as part of putting the trigger on the stack, and with a variable number of targets the player announces how many they'll choose — here, zero [603.3d] [601.2c].

On resolution, Territorial Kavu's ability simply does nothing, since there is no card to exile [608.2d]. Note also that once the mode is chosen it's locked in; effects that change targets can't change the mode [115.8].

This works identically in two-player and multiplayer games — "a graveyard" includes every player's graveyard, and in a multiplayer game you'd still be free to pick zero targets even if some opponent's graveyard later filled up.

entries.question: Adriel currently controls Nico's commander. Can Adriel cast [Deadly Rollick] for its alternative cost?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Adriel can pay the alternative cost because they control a commander permanent (even if it’s Nico’s).
entries.answer:
Yes. Adriel can cast Deadly Rollick without paying its mana cost. Deadly Rollick's alternative cost condition is "If you control a commander" — it doesn't say "your commander," so any commander permanent Adriel controls satisfies it, including Nico's commander that Adriel has gained control of.

Why: rule 903.3d says that when an effect refers to controlling a commander, it refers to a permanent on the battlefield that is a commander — being a commander is an attribute of the card that follows it between zones, independent of who currently controls the permanent. "You" on Deadly Rollick means its would-be controller, i.e., Adriel while casting it (109.5, You/Your). So the check is purely "does Adriel control a permanent that is a commander," and Nico's commander under Adriel's control answers yes.

Mechanics of the cast: Adriel announces the intent to use the alternative cost as part of proposing the spell (118.9a, 601.2b), and the total cost is then locked in (601.2f). Per Deadly Rollick ruling #1, once Adriel begins casting it, no other player can respond — Nico can't try to take back or remove the commander mid-cast to force Adriel to pay {3}{B}. Note the condition is only checked as the spell is cast; if the commander leaves Adriel's control afterward, the already-cast Deadly Rollick still resolves and exiles the target creature.

Multiplayer: this works identically at any table size — the rule and the card care only about whether the caster controls a commander permanent, not about how many opponents there are. (Control-changing situations like this are also common in Commander, which is typically multiplayer.)

entries.answer_gold: Yes. Deadly Rollick alternative cost works if Adriel controls any commander, not necessarily theirs.

entries.question: Ashley attacks Natalie with [Frenzied Raptor] and [Knight Errant]. Can Natalie block Frenzied Raptor with [Ogre Resister], cast [Displace] targeting Ogre Resister, then block Knight Errant with Ogre Resister too?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that blockers are declared only once in the declare blockers step and that exiling and returning Ogre Resister with Displace removes it from combat but does not allow it to be declared as a blocker again against Knight Errant.
entries.answer:
No. Once blockers are declared, Natalie can't re-declare Ogre Resister as a blocker, and casting Displace on Ogre Resister only removes it from combat entirely.

Here's the sequence:

1. In the declare blockers step Natalie declares Ogre Resister as a blocker for Frenzied Raptor. Ogre Resister becomes a blocking creature and Frenzied Raptor becomes a blocked creature [509.1g] [509.1h].
2. Natalie then casts Displace targeting Ogre Resister. Displace exiles Ogre Resister and returns it to the battlefield. Leaving the battlefield removes Ogre Resister from combat, so it stops being a blocking creature [506.4] [506.4a]. The card that returns is a brand-new object, and nothing about Displace says it enters blocking, so it is simply on the battlefield doing nothing in combat.
3. There is no second declaration of blockers. Blocking is a turn-based action that happens once, at the start of the declare blockers step [509.1h] [Declare Blockers]. Only an effect that specifically puts a creature onto the battlefield blocking could make a creature block outside that declaration [509.4a] [509.4b], and Displace is not such an effect — it just returns the creature to the battlefield.

Results for combat damage:
- Frenzied Raptor stays a blocked creature even though the only creature blocking it is gone [509.1h]. Because no creature is currently blocking it, Frenzied Raptor assigns no combat damage at all — it does not hit Natalie [510.1c].
- Ogre Resister, no longer blocking anything, assigns no combat damage [510.1d].
- Knight Errant was never blocked, so it deals its 2 damage to Natalie.

So the Displace trick does "fog" Frenzied Raptor's 4 damage, but it cannot redirect Ogre Resister onto Knight Errant.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming Displace is cast after blockers are declared (as described). If Natalie instead cast Displace before the declare blockers step, Ogre Resister would return as a new object and could be declared as a blocker normally — but still only against one attacker per declaration unless it had an ability letting it block additional creatures.

Multiplayer note: this answer doesn't depend on the player count — Natalie is the defending player either way. The only variant provided that changes blocking is the shared team turns option, where a defending team makes one combined block covering all its players' attackers [805.10d]; even there, blockers are still declared only once.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Declaring blockers is a turn-based action at the beginning of the declare blockers step.. All blockers are declared at the same time, and additional blockers can't be declared after this point. By the time Natalie could cast Displace, the opportunity to declare blockers has already passed, so Ogre Resister wouldn't be able to block an additional creature.

entries.question: Ari controls [Chronicle of Victory] and the chosen creature type is Insect. When Ari casts [Grist, the Hunger Tide], will it trigger Chronicle of Victory?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference — Grist is an Insect while on the stack, so casting it will trigger Chronicle of Victory.
entries.answer:
Yes. Chronicle of Victory's third ability triggers and Ari draws a card.

Chronicle of Victory reads "Whenever you cast a spell of the chosen type, draw a card," and the chosen type here is Insect. While Grist, the Hunger Tide is anywhere other than the battlefield — including on the stack as a spell being cast — its own static ability makes it a 1/1 Insect creature in addition to its other types, so the spell is a Legendary Planeswalker Creature — Grist Insect [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #3]. That satisfies Chronicle of Victory's trigger condition at the time Grist, the Hunger Tide is cast.

Note what does *not* happen: once Grist, the Hunger Tide resolves and is on the battlefield it stops being a creature and is only a planeswalker [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #3], so it never gets the +2/+2, first strike, and trample from Chronicle of Victory's second ability. The draw trigger already happened on cast and is unaffected by that later change.

Also, the type choice for Chronicle of Victory was locked in as it entered the battlefield, and players can't act between that choice and the effect applying [Chronicle of Victory ruling #2]; here it's already set to Insect.

This works the same at any table size — Chronicle of Victory only cares about spells Ari casts, so player count doesn't change the outcome.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. Grist, the Hunger Tide states that it's an Insect creature when not on the battlefield, which includes the stack.

entries.question: Angela attacks with [Mons's Goblin Raiders]. Nico blocks with [Pikemen]. Angela uses [Armored Guardian] to give Mons's Goblin Raiders protection from white. What happens?
entries.reason: Both conclude the block stands and Mons's Goblin Raiders deals its damage to Pikemen while all damage from the white Pikemen is prevented by protection from white.
entries.answer:
Mons's Goblin Raiders stays blocked by Pikemen; protection from white does not undo the block. It just means Pikemen's combat damage to Mons's Goblin Raiders is prevented.

Details:
- Protection from white gives Mons's Goblin Raiders, among other things, the evasion restriction that white creatures can't block it — but that restriction only matters at the moment blockers are declared. Once Pikemen has been declared as a blocker, gaining or losing an evasion ability afterward doesn't affect that block [509.1b]. Nothing here removes Pikemen from combat either [506.4, 506.4a], and a blocked creature stays blocked until removed from combat or end of combat [509.1h].
- So Mons's Goblin Raiders is still a blocked creature and will deal no damage to Nico.
- In the combat damage step, Pikemen has first strike and would deal 1 damage first, but Pikemen is a white source, and protection from white prevents damage from white sources [702.16f, 609.7b]. That damage is prevented, so Mons's Goblin Raiders survives.
- Mons's Goblin Raiders then deals its 1 damage in the regular damage step to Pikemen (a 1/1), destroying it. Because Pikemen has banding, its controller Nico divides the damage of the creature it's blocking; with Pikemen as the only blocker, all 1 damage goes to Pikemen anyway (per Pikemen's own text).
- Costs note: Armored Guardian's ability costs {1}{W}{W} — one generic plus two white specifically.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Armored Guardian's ability resolved after blockers were declared, as stated. If instead it resolved before the declare blockers step, Nico simply couldn't legally declare Pikemen (a white creature) as a blocker for Mons's Goblin Raiders [702.16f, 509.1b], and Mons's Goblin Raiders would be unblocked.

This works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table; only the one defending player who controls Pikemen is involved [509.1g].

entries.answer_gold: Mons's Goblin Raiders will deal combat damage to Pikemen but Pikemen will not deal any damage to Mons's Goblin Raiders. Because Mons's Goblin Raiders gained protection from white, all damage from white sources will be prevented.

entries.question: Arya casts [Force of Despair] for its alternative cost, exiling [Gibbering Descent] from their hand. Can they then cast Gibbering Descent for madness?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Force of Despair's alternative cost exiles the card rather than discarding it, so madness does not apply and Gibbering Descent cannot be cast for madness.
entries.answer:
No. Arya cannot cast Gibbering Descent for its madness cost in this situation.

Why: Madness is a keyword with two parts — a static ability that replaces a discard ("If a player would discard this card, that player discards it, but exiles it instead of putting it into their graveyard") and a triggered ability that fires "when this card is exiled this way," letting the owner cast it for the madness cost ([702.35a]). The trigger is strictly keyed to the card being *discarded*; madness works regardless of why the discard happens (cost, spell instruction, cleanup-step hand size), but there must be a discard ([Gibbering Descent ruling #8]).

Force of Despair's alternative cost is "you may exile a black card from your hand rather than pay this spell's mana cost." That's an exile, not a discard, so Gibbering Descent's madness replacement effect never applies and no madness trigger is created. Gibbering Descent simply sits in exile with no permission to cast it. Applying that alternative cost is legal and normal ([601.2b], [601.2f], [113.2b]) — it just doesn't turn on madness.

Note also that even if madness had triggered, madness is a one-shot window: if the card isn't cast when the trigger resolves it goes to the graveyard and you don't get another chance ([Gibbering Descent ruling #1]).

This answer doesn't depend on player count — it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table. (Force of Despair's alternative cost does require it not to be your turn, which just means Arya is casting it during some other player's turn; with more than two players, any opponent's turn works.)

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Madness only applies to discarding the card, not exiling it.

entries.question: Alejandro controls [Archon of Sun's Grace] and casts [Thassa's Emissary]. Do they make a token?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference: Thassa's Emissary entering as an enchantment creature triggers Archon of Sun's Grace and creates the 2/2 Pegasus token.
entries.answer:
Yes — Alejandro creates a 2/2 white Pegasus creature token with flying.

Archon of Sun's Grace has the Constellation ability "Whenever an enchantment you control enters, create a 2/2 white Pegasus creature token with flying." Thassa's Emissary is an Enchantment Creature — Crab, so when the Thassa's Emissary spell resolves and its controller puts it onto the battlefield (rule 303.2), an enchantment Alejandro controls has entered the battlefield. Enters-the-battlefield triggers are checked against all permanents already on the battlefield, including Archon of Sun's Grace, when the event happens (rule 603.6a), so Constellation triggers and goes on the stack.

This holds whether Thassa's Emissary is cast for its normal {3}{U} cost as an enchantment creature, or for its bestow cost of {5}{U} as an Aura spell — an Aura is still an enchantment, and it enters the battlefield attached to the enchanted creature (rules 303.4, 303.4a), which still satisfies "an enchantment you control enters."

The token is created by the triggered ability resolving, so it appears after Thassa's Emissary is already on the battlefield; anyone can respond to the Constellation trigger before it resolves. Note also that Archon of Sun's Grace gives Pegasus creatures you control lifelink, so the new token has flying and lifelink.

This answer doesn't depend on player count — it works identically in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table, since the trigger only cares about enchantments Alejandro controls.
