entries.answer_gold: Yes. Archon of Sun's Grace's ability triggers if any enchantment enters the battlefield. It doesn't matter if that enchantment is also a creature.

entries.question: Avery casts [Screamreach Brawler] for its Dash cost, and attacks. Norah casts [Turn Against] to take control of Screamreach Brawler. What happens at the end of Avery's turn?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same ruling: the Dash delayed trigger returns Screamreach Brawler to its owner's (Avery's) hand at the beginning of the end step even if Norah controls it.
entries.answer:
Screamreach Brawler is returned to Avery's hand at the beginning of the end step, even though Norah controls it at that moment.

Why: Dash gives the spell a delayed triggered ability, "If this spell's dash cost was paid, return the permanent this spell becomes to its owner's hand at the beginning of the next end step" [702.109a]. That delayed trigger is controlled by Avery and refers to a specific object; it still affects Screamreach Brawler even though its characteristics or controller have changed, as long as the permanent is still on the battlefield when the ability resolves [603.7c] [Screamreach Brawler ruling #0]. Gaining control does not change ownership — Avery owns the card [110.2b] — and a card that would go to a hand other than its owner's goes to its owner's hand instead [400.3]. So it goes to Avery's hand, not Norah's.

Timing note: Turn Against's control effect lasts "until end of turn," which ends during the cleanup step — after the end step. So the dash trigger resolves while Norah still controls Screamreach Brawler, and the card leaves the battlefield before Turn Against's effect would have ended. (Had Screamreach Brawler died or otherwise left the battlefield before the end step, the dash trigger would do nothing [Screamreach Brawler ruling #0] [603.7c].)

Also note Screamreach Brawler had haste from dash while Avery controlled it [702.109a], and Turn Against separately untaps it and gives it haste until end of turn.

Multiplayer: the answer is the same with more than two players — the card returns to its owner Avery's hand regardless of who gained control [400.3] [110.2b]. One extra wrinkle exists only in multiplayer: if the player who controlled the permanent by default had left the game and a control effect ended, the object would be exiled instead [800.4c], but that doesn't apply here since Avery is still in the game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Screamreach Brawler will be returned to Avery's hand at the beginning of their end step. ([702.109a]) Screamreach Brawler's Dash ability creates a delayed trigger that will go on the stack at the beginning of the next end step, it doesn't matter who controls the creature at that point.

entries.question: Angelique casts [Poison the Waters] targeting Nico. Can they choose [Grist, the Hunger Tide] from Nico's hand?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Grist is a creature in hand due to its static ability and thus can be chosen by Poison the Waters' second mode.
entries.answer:
Yes. In Nico's hand, Grist, the Hunger Tide is a creature card, so Angelique can choose it with Poison the Waters' second mode and Nico must discard it.

Why: Grist, the Hunger Tide's own text says "As long as Grist isn't on the battlefield, it's a 1/1 Insect creature in addition to its other types." That card text overrides the general expectation that a planeswalker card is only a planeswalker: anywhere other than the battlefield (including hand), it is a Legendary Planeswalker Creature — Grist Insect [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #3]. Poison the Waters' second mode lets you "choose an artifact or creature card" from the revealed hand, and Grist, the Hunger Tide qualifies as a creature card there.

Assumptions and details:
- Angelique must have chosen the second mode ("Target player reveals their hand...") when casting Poison the Waters; modes are chosen as the spell is put on the stack and can't be changed later [700.2, 700.2e, 115.8]. If Angelique instead chose the first mode (all creatures get -1/-1), there is no target player and no discard at all — that mode only affects creatures on the battlefield, and Grist, the Hunger Tide in hand is untouched.
- Only Nico is targeted by Poison the Waters; the card chosen from hand is not a target, it's chosen on resolution by Angelique [115.1, 115.10, 115.10a, 608.1].
- Because Poison the Waters targets an opponent, casting it is a crime for Angelique [700.13, Crime].
- Multiplayer: nothing changes. "Target player" can be any player at the table, so in a game with more than two players Angelique simply picks Nico as that target; the only special case is the optional limited range of influence variant, where a chosen player must be within Angelique's range of influence [801.5a].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Grist, the Hunger Tide's first ability makes it a creature while in all zones other than the battlefield, including the hand.

entries.question: Augustine casts [Energy Tap] targeting their [Aclazotz, Deepest Betrayal]. Unfortunately, Aclazotz, Deepest Betrayal dies before Energy Tap resolves. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Energy Tap does nothing and Augustine gets no mana because its only target died and the spell is removed from the stack as an illegal-target situation.
entries.answer:
Energy Tap doesn't resolve at all. Aclazotz, Deepest Betrayal was Energy Tap's only target, and when Aclazotz, Deepest Betrayal dies it leaves the battlefield — a target that's no longer in the zone it was in when it was targeted is an illegal target [608.2b, Illegal Target]. Since every instance of the word "target" on Energy Tap is now illegal, Energy Tap is removed from the stack and put into Augustine's graveyard without any of its effects happening [608.2b, 608.2n]. Augustine taps nothing and adds no mana — not even one {C}. (Had it resolved on a legal Aclazotz, Deepest Betrayal, it would have added five {C}, matching that card's mana value of 5; {C} is colorless mana specifically, not generic.)

Note the death trigger: "When Aclazotz dies, return it to the battlefield tapped and transformed" brings it back as Temple of the Dead. That returned permanent is a new object and is not the thing Energy Tap targeted, so it can't rescue the spell — and it's a land, not an untapped creature you control, so it wouldn't be a legal target anyway. Also, nothing here lets Augustine retarget: effects that change targets are separate effects, and a target can only be changed to another legal target [115.7a].

This outcome is identical in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; the rule about illegal targets doesn't depend on the number of players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Augustine won't get any colorless mana. If a spell lacks targets when it goes to resolve, it won't do anything.

entries.question: Antoine controls [Aang and La, Ocean's Fury] and [Embodiment of Insight]. Does Aang and La, Ocean's Fury have vigilance?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Aang and La is not a land creature and therefore does not gain vigilance from Embodiment of Insight's static ability.
entries.answer:
No. Aang and La, Ocean's Fury does not have vigilance.

Embodiment of Insight's own vigilance is a printed ability of Embodiment of Insight only; it doesn't spread to your other creatures. Its second ability, "Land creatures you control have vigilance," is a static ability generating a continuous effect that applies at any given moment to whatever its text indicates (CR 611.3a/611.3b, 604.1, 113.3d) — namely permanents you control that are both lands and creatures. Aang and La, Ocean's Fury is a Legendary Creature — Avatar Spirit Ally with no land type, so it is not a "land creature" and is not in the set of objects that effect applies to. Aang and La, Ocean's Fury therefore has only reach and trample (plus whatever else grants it abilities).

If Embodiment of Insight's landfall trigger animates one of your lands into a 3/3 Elemental creature that's still a land, that land immediately becomes a land creature and picks up vigilance from the static ability (CR 611.3a) — but that has no bearing on Aang and La, Ocean's Fury.

This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games; the effect is limited to lands their controller (Antoine) controls, regardless of the number of players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. "Land creature" refers to a creature that's also a land, not a creature that doesn't have flying.

entries.question: Nico casts [Ashcoat Bear] before blockers are declared. Can Aron use [Kytheon's Irregulars]'s ability to tap Ashcoat Bear before it can be declared as a blocker?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Aron can tap Ashcoat Bear with Kytheon's Irregulars before blockers are declared (players get priority after the spell resolves and before the declare blockers step), preventing it from being declared as a blocker.
entries.answer:
Yes. If Aron activates Kytheon's Irregulars's ability ({W}{W}: Tap target creature) targeting Ashcoat Bear and it resolves before the declare blockers step begins, Ashcoat Bear will be tapped and therefore cannot be declared as a blocker: when the defending player declares blockers, the creatures chosen must be untapped (and can't be battles) [509.1a].

Details and timing:
- Ashcoat Bear has flash, so Nico can cast it any time he could cast an instant; assume it resolved and is on the battlefield untapped before the declare blockers step.
- Kytheon's Irregulars's ability costs only {W}{W} — that's two white mana specifically, not generic — and has no {T} in its cost, so the "summoning sickness" restriction of rule [602.5a] doesn't apply to activating it even if Kytheon's Irregulars just came under Aron's control.
- Windows: Aron can activate it during the declare attackers step (or the beginning of combat step) while players have priority. As long as the ability resolves before the declare blockers step's turn-based action of declaring blockers — which doesn't use the stack — Ashcoat Bear is locked out of blocking [509.1].
- If Aron instead waits and taps Ashcoat Bear after it has already been declared as a blocker, it's too late: tapping a creature already declared as an attacker or blocker doesn't remove it from combat and doesn't prevent its combat damage [506.4b], and effects that would have kept a creature from blocking don't remove it from combat once it's blocking [506.4a].
- Note Ashcoat Bear must be blocking a creature attacking Aron (or a planeswalker/battle Aron controls or protects) in the first place [509.1a] — i.e., Nico would need to be the defending player against Aron's attack for this to matter.

Multiplayer: the rules given here work the same with more than two players — blockers are declared by each defending player for creatures attacking them, so tapping Ashcoat Bear before the declare blockers step still stops it from blocking. One exception in the provided rules: under the shared team turns option, the defending team makes one combined block, but the same untapped requirement of [509.1a] applies [805.10d].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. If Nico made no indication they were going to declare blockers, then it's likely they were casting Ashcoat Bear in the declare attackers step. After it resolves both players will get priority before the declare blockers step.

entries.question: Alberto controls a tapped [Kalamax, the Stormsire] and casts [Teach by Example]. After that resolves they cast [Soul Partition]. How many +1/+1 counters will Kalamax, the Stormsire get, and how many Soul Partitions will Alberto get?
entries.reason: Both conclude Kalamax gets three +1/+1 counters and Alberto ends up with three Soul Partition spells total (the original plus two copies).
entries.answer:
Kalamax, the Stormsire ends up with 3 +1/+1 counters, and Alberto gets 3 total Soul Partition resolutions (the original plus 2 copies).

Step by step:

1. Teach by Example is Alberto's first instant spell of the turn and Kalamax, the Stormsire is tapped, so Kalamax, the Stormsire's first ability triggers and copies Teach by Example. That copy is put on the stack, is itself a spell, and isn't cast [707.10b, 112.1a]. Because an instant spell was copied, Kalamax, the Stormsire's second ability triggers once — counter #1.
2. The copy of Teach by Example and the original Teach by Example both resolve. Each sets up its own delayed trigger: "When you next cast an instant or sorcery spell this turn, copy that spell." So Alberto has two such pending effects.
3. Alberto casts Soul Partition. This is his second instant of the turn, so Kalamax, the Stormsire's first ability does not trigger again. But both Teach by Example delayed triggers trigger, and each one copies Soul Partition — 2 copies on the stack, and Alberto may choose new targets for each [707.10b].
4. Kalamax, the Stormsire's second ability triggers once per copy event, so it triggers twice more — counters #2 and #3. (Compare Kalamax, the Stormsire ruling #3: if an effect copies an instant multiple times, the last ability triggers that many times.)

So: 3 counters (Kalamax, the Stormsire becomes 7/7 if it started 4/4), and 3 Soul Partition effects — up to three different nonland permanents exiled, since each copy can be given a new target.

Timing note: I'm assuming, as stated, that Teach by Example and its copy both fully resolved before Soul Partition was cast. If Soul Partition were somehow cast before those resolved, the delayed triggers wouldn't exist yet and it wouldn't be copied at all.

Player count doesn't change any of this — nothing here references opponents or a defending player, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table (only who you may target with the copies of Soul Partition differs).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Alberto will get a total of three Soul Partitions (the original and three copies), and Kalamax, the Stormsire will get three +1/+1 counters. (One for copying Teach by Example, and two for the two copies of Soul Partition.)

entries.question: Anderson controls [The Ozolith] and [Gideon Jura], which has 5 loyalty counters on it. They use Gideon Jura's ability to turn it into creature, and then it dies. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling that The Ozolith ends up with Gideon Jura's five loyalty counters (assuming they were still on him when he left), matching the reference.
entries.answer:
The Ozolith's first ability triggers and Anderson puts five loyalty counters on The Ozolith.

Why: Gideon Jura's 0 ability makes Gideon Jura "a 6/6 Human Soldier creature that's still a planeswalker," so while that effect lasts Gideon Jura is a creature Anderson controls. When Gideon Jura leaves the battlefield having counters on it, The Ozolith's trigger condition is met. Loyalty counters are counters like any other (122.1e, 306.5c), so they qualify.

How many and which counters: The Ozolith doesn't literally move counters off Gideon Jura — Gideon Jura's counters ceased to exist when it changed zones (122.2, 400.7). Instead Anderson puts the same number of each kind of counter Gideon Jura had onto The Ozolith (122.8, The Ozolith ruling #3). That count is taken from Gideon Jura's last known information on the battlefield (704.8). So if Gideon Jura still had 5 loyalty counters when it left, The Ozolith gets 5 loyalty counters.

Important timing caveat: I'm assuming Gideon Jura died to something other than loss of loyalty — e.g., it was destroyed by lethal damage marked on it as a creature, or by a destroy/sacrifice effect — while still having 5 loyalty counters. If instead Gideon Jura went to the graveyard because its loyalty hit 0 (damage removes loyalty counters, 306.8/120.3c, and a planeswalker with 0 loyalty is put into the graveyard as a state-based action, 704.5i/306.9), then it had no counters when it left and The Ozolith's ability does nothing (it has an intervening "if it had counters on it" clause). Note also that Gideon Jura's own 0 ability prevents all damage to him that turn, so damage-based loyalty loss generally won't happen that turn (see Gideon Jura ruling #0 for unpreventable damage).

What the counters do on The Ozolith: nothing, in practice. Loyalty is a characteristic only planeswalkers have (306.5), and The Ozolith is a Legendary Artifact, not a planeswalker, so loyalty counters sitting on it have no effect (compare The Ozolith ruling #1). At the beginning of combat on Anderson's turn, The Ozolith's second ability triggers and Anderson may move all counters onto a target creature — but loyalty counters on an ordinary creature likewise do nothing unless that permanent is a planeswalker.

Player count doesn't change any of this; the rules cited apply the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Anderson will move the loyalty counters from Gideon Jura onto The Ozolith. The Ozolith doesn't have any restrictions on the kind of counters that can be placed on it.

entries.question: Ariel casts [Forfend], casts [Anhelo, the Painter]. If Ariel then casts another Forfend, will it have casualty 2?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the second Forfend won't have casualty 2 because Anhelo only grants casualty to the first instant or sorcery you cast each turn.
entries.answer:
No. The second Forfend will not have casualty 2.

Anhelo, the Painter grants casualty 2 only to "the first instant or sorcery spell you cast each turn." That wording looks back at what Ariel has already cast this turn, and it doesn't require Anhelo, the Painter to have been on the battlefield at the time. Ariel's first Forfend was the first instant or sorcery spell cast this turn, so the second Forfend is the second such spell and gets nothing from Anhelo, the Painter. Effects that ask the game for information about earlier actions this turn count those actions even though the relevant objects/permanents weren't in the same state (or on the battlefield) at that time [608.2i].

Note also that even if Anhelo, the Painter had somehow applied, it couldn't have retroactively changed the first Forfend, since casting something that alters costs doesn't affect spells already on the stack [601.8].

For completeness, casualty 2 would mean: as an additional cost to cast the spell, you may sacrifice a creature with power 2 or greater; if you do, a triggered ability copies the spell (and the copy resolves first) [702.153a] [Anhelo, the Painter ruling #3] [Anhelo, the Painter ruling #0]. Forfend's cost stays {1}{W} either way — casualty is a sacrifice cost, not a mana cost change.

This answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. It's the second instant or sorcery spell Ariel cast this turn, not the first.

entries.question: Azariah attacks with a [Barrage Tyrant] and Nico blocks with a [Kor Firewalker]. Does the Kor Firewalker die?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same ruling—that Barrage Tyrant's devoid makes it colorless (not red), so Kor Firewalker's protection from red doesn't apply and it dies in combat.
entries.answer:
Yes — Kor Firewalker dies. Barrage Tyrant has devoid, so its printed text states "This card has no color"; Barrage Tyrant is a colorless creature, not a red one. Kor Firewalker's protection from red therefore does nothing against Barrage Tyrant's combat damage.

In the combat damage step, each attacking and blocking creature deals combat damage equal to its power [120.2a]. Neither creature has first strike or double strike, so there is a single combat damage step and both assign damage at the same time [506.1], [510.1], and all of it is dealt simultaneously with no chance to respond in between [510.2], [703.4k], [703.4m]. Barrage Tyrant (5/3) assigns 5 damage to Kor Firewalker (2/2), which is lethal, and Kor Firewalker assigns 2 damage to Barrage Tyrant, which is not enough to destroy its 3 toughness. Result: Kor Firewalker is destroyed, Barrage Tyrant survives with 2 damage marked.

Note this is purely a blocking/damage interaction and doesn't depend on the number of players at the table; it works the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game (Nico is simply the defending player or a creature controlled by a defending player).

Separately, Barrage Tyrant's activated ability ({2}{R}, Sacrifice another colorless creature) also deals damage from Barrage Tyrant itself, not from the sacrificed creature [Barrage Tyrant ruling #1] — and that damage would likewise not be stopped by protection from red, since the source, Barrage Tyrant, is colorless. Kor Firewalker's second ability triggers on a player casting a red spell; Barrage Tyrant is colorless, so casting Barrage Tyrant would not trigger it.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Devoid is a keyword that means "this card has no color". Kor Firewalker doesn't have protection from the Barrage Tyrant.

entries.question: Both Augustus and Nico control a [Thraben Purebloods]. Nico casts [Unholy Hunger] targeting Augustus's Thraben Purebloods and in response Augustus casts [Unified Will] targeting Unholy Hunger. What happens?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling that Unified Will does not counter Unholy Hunger on a tie (so it does nothing) and Unholy Hunger then resolves and destroys Thraben Purebloods.
entries.answer:
Unified Will resolves first and does nothing, then Unholy Hunger resolves and destroys Augustus's Thraben Purebloods.

Why: Unified Will only counters the target spell "if you control more creatures than that spell's controller," and that comparison is checked only as Unified Will resolves ([Unified Will ruling #0]). At that moment Augustus controls one creature (his Thraben Purebloods) and Nico controls one creature (Nico's Thraben Purebloods). That's equal, not more, so Unified Will simply has no effect; Unholy Hunger is not countered and stays on the stack. (Countering would have removed it from the stack without any of its effects — see rule 701.6a.)

Unholy Hunger then resolves. Its target, Augustus's Thraben Purebloods, is still a legal target (still on the battlefield, still a creature), so the spell resolves and destroys it (608.2b). Nico also gains 2 life if there are two or more instant and/or sorcery cards in Nico's graveyard when Unholy Hunger resolves (spell mastery); note Unholy Hunger itself is still on the stack at that time and doesn't count.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming no other creatures enter or leave before Unified Will resolves. If Augustus gets a second creature (or Nico loses his Thraben Purebloods) before Unified Will resolves, Augustus would then control more creatures and Unified Will would counter Unholy Hunger, putting it into Nico's graveyard, and Augustus's Thraben Purebloods would survive.

This analysis doesn't depend on the number of players — Unified Will compares only its controller's creature count to the targeted spell's controller's creature count, so it works identically at a two-player or multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Unified Will resolves and does nothing. Unified Will checks on resolution to see if Augustus controls more creatures than Nico, and since a tie isn't "more than" it does not counter Unholy Hunger.

entries.question: In a Commander game, how much life does each player begin the game with?
entries.reason: The candidate states each player starts at 40 life in Commander, matching the reference's correct ruling.
entries.answer:
Each player begins a Commander game with a starting life total of 40 [103.4c] [119.1c]. This is one of the Commander variant's additions to the normal rules, which otherwise default to a 20-life start [103.4]. Mechanically, once the starting player has been determined, each player sets their life total to 40 and draws a hand of seven cards [903.7].

This applies regardless of the number of players \or a multiplayer table \u2014 Commander games are commonly multiplayer, and every player individually starts at 40; there is no shared life total. Note two related variants in the provided rules: under the Brawl option, starting life is 25 in a two-player game and 30 in a multiplayer game [903.12f], and under the Archenemy Commander option the archenemy starts at 60 life while the opposing team shares a 60-life total [904.13b].

entries.question: Andrew attacks with [Caravan Hurda] that's enchanted with [Spirit Link]. How much life will they gain?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Andrew gains two life total: one from Caravan Hurda's lifelink (damage event) and one from Spirit Link's triggered ability.
entries.answer:
Andrew gains 2 life total — 1 from Caravan Hurda's lifelink and 1 more from Spirit Link's triggered ability (assuming Andrew controls the Spirit Link; the Aura's controller is who gains that life). These are two separate life-gain events, not one gain of 2.

Why: Caravan Hurda is a 1/5, so it deals 1 combat damage (whether it's unblocked and hits a defending player, or is blocked and deals its damage to a blocking creature — the amount is the same). Lifelink means damage dealt by that source causes its controller to gain that much life in addition to the damage's normal results [702.15b, 120.3f], so Andrew gains 1 as part of the damage event itself, with no trigger and no chance to respond [120.4c, 120.4d].

Spirit Link reads "Whenever enchanted creature deals damage, you gain that much life." That's a separate triggered ability that goes on the stack and can be responded to [Spirit Link ruling #1], so its 1 life arrives later, after the combat damage step's triggers resolve. Because the lifelink gain and the Spirit Link gain are distinct life-gain events, any "whenever you gain life" trigger Andrew controls would trigger twice [702.15e, 119.9, 119.3].

If Caravan Hurda's damage is somehow prevented or reduced to 0, no life gain occurs from either source [119.9]. If Andrew's life total would hit 0 from simultaneous damage, the lifelink life is gained as part of the same damage event, but Spirit Link's life comes too late to save him [Spirit Link ruling #1].

This works the same in a two-player or multiplayer game; the number of opponents doesn't change the amount, only which player or creature is dealt the 1 damage.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Two life. Andrew will gain one life from Spirit Link's keyword ability, and one life from Caravan Hurda's triggered ability.

entries.question: Alex controls [Soul-Scar Mage] and casts [Puncturing Blow] targeting Natalia's [Elvish Ranger]. What zone does it move to?
entries.reason: Both conclude the Elvish Ranger is exiled because Puncturing Blow's replacement effect applies to the creature "would die" event even though Soul-Scar Mage replaced the damage with -1/-1 counters.
entries.answer:
Elvish Ranger goes to exile, not to Natalia's graveyard.

Step by step:

1. Puncturing Blow would deal 5 noncombat damage to Elvish Ranger. Soul-Scar Mage's static ability is a replacement effect (rule 614.1): "If a source you control would deal noncombat damage to a creature an opponent controls, put that many -1/-1 counters on that creature instead." Since Alex controls both Soul-Scar Mage and the source (Puncturing Blow), and Elvish Ranger is controlled by an opponent, no damage is dealt at all — instead Elvish Ranger gets five -1/-1 counters. (Per Soul-Scar Mage ruling #1, this is a replacement, not a prevention effect.)

2. Elvish Ranger is 4/1, so with five -1/-1 counters it becomes -1/-4. Its toughness is 0 or less, so the next time state-based actions are checked it is put into its owner's graveyard (rule 704.5f). Note this is the toughness-0 state-based action, not the lethal-damage one (rule 704.5g) — no damage was marked, and regeneration cannot replace it. State-based actions happen automatically before any player would receive priority (rules 704.1, 117.2d).

3. However, Puncturing Blow's own text says "If that creature would die this turn, exile it instead." Dying means moving to the graveyard, so that move event is replaced and Elvish Ranger is exiled instead. Puncturing Blow ruling #0 states explicitly that this replacement applies if the creature would die this turn for any reason — not just from lethal damage — and applies even if Puncturing Blow dealt it no damage. Here the card text overrides the ordinary outcome of the state-based action, which would otherwise send Elvish Ranger to the graveyard.

So the final zone is exile. This works the same regardless of the number of players at the table; nothing here depends on player count.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Exile. Puncturing Blow says to exile the creature if it would die this turn. It doesn't matter if it was dealt the damage or not.

entries.question: Nathaniel casts [The Wandering Emperor]. Avery then plays [Teferi, Time Raveler]. After it resolves, can Nathaniel activate The Wandering Emperor's abilities this turn?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Teferi, Time Raveler only restricts casting spells and does not stop activating The Wandering Emperor's loyalty abilities, so Nathaniel may activate them this turn.
entries.answer:
Yes. Teferi, Time Raveler doesn't stop Nathaniel from activating The Wandering Emperor's loyalty abilities — it only restricts when opponents can *cast spells*, and activating a loyalty ability is not casting a spell.

Details:
- Teferi, Time Raveler's static ability reads "Each opponent can cast spells only any time they could cast a sorcery." That is a casting restriction only; loyalty abilities are activated abilities ([606.1], [606.2], [209.2]), and a player may activate an activated ability any time they have priority ([117.1b]).
- Because Avery playing Teferi, Time Raveler as a planeswalker spell happens during Avery's own main phase with an empty stack ([306.1]), Nathaniel is not in his own main phase. Normally rule [606.3]/[306.5d] would forbid activating a loyalty ability outside your own main phase with an empty stack. But The Wandering Emperor's own text — "As long as The Wandering Emperor entered this turn, you may activate her loyalty abilities any time you could cast an instant" — overrides that general timing rule. So on the turn she entered, Nathaniel can activate a loyalty ability at instant speed, including on Avery's turn after Teferi, Time Raveler resolves.
- Limit: only one. Per [606.3] and [The Wandering Emperor ruling #0], no loyalty ability of that permanent may have been activated already that turn. So if Nathaniel already used one of her abilities this turn, he gets no more; otherwise he may use exactly one of +1, −1, or −2.
- Timing assumption: I'm reading it as Nathaniel flashing in The Wandering Emperor during Avery's turn, then Avery casting Teferi, Time Raveler in a main phase. If instead this all happened on Nathaniel's own turn (Avery couldn't cast a planeswalker then anyway, absent an effect), Nathaniel could still activate one loyalty ability in his main phase with an empty stack under [306.5d].
- Multiplayer: no difference. Teferi, Time Raveler applies to "each opponent," so every opponent is restricted on casting spells, but none of them is restricted on activating loyalty abilities.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Teferi, Time Raveler only prevents casting spells, not activating abilities.

entries.question: Ariel controls a [Mistvein Borderpost]. Nina controls a [Stony Silence]. Can Ariel tap Mistvein Borderpost for mana?
entries.reason: Both conclude that Stony Silence prevents activating artifact activated abilities, so Ariel cannot activate Mistvein Borderpost's {T}: Add {U} or {B} ability to tap it for mana.
entries.answer:
No. Stony Silence says "Activated abilities of artifacts can't be activated," and Mistvein Borderpost is an artifact, so its "{T}: Add {U} or {B}" ability can't be activated at all.

Details:
- "Tapping a permanent for mana" means activating a mana ability of that permanent that includes {T} in its cost [106.12]. Mistvein Borderpost's {T}: Add {U} or {B} is exactly such an activated mana ability [113.4], [605.1].
- Mana abilities are still activated abilities; they just don't use the stack and resolve immediately [605.3b], [405.6c]. That special handling doesn't exempt them from a prohibition, and Stony Silence ruling #1 states explicitly that no abilities of artifacts can be activated, including mana abilities.
- A player can't even begin to activate an ability that's prohibited from being activated [602.5], so Ariel can't announce it, and nothing about Mistvein Borderpost being untapped or tapped changes that.
- Stony Silence only shuts off activated abilities of artifacts on the battlefield; triggered abilities and abilities that function in other zones are unaffected (Stony Silence ruling #2).
- Note the ownership doesn't matter: Stony Silence affects all artifacts, not just its controller's or opponents'. This is the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table — every player's artifacts are shut off.

Ariel can still cast Mistvein Borderpost (casting isn't an activated ability) and it will still enter tapped, but it can never be tapped for {U} or {B} while Stony Silence is on the battlefield.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Tapping the Mistvein Borderpost for mana is an activated ability.

entries.question: In a Two-Headed Giant game, how much life does each team begin the game with?
entries.reason: The candidate correctly states that each Two-Headed Giant team begins with a shared starting life total of 30, matching the reference.
entries.answer:
Each team begins a Two-Headed Giant game with a shared life total of 30 life [810.4], [119.1a], [103.4a]. Note that in Two-Headed Giant, life is a single "shared life total" for the team rather than each player having their own total [Two-Headed Giant Variant], [Shared Life Total]. Damage, life loss, and life gain happen to each player individually, but the result is applied to the team's shared total \u2014 so a spell dealing 4 damage to each player costs a two-player team 8 life [810.9]. A team loses the game when its shared life total is 0 or less [704.6a].

Standard Two-Headed Giant is played with two teams of two players each [810.1]. If you play the variant with larger, equally sized teams (Three-Headed Giant, Four-Headed Giant, etc.), the starting life total increases by 15 for each player beyond the second \u2014 so 45 for three-player teams, 60 for four-player teams \u2014 and the poison counters needed to lose goes up by five per extra player [810.11].

entries.question: Ariel is at 1 life, controls [City of Brass], and has [Angel's Grace] in their hand. Can they tap City of Brass for {W} and then use that {W} to cast Angel's Grace and not lose the game?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion — you can tap City of Brass and cast Angel's Grace before its damage trigger resolves to avoid losing, and correctly notes that tapping it while paying for the spell would put the trigger above the spell and cause you to lose.
entries.answer:
Yes — but only if Ariel taps City of Brass as a separate action *before* starting to cast Angel's Grace, not while casting it.

How it works:

1. Ariel activates City of Brass's mana ability, adding {W}. City of Brass's triggered ability ("deals 1 damage to you") triggers and is put on the stack. Ariel is still at 1 life, so no state-based action makes them lose (704.5a, 119.6, 104.3b).
2. With City of Brass's trigger on the stack, Ariel responds by casting Angel's Grace with that {W} ([City of Brass ruling #0] explicitly allows this and says the instant resolves first). Angel's Grace has split second, so nothing else can be cast in response, and it resolves first.
3. Angel's Grace resolves: Ariel can't lose the game this turn, and until end of turn damage that would reduce their life total to less than 1 reduces it to 1 instead.
4. City of Brass's trigger then resolves and deals 1 damage. That damage would take Ariel to 0, so instead their life total is set to 1. State-based actions see 1 life, so no loss (704.5a, 117.5, 704.1).

The trap: if Ariel taps City of Brass *during* the casting of Angel's Grace (using it as a mana ability to pay the cost), City of Brass's trigger waits and is then put on the stack on top of Angel's Grace, so the damage trigger resolves FIRST ([City of Brass ruling #2]). Ariel would drop to 0 life, and the next time state-based actions are checked — before any player gets priority — Ariel loses the game (117.5, 704.5a, 119.6). Angel's Grace would still be sitting on the stack, and a replacement effect can't retroactively undo a loss that already happened (614.4).

Note also that Angel's Grace doesn't prevent the damage; it only changes the result ([Angel's Grace ruling #3]), and it wouldn't help against effects that say "you lose life" ([Angel's Grace ruling #9]) — City of Brass deals damage, so it is covered.

Multiplayer: nothing here depends on the number of players; the same sequencing applies at a two-player or multiplayer table (the "your opponents can't win" clause simply applies to all opponents).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. When Ariel taps City of Brass, the trigger to deal 1 damage is put onto the stack.Ariel may cast Angel's Grace before it resolves.

entries.question: Anderson controls a 0/1 red Elemental creature token with "At the beginning of your upkeep, sacrifice this creature and return target card named [Rekindling Phoenix] from your graveyard to the battlefield. It gains haste until end of turn." and has a Rekindling Phoenix in their graveyard. During Anderson's upkeep with the token's trigger on the stack, Nia casts [Surgical Extraction] targeting Rekindling Phoenix and chooses to exile it as Surgical Extraction resolves. What happens when the Elemental token's trigger resolves?
entries.reason: Both conclude the trigger is removed as its target is illegal when it would resolve, so it does nothing (the token isn't sacrificed and will trigger again next upkeep).
entries.answer:
The Elemental token's trigger doesn't resolve at all, and Anderson does NOT sacrifice the token. The token stays on the battlefield and its ability will trigger again at the beginning of Anderson's next upkeep.

Why: the token's ability targets a card named Rekindling Phoenix in Anderson's graveyard. When Nia's Surgical Extraction resolves and exiles that Rekindling Phoenix card, the target leaves the graveyard — the zone it was in when it was targeted — so it is an illegal target (608.2b). A target that's no longer in the zone it was in when targeted is illegal, and since that's the ability's only target, the ability is removed from the stack and does nothing (608.2b). Because the sacrifice is part of the ability's effect and the ability never resolves, nothing about it happens: no sacrifice, no return, no haste. This is confirmed directly by [Rekindling Phoenix ruling #0], which states that if the target becomes illegal after the ability has triggered but before it resolves, you won't sacrifice the Elemental token, and it will trigger again during your next upkeep. Note also that the exiled Rekindling Phoenix is a new object in exile with no relation to the graveyard card (400.7), so the ability cannot follow it.

Same ruling in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table — nothing here depends on the number of players.

Timing note: I'm assuming Surgical Extraction was cast and fully resolved while the token's trigger was still on the stack (the trigger resolves after, since Surgical Extraction was put on the stack later). If instead the Rekindling Phoenix card were somehow still in Anderson's graveyard when the trigger resolved, the trigger would resolve normally: Anderson sacrifices the token and returns Rekindling Phoenix to the battlefield with haste.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The token's trigger will be removed from the stack when it tries to resolve as all of its targets are now illegal. The token is not sacrificed.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Kozilek, Butcher of Truth] which has been mutated with [Everquill Phoenix]. Kozilek, Butcher of Truth dies. Will Everquill Phoenix also be shuffled into their deck?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that the mutated permanent's cards (Kozilek and Everquill Phoenix) go to Autumn's graveyard when it dies and Kozilek's triggered ability shuffles that graveyard (including Everquill Phoenix) into their library.
entries.answer:
Yes — Everquill Phoenix ends up shuffled into the library, but by way of the graveyard, not as a special "mutate" effect.

How it works:

1. A mutated permanent is a single permanent represented by more than one card (rule 702.140c, 730.1), and it has all abilities of each card representing it (rule 702.140e). So the permanent has Kozilek, Butcher of Truth's "When Kozilek is put into a graveyard from anywhere, its owner shuffles their graveyard into their library" ability whether Kozilek, Butcher of Truth is the top or bottom card.
2. When the merged permanent dies, one permanent leaves the battlefield but each component is put into the appropriate zone individually (rule 730.3). So both the Kozilek, Butcher of Truth card and the Everquill Phoenix card go to their owner's graveyard. If they're both owned by Autumn, Autumn may arrange them in either order in the graveyard (rule 730.3a).
3. Kozilek, Butcher of Truth's ability triggers on it being put into a graveyard from anywhere, so it triggers and, on resolution, its owner shuffles their graveyard into their library. Everquill Phoenix is in that graveyard at that time (assuming nothing moves it out first), so it gets shuffled in along with everything else in that graveyard.

Assumption on timing: I'm assuming both cards hit the graveyard simultaneously as the merged permanent dies, and that nothing responds to the trigger by moving Everquill Phoenix elsewhere. If something exiles or reanimates Everquill Phoenix from the graveyard in response to Kozilek, Butcher of Truth's trigger, it obviously won't be in the graveyard to be shuffled. Also note this shuffle affects only the owner's own graveyard and library — in a multiplayer game, other players' graveyards are untouched, and if Everquill Phoenix were owned by a different player it would go to that player's graveyard and would not be shuffled by Kozilek, Butcher of Truth's ability.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Yes, Everquill Phoenix will get shuffled into Autumn's library.

When Kozilek, Butcher of Truth dies, both Kozilek, Butcher of Truth and Everquill Phoenix are put into Autumn's graveyard. Kozilek, Butcher of Truth then triggers. All cards in Autumn's graveyard will be shuffled into their library when the trigger resolves.

entries.question: Aldo controls [Bubble Matrix] and [Aegar, the Freezing Flame], Nico controls [Toralf, God of Fury]. Aldo casts [Ultimate Magic: Meteor]. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Bubble Matrix prevents all damage from Ultimate Magic: Meteor so no damage is dealt and neither Aegar nor Toralf's excess-damage triggers occur.
entries.answer:
Nothing dies and no damage is dealt: Bubble Matrix prevents all of Ultimate Magic: Meteor's damage to every creature, so neither Aegar, the Freezing Flame nor Toralf, God of Fury triggers.

Step by step:

1. Ultimate Magic: Meteor resolves and would deal 7 damage to each creature (including Aegar, the Freezing Flame and Toralf, God of Fury). Damage is processed in a four-part sequence; in the second part, damage is dealt as modified by replacement and prevention effects [120.4b]. Prevention effects act as shields that watch for the damage event and prevent it [615.1].
2. Bubble Matrix's static ability ("Prevent all damage that would be dealt to creatures") prevents all 7 damage to each creature. Since no damage is actually dealt, nothing is marked on any creature [120.3e, 302.7], and no creature is destroyed by state-based actions [704.5g].
3. Aegar, the Freezing Flame triggers only when a creature or planeswalker an opponent controls is dealt excess damage. Excess-damage checks look at damage actually dealt to the permanent [120.10]; because all of it was prevented, zero damage was dealt, so there is no excess and Aegar, the Freezing Flame does not trigger. (Note also that Aegar, the Freezing Flame is Aldo's own creature, and Aldo controls it, so damage to Aegar, the Freezing Flame itself could never trigger it.)
4. Toralf, God of Fury triggers only on excess *noncombat* damage dealt to a creature or planeswalker an opponent controls. Nico controls Toralf, God of Fury; Aldo's creatures took no damage at all, so there is no excess and Toralf, God of Fury does not trigger either. (Toralf, God of Fury also takes no damage itself.)
5. Any "damage was prevented" triggers would still trigger if someone had one [615.13], but neither Aegar, the Freezing Flame nor Toralf, God of Fury is such an ability.
6. Ultimate Magic: Meteor's second sentence only applies if it was cast from exile (e.g., via its Foretell {5}{R} cost). Assuming Aldo cast it from hand for {5}{R}, nothing is destroyed. If Aldo instead cast it from exile, then for each opponent Aldo chooses an artifact or land that player controls and destroys the chosen permanents — that part is unaffected by Bubble Matrix, since it's destruction, not damage.

Multiplayer note: the damage/prevention analysis is identical regardless of player count. Only the from-exile clause scales — with more than two players, Aldo would choose one artifact or land controlled by each opponent, not just Nico's.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Nothing. Bubble Matrix's replacement effect prevents the damage Ultimate Magic: Meteor would deal, and so neither of the triggered abilities will happen, because no excess damage is being dealt.

entries.question: Ariel attacks with [Stoneforge Mystic] that's equipped with [Colossus Hammer]. Nathaniel blocks with [Priest of Ancient Lore]. After combat, Ariel equips Colossus Hammer to another creature. Does Stoneforge Mystic die?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that the 2 combat damage remains marked after combat and when Colossus Hammer is removed the Mystic becomes a 1/2 with 2 damage marked and is destroyed by state-based actions.
entries.answer:
Yes — Stoneforge Mystic dies as soon as Colossus Hammer leaves it.

Why: while equipped, Stoneforge Mystic is a 1/2 plus +10/+10, so an 11/12. Priest of Ancient Lore (2/1) deals 2 combat damage to it in the combat damage step [510.2, 703.4m]. That damage isn't enough to be lethal against toughness 12, but it stays marked on Stoneforge Mystic — marked damage is only removed by regeneration or in the cleanup step [120.6, 302.7, 514.2].

When Ariel activates Colossus Hammer's Equip {8} in the postcombat main phase (equip is sorcery-speed only, and the postcombat main phase follows the combat phase [505.1, 511.3]), Colossus Hammer becomes attached to the other creature and unattached from Stoneforge Mystic [301.5c, 701.3d]. Stoneforge Mystic immediately reverts to 1/2 while still carrying 2 marked damage. State-based actions are checked before any player gets priority, and since damage marked (2) is greater than or equal to its toughness (2), Stoneforge Mystic is destroyed as a state-based action [704.5g, 704.1]. Regeneration or a toughness boost in response isn't possible here, because state-based actions don't use the stack and nobody gets priority between the equip resolving and the check.

Timing note: I'm assuming the equip happens in the postcombat main phase of the same turn, before the cleanup step. If instead Ariel waited until a later turn (after that turn's cleanup step removed all marked damage [514.2]), Stoneforge Mystic would have no damage marked and would survive losing Colossus Hammer.

This works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table; nothing here depends on the number of players.

entries.question: Aydan has searched their library this turn with [Aang's Journey]. During their end step, Nathaly casts [Mission Briefing]. Can they use it to cast [Archive Trap] from their graveyard for free?

Note the alternative cost doesn't change Archive Trap's mana cost or mana value of {3}{U}{U} / MV 5 — only what Nathaly actually pays [Archive Trap ruling #3]. Archive Trap is an instant, so casting it during Nathaly's... during the end step is fine — a sorcery, by contrast, would have had to wait for Nathaly's own main phase with an empty stack [307.5a]. entries.question: Noah controls [Solitary Confinement]. Avery attacks with [Vault Guardsman] and casts [Skullcrack] targeting themselves. Does Noah lose life?

entries.answer:
Yes — if Skullcrack resolves before combat damage, Noah takes 3 damage from Vault Guardsman and loses 3 life. Skullcrack's second sentence, "Damage can't be prevented this turn," shuts off Solitary Confinement's "Prevent all damage that would be dealt to you" for the rest of that turn. Solitary Confinement's prevention shield still exists but simply does nothing (Skullcrack ruling #1: damage-prevention effects still resolve/exist, but the prevention part has no effect). With no prevention applying, Vault Guardsman's 3 combat damage to Noah, from a source without infect, causes Noah to lose 3 life (rules 120.3a, 119.3, 615.1/615.1a).

Timing note: I'm assuming Skullcrack resolved before combat damage was dealt (e.g., cast in the declare attackers or declare blockers step). Since Skullcrack's effect lasts the whole turn, the same result holds even if it resolves before combat begins. If instead combat damage had already been dealt before Skullcrack resolved, Solitary Confinement would have prevented that earlier damage and Noah would have lost no life from that damage — Skullcrack does not undo prevention that already happened.

Other points: Solitary Confinement also gives Noah shroud, but that's irrelevant here because Avery targeted themselves, not Noah, and Skullcrack targets only the player or planeswalker (Skullcrack ruling #2). Avery takes 3 damage from their own Skullcrack. Also, no one can gain life this turn, so any lifelink-style gain or life-gain replacement effects do nothing (Skullcrack ruling #0, rules 119.7, 119.10). If Vault Guardsman is blocked, Noah takes no combat damage from it unless it has trample or a similar ability.

Multiplayer: nothing here changes with more than two players — Skullcrack's "damage can't be prevented" and "players can't gain life" apply to the whole table, and each player's damage/life loss is tracked individually. In Two-Headed Giant, life loss is applied to the team's shared life total (rule 810.9g/810.9h).

entries.answer_gold: Yes. Skullcrack says that damage can't be prevented, so Solitary Confinement doesn't prevent it.

entries.question: Allan controls [City of Traitors], and Nala casts [Crop Rotation] finding [Birnin Zana Plaza]. Can Nala choose to have the Birnin Zana Plaza enter under Allan's control, making them sacrifice City of Traitors?

Crop Rotation says "Search your library for a land card, put that card onto the battlefield, then shuffle" — it doesn't say "under another player's control," so Birnin Zana Plaza enters under Nala's control. Rule 110.2a states that when an effect instructs a player to put an object onto the battlefield, it enters under that player's control unless the effect states otherwise, and there is no choice offered here.

Even if Birnin Zana Plaza somehow did enter under Allan's control, City of Traitors still wouldn't be sacrificed. City of Traitors triggers only "When you play another land." Putting a land onto the battlefield with Crop Rotation is not playing a land (rule 305.4), and City of Traitors explicitly does not trigger on lands that are put onto the battlefield without being played (City of Traitors ruling #0). Note also that City of Traitors' trigger condition is "you play another land" — it cares about its own controller (Allan) playing a land, not about Nala's actions.

The only way to redirect where Birnin Zana Plaza enters would be a replacement effect that changes under whose control it enters (see rule 616.1b for how such effects are handled); nothing in Crop Rotation or Birnin Zana Plaza provides one.

This answer is the same whether the table is two players or multiplayer — Crop Rotation's controller (Nala) gets Birnin Zana Plaza regardless of how many opponents there are.

entries.answer_gold: No. If a player is instructed to put something onto the battlefield, it enters under their control. And City of Traitors only triggers when Allan takes the turn-based action of playing a land, not just having one enter the battlefield under their control.

entries.question: Addison controls [Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider] and two [Flensermite]s. If Addison deals combat damage with both Flensermites, how many poison counters will Natasha get?

Why: Infect means damage dealt to a player by a source with infect doesn't cause life loss; instead the source's controller (Addison) gives that player that many poison counters [702.90b] [120.3b]. Each Flensermite is a 1/1, so each deals 1 combat damage, which becomes an instruction for Addison to give Natasha 1 poison counter.

Because Addison controls Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider, its second ability applies: "If you would put one or more counters on a permanent or player, put twice that many of each of those kinds of counters on that permanent or player instead." Addison is the one putting the counters, which is exactly what matters for which of Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider's two abilities applies [Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider ruling #1]. So each Flensermite's 1 poison counter becomes 2.

The two Flensermites deal damage as separate sources, so there are two separate counter-placement events, each doubled once: 2 + 2 = 4 poison counters. Vorinclex, Monstrous Raider's replacement effect doesn't reapply to its own output — a replacement effect gets only one opportunity to affect a given event [614.5].

Side notes: Flensermite also has lifelink, so Addison gains 2 life total from the 2 damage dealt. Natasha loses no life from the combat damage [702.90b]. Natasha loses the game as a state-based action once she has ten or more poison counters [122.1f] [104.3d] [704.1]. In a Two-Headed Giant game the answer changes in presentation only: poison counters are shared by the team, so the 4 counters would count toward Natasha's team total [810.10] [810.10a].

entries.answer_gold: Two damage will be dealt to Natasha and they will get four poison counters. ([702.164c], [702.90b])

entries.question: Aubrey controls [Leonin Shikari] and [Mjölnir, Storm Hammer] attached to [Urbis Protector]. They attack with Urbis Protector and [The Ninth Doctor]. After blockers have been declared, can Aubrey reequip Mjölnir, Storm Hammer to The Ninth Doctor?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference — Leonin Shikari permits activating equip during the declare blockers step, so Mjölnir can be moved to The Ninth Doctor.
entries.answer:
Yes. Leonin Shikari's text — "You may activate equip abilities any time you could cast an instant" — overrides the normal restriction in the equip keyword that it can only be activated as a sorcery (702.6a), so Aubrey can pay Mjölnir, Storm Hammer's Equip {4} (four generic mana, payable with any colors or colorless) during the declare blockers step and attach Mjölnir, Storm Hammer to The Ninth Doctor. The Ninth Doctor is a creature Aubrey controls, which is all Equip {4} requires as a legal target (702.6a, 301.5c); Mjölnir, Storm Hammer's "attach to target legendary creature you control" clause is only on its enters-the-battlefield trigger, not on its equip ability, so it isn't a restriction here (though The Ninth Doctor is legendary anyway).

A few consequences:
- Moving Mjölnir, Storm Hammer does not remove Urbis Protector or The Ninth Doctor from combat; neither leaves the battlefield, changes control, or stops being a creature (506.4b). Both remain attacking, and Urbis Protector remains blocked or unblocked as declared.
- No new attack trigger. Mjölnir, Storm Hammer's "Whenever equipped creature attacks" triggers only at the declaration of attackers; The Ninth Doctor was already declared as an attacker earlier in the turn, so attaching Mjölnir, Storm Hammer now does not cause that ability to trigger again. Any instance of the trigger from Urbis Protector attacking has already been put on the stack and resolves (or resolved) independently of where Mjölnir, Storm Hammer is attached (Mjölnir, Storm Hammer ruling #0 covers only what happens if its target creature becomes illegal).
- Leonin Shikari lifts only the sorcery-speed timing restriction; Aubrey still needs priority and must still obey any other restrictions on the equip ability (Leonin Shikari ruling #1).

Timing assumption: I'm reading this as after blockers are declared but before combat damage, with Aubrey holding priority in the declare blockers step. If instead this were attempted after combat damage had already been dealt, the answer to "can she move it" is still yes, but it would obviously no longer change how damage was dealt.

Multiplayer note: nothing here changes with more than two players. Equip only cares that the target creature is one Aubrey controls; the number of opponents matters only for the damage portion of Mjölnir, Storm Hammer's attack trigger, which has already triggered (or not) based on the declaration of attackers.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. Players receive priority in the declare blockers step to cast spells and activate abilities, and Leonin Shikari allows them to activate equip abilities any time they have priority.

entries.question: Can Alex attach [Cranial Plating] at instant speed?

entries.answer:
Yes. Cranial Plating's {B}{B} ability — "{B}{B}: Attach this Equipment to target creature you control" — has no "Activate only as a sorcery" restriction, so Alex can activate it any time he has priority and could cast an instant, including during another player's turn or in combat [Cranial Plating ruling #1].

Why: a true equip ability means "[Cost]: Attach this permanent to target creature you control. Activate only as a sorcery" [702.6a]. Cranial Plating's Equip {1} is that sorcery-speed ability. But its {B}{B} ability, while similar in effect, is not an equip ability and carries no such timing restriction [Cranial Plating ruling #1]. Note the cost is two black mana specifically, {B}{B} — it cannot be paid with generic or colorless mana; the separate Equip {1} costs one generic mana.

The target must be a creature Alex controls, and Cranial Plating can't be attached to a noncreature permanent or to itself [301.5, 301.5c, 701.3a]. If the target creature is gone or illegal on resolution, nothing happens; if Cranial Plating ends up attached to an illegal permanent, it becomes unattached as a state-based action but stays on the battlefield [301.5c, 704.1]. Moving Cranial Plating to a new creature gives it a new timestamp [701.3c]. Cranial Plating can only equip one creature at a time, so activating the ability moves it off whatever it was attached to [301.5c].

This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games — the ability targets a creature Alex controls, so the number of opponents doesn't change anything, other than that there are more opponents' turns during which he can activate it.

entries.answer_gold: Yes, if they pay {B}{B}. Equip is sorcery speed, but Cranial Plating's second ability is a regular activated ability, which can be activated any time Alex has priority.

entries.question: Andres controls two [Ruin Crab]s and plays a land. Can they cast [Extirpate] targeting something in the first three cards milled, before the next three are milled?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion that the two Ruin Crab triggers resolve separately and Andres may cast Extirpate after the first trigger resolves and before the second resolves.
entries.answer:
Yes. The two Ruin Crab landfall triggers are separate objects on the stack, and they resolve one at a time; after the first Ruin Crab trigger finishes resolving (milling three cards from each opponent), players receive priority again before the second Ruin Crab trigger resolves, and Andres can cast Extirpate then, targeting one of the cards just milled.

Why: when Andres plays the land, both Ruin Crab abilities trigger on the same event. They're put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority, and since Andres controls both, he puts them on the stack in any order he chooses [603.3b] [117.5]. Only the top object resolves each time all players pass [608.1]; the second Ruin Crab trigger is still waiting on the stack. Once the first Ruin Crab trigger has fully resolved, the active player gets priority [117.1], and casting Extirpate at that point means it's cast "in response to" the remaining Ruin Crab trigger and will resolve before it [117.7]. Extirpate is an instant, so timing is legal, and its split second only stops other players from casting spells or activating non-mana abilities while Extirpate is on the stack — it doesn't stop the second Ruin Crab trigger from resolving afterward (Card data: Extirpate).

Targeting requirements: Extirpate needs a target card in a graveyard other than a basic land card, so you can't grab a basic land that got milled; a nonbasic land or any other milled card is fine. It then exiles all cards with that name from that player's graveyard, hand, and library, so doing it before the remaining three cards are milled is generally to your advantage.

Multiplayer note: Ruin Crab mills each opponent, so in a game with more than two players every opponent mills three from the first Ruin Crab trigger, and Andres may pick a milled card from any one of those graveyards as Extirpate's target [101.4]. The sequencing answer is identical with two players or more.

entries.answer_gold: Yes. Ruin Crab has a triggered ability, which each resolve one at a time. Players may cast spells in between.

entries.question: Alonzo attacks with a [Kraken Hatchling] that is equipped with [Barrow-Blade], and Nia blocks with an [Oreskos Swiftclaw] enchanted with [Greel's Caress]. After Barrow-Blade's triggered ability resolves, what are the power and toughness of Oreskos Swiftclaw?

entries.question: Aliza sacrifices [Lembas] to gain life. Can Nasir exile it in response with [Cling to Dust]?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Nasir can respond and exile Lembas while it is in the graveyard after being sacrificed, so Cling to Dust can be cast in response.
entries.answer:
Yes — Aliza sacrificing Lembas puts it into her graveyard immediately (sacrificing moves the permanent from the battlefield directly to its owner's graveyard, rule 701.21a, 404.1), so while it sits there Nasir can cast Cling to Dust targeting Lembas and exile it.

Details and timing:

1. Sacrificing Lembas is part of the cost of its "{2}, {T}, Sacrifice this artifact: You gain 3 life" ability, so Lembas is already in the graveyard as soon as that ability is activated. That also triggers Lembas's own ability, "When this artifact is put into a graveyard from the battlefield, its owner shuffles it into their library." That trigger goes on the stack above the life-gain ability, and players then get priority.

2. If Nasir casts Cling to Dust ({B}) at that point, targeting Lembas in Aliza's graveyard, Cling to Dust is on top of the stack and resolves first. Lembas is still in the graveyard, so it's a legal target: it is exiled, and since Lembas is not a creature card, Nasir draws a card (he does not gain 3 life).

3. The Lembas shuffle trigger then resolves with Lembas already in exile. Per rule 701.24c, the library is still shuffled even though the specific object isn't in the expected zone — Lembas itself stays exiled. Aliza's life-gain ability then resolves and she gains 3 life; exiling Lembas doesn't counter that ability, because the cost was already paid.

Timing caveat: this assumes Nasir responds while the shuffle trigger is still on the stack. If instead he waits until Lembas's shuffle trigger has resolved, Lembas is in Aliza's library, no longer a legal target — and if it was targeted before leaving the graveyard, Cling to Dust simply won't resolve at all: no life gain and no card drawn (rule 608.2b; Cling to Dust ruling #0). Also note Cling to Dust ruling #3: if Nasir is casting it for its escape cost, he must not target a card he's exiling to pay that cost, or the spell won't resolve.

Player count doesn't matter here: the rules used apply the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; Nasir just needs priority with Lembas in the graveyard.

entries.question: Arabella casts [Tandem Takedown], granting their two [Zombie Goliath] +1/+0. Can each Zombie Goliath deal damage to a different one of Nickolas's creatures?
