Yes. Chandra, Hope's Beacon's −X ability with X=1 deals damage to "each of up to two targets," and Nick and Noemi are two separate legal targets, so Ashley may choose both. Each of them is dealt 1 damage individually, and because in Two-Headed Giant damage happens to each player individually but is applied to the team's shared life total, Nick and Noemi's team loses a total of 2 life [810.9]. This is the same math as the Flame Rift example in [810.9], where 4 damage to each player means 8 damage to a team.

Note the restrictions that exist elsewhere in Two-Headed Giant do not apply here: the "only one member of each team" limits are specifically for effects that set each player's life total to a number [810.9d] and for effects that redistribute life totals [810.9f]. Plain damage has no such limit. Likewise, poison-counter proliferation has a one-per-team rule [701.34b], but again that doesn't restrict damage.

One caveat: "any target" style targeting requires each of the two targets to be different objects/players, so Ashley can't pick the same player twice to double up — but Nick and Noemi are distinct players, so that's fine. Outside Two-Headed Giant (in a normal two-player or free-for-all game), the same targeting works, but each player would simply lose life from their own individual life total rather than a shared one [Shared Life Total].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Each member of a team is a separate player and is targeted independently.

entries.question: If Aaden casts [Chord of Calling] with X=2 by tapping 5 green creatures, does it trigger Nathaly's [Roiling Vortex]?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference — convoke paid the entire cost so no mana was spent and Roiling Vortex triggers to deal 5 damage to the caster (Aaden).
entries.answer:
Yes — Roiling Vortex triggers and deals 5 damage to Aaden.

Why: with X=2, Chord of Calling's total cost is {2}{G}{G}{G} — five symbols in all (two generic plus three green). Convoke on Chord of Calling says "Each creature you tap while casting this spell pays for {1} or one mana of that creature's color," so tapping five green creatures pays all five symbols directly. Convoke creatures do not produce mana; they pay part of the cost instead, so no mana is actually spent to cast Chord of Calling. Roiling Vortex's second ability reads "Whenever a player casts a spell, if no mana was spent to cast that spell, this enchantment deals 5 damage to that player" — that condition is met, and the damage goes to Aaden (the caster), not to Nathaly, even though Nathaly controls Roiling Vortex.

A couple of notes on the mechanics: X must be chosen at announcement, before you tap creatures for convoke, and X plus any cost changes determines the total cost you then pay off with convoke [Chord of Calling ruling #6]. Also, a creature already tapped for a mana ability can't also be tapped for convoke [Chord of Calling ruling #5]; if Aaden had tapped even one creature for mana and spent that mana on Chord of Calling, mana would have been spent and Roiling Vortex would not trigger. Convoke is not an alternative cost — Chord of Calling still has its normal mana cost, and convoke merely helps pay the total cost determined under rule 601.2f.

Multiplayer: Roiling Vortex's trigger is worded for "a player" casting a spell, so it behaves identically with two players or more — it triggers on the caster and damages that caster, whoever they are.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. No mana was spent to cast Chord of Calling.

entries.question: Does Nasir have a chance to cast [Surgical Extraction] after Addison has drawn for turn but before they have a chance to cast a sorcery?
entries.reason: Both say yes — after the draw the active player receives priority and if they pass opponents (including Nasir) may cast instants like Surgical Extraction before any sorcery window opens.
entries.answer:
Yes. Addison's draw happens as a turn-based action immediately when the draw step begins ([703.4d], [504.1]), and it doesn't use the stack ([703.1]). Then Addison (the active player) gets priority ([504.2], [117.3a]). If Addison passes priority, priority passes to Nasir, and since Surgical Extraction is an instant, Nasir may cast it any time he has priority ([117.1], [117.1a]) — including there in the draw step, which is before Addison's precombat main phase where a sorcery could be cast (a noninstant spell requires the caster's own main phase with an empty stack, [117.1a]).

A few practical notes:
- Addison gets priority first in the draw step, so Addison could act before Nasir, but Addison still can't cast a sorcery during the draw step. Nasir's window exists as soon as Addison passes.
- Nasir also has windows in the upkeep step ([503.1], [503.1a]) — after the untap step, during which no one gets priority ([502.4]) — though those are before the draw, not after it.
- If Nasir casts Surgical Extraction, it resolves once all players pass in succession ([608.1]); Addison could respond, but again not with a sorcery.
- Multiplayer: the same works, but priority passes in turn order starting after the active player, so Nasir's window comes when priority reaches him, and every other opponent likewise gets a chance to act before Addison's main phase.
- Timing assumption: I'm reading "after Addison has drawn" as after the draw step's turn-based draw. If instead Addison drew from a spell or ability resolving elsewhere, the answer is the same in substance — Nasir gets priority before any sorcery can be cast, since sorceries only go on an empty stack in Addison's main phase.

Cost note: Surgical Extraction costs {B/P}, payable with one black mana or 2 life; there is no generic component.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Players receive priority in the draw step after a card has been drawn.

entries.question: Abril casts [Blot Out] targeting Nikolas. In response, Nikolas casts [Veil of Summer]. Abril responds with their own Veil of Summer. What happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Abril's Veil resolves first, then Nikolas's resolves (drawing a card), and Blot Out subsequently fails to resolve and is put into Abril's graveyard because Nikolas now has hexproof from black, making the target illegal.
entries.answer:
Blot Out is removed from the stack and put into Abril's graveyard with no effect; Nikolas exiles nothing.

Order of resolution (last on, first off — rule 405.2, 405.5, 117.7):

1. **Abril's Veil of Summer** resolves first. Abril draws a card only if an *opponent* cast a blue or black spell this turn — Abril's own Blot Out doesn't count, and Nikolas's Veil of Summer is green, so Abril most likely draws nothing (unless some other opponent cast a blue/black spell earlier this turn). Abril and Abril's permanents gain hexproof from blue and from black, and spells Abril controls can't be countered this turn. None of that protects Blot Out's target.
2. **Nikolas's Veil of Summer** resolves next. Nikolas draws a card, because Abril (an opponent of Nikolas) cast Blot Out, a black spell, this turn. Nikolas and Nikolas's permanents gain hexproof from blue and from black until end of turn — meaning they can't be targeted by blue or black spells or abilities Nikolas's opponents control.
3. **Blot Out** then tries to resolve. On resolution the game rechecks targets (608.2b). Blot Out is a black spell controlled by Abril, an opponent of Nikolas, and its only target is Nikolas, who now has hexproof from black. That target is illegal, and since every instance of "target" is illegal, Blot Out doesn't resolve and is put into Abril's graveyard (608.2b, 608.2n).

Note that Blot Out targets only the player, not the permanent (Blot Out ruling #0), so Nikolas's own hexproof — not any creature's — is what matters. Also, Veil of Summer had no effect while it was still on the stack (Veil of Summer ruling #2). Abril's Veil of Summer's "spells you control can't be countered" clause is irrelevant here: Blot Out isn't countered, it simply fails to resolve for lack of a legal target.

This works the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer; the only multiplayer wrinkle is that other opponents' earlier blue or black spells could give Abril's Veil of Summer a card draw, and priority passes through all players in turn order before each object resolves (101.4).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold:
Abril's Veil of Summer resolves first. Then Nikolas's resolves and draws them a card. Then Blot Out tries to resolve and fails, since it has an illegal target.

(Abril's Veil of Summer didn't accomplish anything useful.)

entries.question: Abril controls [Painter's Servant], naming "blue". Can they exile [Archangel] to cast [Misdirection]?
entries.reason: Both conclude Painter's Servant makes Archangel blue while in hand, so Abril can exile it to pay Misdirection's alternative cost.
entries.answer:
Yes. With Painter's Servant on the battlefield naming blue, every card not on the battlefield — including Archangel in Abril's hand — is blue in addition to its other colors, so Archangel is a blue card and can be exiled to pay Misdirection's alternative cost.

Details:
- An object is normally the color of the mana symbols in its mana cost [202.2, 105.2]; Archangel's cost is {5}{W}{W}, so it's white. Painter's Servant's second ability adds blue to it while Archangel is in hand, making Archangel white and blue.
- Misdirection's text "You may exile a blue card from your hand rather than pay this spell's mana cost" is an alternative cost [118.9b/118.9c], announced as Abril proposes Misdirection [601.2b] and paid during cost payment [601.2f]. Exiling the now-blue Archangel satisfies it. Paying the alternative cost doesn't change Misdirection's mana cost of {3}{U}{U}; anything that asks for that mana cost still sees {3}{U}{U} [118.9c].
- Caveat: if some other effect sets Archangel's color (rather than adding to it), it can overwrite Painter's Servant's effect and Archangel might not be blue [Painter's Servant ruling #4].

This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games; Painter's Servant affects all cards, not just Abril's, so opponents' cards are blue too.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Archangel is blue due to Painter's Servant.

entries.question: Natalee controls [Giant Solifuge]. Can Avery cast [Geth's Verdict]? If so, what happens?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Avery targets Natalee (not the creature) with Geth's Verdict, so Natalee must sacrifice Giant Solifuge if it’s her only creature and then lose 1 life.
entries.answer:
Yes. Avery can cast Geth's Verdict targeting Natalee, and if Giant Solifuge is Natalee's only creature, Natalee must sacrifice Giant Solifuge and lose 1 life.

Why shroud doesn't help: Giant Solifuge's shroud means it can't be the target of spells or abilities. But Geth's Verdict says "Target player sacrifices a creature of their choice and loses 1 life" — the only target is the player, Natalee. Giant Solifuge is never targeted, so shroud is irrelevant here. Targets are only checked for legality on resolution for the things actually targeted (rule 608.2b), and Natalee remains a legal target.

On resolution, Natalee follows the instruction: she chooses one creature she controls and sacrifices it — moving it from the battlefield directly to its owner's graveyard (rule 701.21a). The choice of which creature is Natalee's, made as Geth's Verdict resolves (rule 608.2d), so with other creatures on her battlefield she may keep Giant Solifuge and sacrifice something else. With Giant Solifuge as her only creature, that's the only legal choice. Sacrificing isn't destruction, so regeneration or destruction-replacement effects won't save Giant Solifuge (rule 701.21a). Natalee then loses 1 life; per the Geth's Verdict ruling, she loses the life even if she controlled no creature at all to sacrifice.

This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games — Geth's Verdict affects only the one targeted player, and Avery chooses that target when casting.

Timing note: I'm assuming Natalee controls Giant Solifuge both when Geth's Verdict is cast and when it resolves. If Giant Solifuge leaves the battlefield before resolution and Natalee controls no other creature, Geth's Verdict still resolves against Natalee, and she just loses 1 life with no sacrifice.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes, Natalee will have to sacrifice Giant Solifuge. Geth's Verdict only targets Natalee, not Giant Solifuge.

entries.question: Audrina controls [Murktide Regent]. Nickolas casts [Extirpate], exiling two [Weight of Spires] from Audrina's graveyard. Does Murktide Regent trigger?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Murktide Regent triggers twice because two instant cards (the two Weight of Spires) left Audrina's graveyard when Extirpate exiled them.
entries.answer:
Yes. Murktide Regent's last ability triggers once for each instant or sorcery card that leaves Audrina's graveyard, so Extirpate exiling two Weight of Spires cards from Audrina's graveyard causes Murktide Regent to trigger twice, putting two +1/+1 counters on Murktide Regent (one per resolution).

Details:
- Weight of Spires is an instant, and Audrina controls Murktide Regent, whose ability reads "Whenever an instant or sorcery card leaves your graveyard, put a +1/+1 counter on this creature." Both copies leaving Audrina's graveyard for exile are two separate leave events, hence two triggers.
- Extirpate's split second only stops players from casting spells or activating non-mana abilities while Extirpate is on the stack; it does not stop triggered abilities from triggering or being put onto the stack. Murktide Regent's triggers go on the stack after Extirpate finishes resolving and resolve normally.
- Only the copies of Weight of Spires exiled from the graveyard matter. Any copies Extirpate finds and exiles from Audrina's hand or library do not trigger Murktide Regent, since they never left the graveyard (and per [Extirpate ruling #4], the graveyard cards must be exiled, while hand/library cards are optional).
- The exiled Weight of Spires cards become new objects in exile with no relation to their previous existence ([400.7k]); this doesn't matter here, because the trigger only cares about the leave-the-graveyard event, and the ability doesn't need to track the cards afterward ([603.6] concerns zone-change triggers that try to act on the moved object — Murktide Regent's ability only adds a counter to itself).
- Note this ability is not linked to Murktide Regent's "enters with a +1/+1 counter for each instant and sorcery card exiled with it" ability ([607.1], [607.2q], [406.6]); cards exiled by Extirpate were not exiled to pay Murktide Regent's delve cost ([702.66a]).

Two players vs. more: the answer is the same at any table size. The only wrinkle would be a variant with limited range of influence, where a trigger only triggers if the event happens entirely within the range of the source's controller ([801.7a]) — in a normal game (including normal multiplayer), Nickolas's Extirpate is within Audrina's range, so Murktide Regent triggers.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Two Instant cards have left Audrina's graveyard.

entries.question: Ari controls [Durkwood Boars] and an [Unlicensed Hearse] which has exiled 2 cards. Nixon casts [Fury Charm], destroying Unlicensed Hearse. Ari casts another Unlicensed Hearse and taps Durkwood Boars to crew it. What are its power and toughness?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling that the newly cast Unlicensed Hearse is 0/0 (having exiled no cards) and will be put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action.
entries.answer:
0/0 — and the new Unlicensed Hearse is put into Ari's graveyard as a state-based action.

Why: Unlicensed Hearse's characteristic-defining ability says "Unlicensed Hearse's power and toughness are each equal to the number of cards exiled with it." That counts only cards exiled with *that* permanent using its own {T} ability. The first Unlicensed Hearse that Nixon destroyed with Fury Charm is a different object; the two cards it exiled are not "exiled with" the newly cast Unlicensed Hearse, which has exiled nothing. So its printed */* evaluates to 0/0 in layer 7 (the value-setting layer, applied by timestamp) [613.4b, 613.7].

While it was just an artifact Vehicle it had no power or toughness at all [208.3, 208.3a, 301.7a]. Tapping Durkwood Boars (power 4, enough for Crew 2) makes Unlicensed Hearse an artifact creature until end of turn [702.122a, 702.122b], at which point it immediately has its power and toughness [301.7b] — here 0/0. Crewing does not grant any power based on the crewing creature's power, so Durkwood Boars' 4 power is irrelevant beyond paying the crew cost. As the Unlicensed Hearse ruling states, a Hearse crewed before exiling any cards is 0/0 and, absent a toughness boost, is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action [Unlicensed Hearse ruling #0].

Timing note: I'm assuming Ari exiled no cards with the *new* Unlicensed Hearse before crewing it. If Ari had first activated its {T} ability to exile cards, it couldn't also be tapped-and-crewed usefully that way, but its power/toughness would equal that number of exiled cards instead of 0.

This analysis doesn't depend on player count — it's the same at a two-player table or in multiplayer.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 0/0. When text on an object refers to itself by name, it is only referring to that specific object, and not other objects with the same name. The second copy of Unlicensed Hearse has not exiled any cards, so it will be 0/0 while crewed. Since it has 0 toughness, it will die as a state-based action.

entries.question: Augustus controls [Mystic Forge], and Nico controls [Grafdigger's Cage]. Can Augustus still cast spells with Mystic Forge?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion — Grafdigger's Cage's prohibition on casting from libraries prevents Mystic Forge's permission to cast spells from the top of the library.
entries.answer:
No. While Nico's Grafdigger's Cage is on the battlefield, Augustus can't cast anything off the top of his library with Mystic Forge.

Mystic Forge says "You may cast artifact spells and colorless spells from the top of your library," which is a permission. Grafdigger's Cage says "Players can't cast spells from graveyards or libraries," which is a prohibition. Rule 601.3 says a player can begin to cast a spell only if a rule or effect allows it AND no rule or effect prohibits it — so the prohibition from Grafdigger's Cage beats the permission from Mystic Forge.

Augustus does keep the rest of Mystic Forge: he may still look at the top card of his library any time (this doesn't use the stack, per Mystic Forge ruling #1), and he can still activate "{T}, Pay 1 life: Exile the top card of your library." Note that Mystic Forge never let him play artifact *lands* from the top anyway, since lands are played, not cast (Mystic Forge ruling #0) — and by the same token Grafdigger's Cage, which only stops casting, wouldn't be what's stopping that.

This works the same at any table size: Grafdigger's Cage says "players," so it shuts off library-casting for Augustus, Nico, and every other player, not just its controller's opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Grafdigger's Cage says that players can't cast spells from libraries.

entries.question: Aspen cast [Summoner's Pact] last turn and is beginning their upkeep. Do they have a chance to cast [Angel's Grace] before losing the game? What happens if they do?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Aspen can cast Angel's Grace in response to Summoner's Pact's upkeep trigger and that when the trigger resolves it will do nothing because Aspen can't lose the game, so the core ruling is the same.
entries.answer:
Yes. Aspen gets priority in their upkeep with Summoner's Pact's delayed triggered ability on the stack, and can cast Angel's Grace then; if they do, they simply don't lose the game this turn even if they never pay {2}{G}{G}.

How it plays out:

1. At the beginning of Aspen's upkeep, the delayed triggered ability from Summoner's Pact ("pay {2}{G}{G}. If you don't, you lose the game") is put onto the stack before the active player gets priority [503.1a]. Note that no one had priority during the untap step, so nothing could be done there [502.4].
2. Aspen, as active player, then receives priority and may cast spells [503.1, 117.1]. That's the window for Angel's Grace. Angel's Grace has split second, so once it's on the stack opponents can't respond with anything but mana abilities.
3. Angel's Grace resolves: "You can't lose the game this turn."
4. Players pass and the Summoner's Pact trigger resolves [608.1]. The "pay {2}{G}{G}" is a cost paid on resolution; the "if you don't" clause checks whether Aspen began paying it [118.12]. If Aspen declines to pay, the ability tries to make them lose the game, but Angel's Grace prevents that, so nothing happens.

Aspen may also cast Angel's Grace after the trigger resolves only if the loss hasn't already happened — it will have, so cast it before the trigger resolves. Casting it in response (or any time in the upkeep before that trigger resolves) is the safe line.

Caveats: the Summoner's Pact trigger is one-shot, so once it's resolved harmlessly Aspen is clear — there's no lingering "lose the game" waiting when Angel's Grace wears off at end of turn. Angel's Grace also doesn't stop life loss from other sources [Angel's Grace ruling #9]. If Summoner's Pact itself had been countered, the delayed trigger wouldn't exist at all [Summoner's Pact ruling #1].

Multiplayer: this works the same at any table size — Aspen is the active player and gets priority first in their own upkeep. Angel's Grace additionally stops all of Aspen's opponents from winning that turn.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Summoner's Pact's trigger is put on the stack at the beginning of the upkeep, and Aspen can respond to it with Angel's Grace. When Summoner's Pact's trigger resolves, it does nothing, since Aspen can't lose the game. Aspen will continue playing indefinitely.

entries.question: Nico controls [Ensnaring Bridge] and has 3 cards in hand. Can Aleena deal 4 damage to Nico by attacking with [Servant of Nefarox]?
entries.reason: Both conclude Ensnaring Bridge only checks at declare attackers so Servant of Nefarox can legally attack as a 3/1, then exalted triggers to make it a 4/2 and it deals 4 damage if unblocked.
entries.answer:
Yes — assuming Servant of Nefarox attacks alone and is unblocked, it deals 4 damage to Nico.

Why: Ensnaring Bridge says "Creatures with power greater than the number of cards in your hand can't attack," and it checks the number of cards in hand only while attackers are being declared [Ensnaring Bridge ruling #0]. At declaration, Servant of Nefarox is a 3/1 and Nico has 3 cards in hand, so its power (3) is not greater than 3 and the attack is legal.

Servant of Nefarox's exalted ability triggers only after attackers are declared ("Whenever a creature you control attacks alone"), so it resolves after the legality check. Once it resolves, Servant of Nefarox is a 4/2. Per that same ruling, changing its power after it has legally attacked won't remove it from combat, and Ensnaring Bridge does not re-check.

In the combat damage step, Servant of Nefarox assigns combat damage equal to its power [510.1a], and since it's unblocked it assigns that damage to the player it's attacking [510.1b] — 4 damage to Nico.

Assumptions and variations: (1) "Attacks alone" means Servant of Nefarox is the only creature Aleena declares as an attacker; if Aleena attacks with anything else, exalted doesn't trigger and it deals only 3. (2) If Nico blocks, Servant of Nefarox must assign its damage to the blocking creature(s) instead [510.1c] — it has no trample, so no damage reaches Nico [702.19b]. (3) If Nico's hand size changes before the declare attackers step (down to 2 or fewer cards), Servant of Nefarox couldn't attack at all.

Multiplayer: the answer is the same. Exalted cares only that the creature attacks alone, and Ensnaring Bridge's "your hand" refers to its controller Nico's hand, so it restricts attacks regardless of which player is being attacked — but the check is still only made at declare attackers.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Ensnaring Bridge only prevents creatures with power > 3 from being declared as attackers. Exalted triggers after the creature attacks and gives it +1/+1. Nothing would remove it from combat at this point.

entries.question: Avery controls [Frogtosser Banneret]. Will it affect the cost of [Nameless Inversion]?
entries.reason: Both conclude Nameless Inversion is a Rogue and that Frogtosser Banneret reduces its cost from {1}{B} to {B}.
entries.answer:
Yes. Nameless Inversion costs {B} instead of {1}{B} while Avery controls Frogtosser Banneret.

Why: Nameless Inversion is a Kindred Instant — Shapeshifter with changeling, which means it is every creature type at all times and in all zones, including on the stack. So it is a Goblin spell and a Rogue spell, and Frogtosser Banneret's ability ("Goblin spells and Rogue spells you cast cost {1} less to cast") applies to it.

The reduction is {1} of generic mana, so it can only remove the generic component: {1}{B} minus {1} generic leaves {B}. The black mana symbol is untouched, because cost reductions expressed in generic mana affect only the generic portion of a cost [118.7a]. The reduction is applied when the total cost is determined and locked in during casting [601.2f].

This works regardless of any alternative or additional costs you might use — Frogtosser Banneret reduces the total cost, not just the printed mana cost [Frogtosser Banneret ruling #1], [118.9d].

Number of players doesn't matter here; the ability only cares about spells Avery casts, so the answer is the same in two-player and multiplayer games.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Nameless Inversion is a Rogue.

entries.question: Ariella casts [Chrome Mox], exiling [Fugitive Droid]. Ariella then uses [Karn, the Great Creator] to put Fugitive Droid into their had. What types of mana can Chrome Mox tap for?
entries.reason: The candidate assumes Chrome Mox exiled an artifact and lost it later, but Chrome Mox cannot imprint an artifact (so the described situation is impossible), making the candidate's ruling inconsistent with the reference.
entries.answer:
None — Chrome Mox can no longer produce any mana at all.

Why: Chrome Mox's Imprint trigger ("you may exile a nonartifact, nonland card from your hand") and its mana ability ("{T}: Add one mana of any of the exiled card's colors") are linked abilities. A linked ability of this kind refers only to cards that are currently in the exile zone as a result of the first ability [607.1, 607.2a]. Once Karn, the Great Creator's −2 puts Fugitive Droid into Ariella's hand, Fugitive Droid is no longer in exile, and it is a new object with no relation to its previous existence [400.7k]. Chrome Mox's mana ability therefore has no exiled card to look at, so it defines no type of mana, and an ability that would produce mana of an undefined type produces no mana instead [106.5]. This matches Chrome Mox ruling #0: if no card is exiled with it, it can't add mana.

Two side notes: (1) Karn, the Great Creator's −2 legitimately works here, since Fugitive Droid is an artifact card Ariella owns, face up in exile — but retrieving it is exactly what turns off Chrome Mox. (2) Even before that, Fugitive Droid is blue ({U}), so Chrome Mox would only ever have tapped for {U}; it can never add {C} (colorless) regardless [Chrome Mox ruling #2]. Karn, the Great Creator's static ability shutting off activated abilities of artifacts only applies to artifacts Ariella's opponents control, so it doesn't stop Ariella from activating Chrome Mox — the activation simply yields nothing.

Assumption on ordering: Chrome Mox's Imprint resolved and exiled Fugitive Droid before Karn, the Great Creator's −2 resolved. If instead you tapped Chrome Mox for mana while Fugitive Droid was still exiled, that activation would have produced {U} normally; only activations after Fugitive Droid leaves exile produce nothing.

This works identically in two-player and multiplayer games; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: This can't happen as described. Chrome Mox can't exile an artifact, even if it's colored.

entries.question: Avery has no cards left in their library. Nala has 1 life. Avery controls [Samwise the Stouthearted], which is their ring-bearer. Avery has been tempted by the ring twice previously. If Avery attacks Nala, who wins the game?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Avery loses due to the Ring-bearer attack trigger forcing a draw from an empty library before combat damage, so Nala wins.
entries.answer:
Nala wins (in a two-player game). Avery loses before combat damage is ever dealt.

Why: Avery has been tempted by the Ring twice, so Avery's emblem The Ring has "Whenever your Ring-bearer attacks, draw a card, then discard a card" [701.54c]. Samwise the Stouthearted is Avery's Ring-bearer, so declaring Samwise the Stouthearted as an attacker triggers that ability. It resolves during the declare attackers step, long before the combat damage step. Avery's library is empty, so Avery attempts to draw from an empty library; the next time state-based actions are checked, Avery loses the game [704.5b]. Nala is never dealt Samwise the Stouthearted's 2 combat damage, so Nala's 1 life is never at risk from this attack.

Note that the two-temptation level is what matters here: the "blocking creature's controller sacrifices it" ability only exists at three or more temptations, and the "each opponent loses 3 life" ability only at four or more [701.54c]. Samwise the Stouthearted is legendary and can't be blocked by creatures with greater power [701.54c], but that's irrelevant once Avery loses.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Avery has no way to respond (no shuffle-back or replacement like the Lich's Mirror-style effect described in [704.7]) between the trigger resolving and state-based actions being checked. If Avery could somehow refill the library or replace the loss before SBAs are checked, Avery would survive and combat damage would proceed, killing Nala at 1 life.

Multiplayer: the question names only Avery and Nala, so the "Nala wins" conclusion is the two-player answer. At a table with more than two players, Avery simply loses and leaves the game [104.3e], and the remaining players (including Nala, still at 1 life) keep playing — nobody wins yet.

entries.answer_gold: Nala wins. When Samwise the Stouthearted attacks, Avery must draw a card. This causes Avery to lose the game before the combat damage step is reached.

entries.question: Axl casts [Deathbringer Liege]? Does it trigger itself?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Deathbringer Liege's triggered abilities only function on the battlefield, so it cannot trigger while it's a spell on the stack.
entries.answer:
No. Casting Deathbringer Liege does not trigger Deathbringer Liege's own "Whenever you cast a white spell" or "Whenever you cast a black spell" abilities.

Why: those are triggered abilities of a permanent card, and abilities of an object other than an instant or sorcery function only while that object is on the battlefield (rule [113.6h]). While Deathbringer Liege is being cast it is a spell on the stack, so its abilities aren't functioning and there is nothing to notice the cast event. The only exceptions are abilities that modify how the object itself enters the battlefield ([113.6h], [614.12]), which these are not. By the time Deathbringer Liege resolves and enters the battlefield ([608.3a]), the casting event is long past, and these triggers look only for future casts.

So: Deathbringer Liege is both white and black (its {W/B} hybrid symbols are colored symbols of both colors), and once it's on the battlefield it will trigger on the next white spell and/or black spell Axl casts — a mono-white spell triggers the tap ability, a mono-black spell triggers the destroy-if-tapped ability, and a spell that's both white and black triggers both. But the Deathbringer Liege spell itself gets no trigger.

This answer doesn't depend on player count — "whenever you cast" only watches Axl's own spells, so it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Deathbringer Liege's abilities only function while it's on the battlefield, and right after Deathbringer Liege has been cast, it's on the stack.

entries.question: Annabelle casts [Shaman of the Pack]. In response to its trigger, Nico kills it with [Deathsprout]. How much life does Nico lose?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: the triggered ability resolves after Deathsprout destroys Shaman of the Pack, so Shaman is not counted and Nico would lose 0 life in that described scenario.
entries.answer:
Nico loses life equal to the number of Elves Annabelle controls at the moment the Shaman of the Pack trigger resolves — and Shaman of the Pack itself is no longer counted, because Deathsprout already destroyed it. If Shaman of the Pack was Annabelle's only Elf, Nico loses 0 life.

Why: Shaman of the Pack's enters ability goes on the stack independently of Shaman of the Pack, and destroying the source afterward doesn't counter or remove the ability [113.7a]. Deathsprout resolving first only kills the creature; the trigger still resolves because its target (Nico, the target opponent) is still legal [608.2b]. The count is made on resolution, not when the ability triggered: Shaman of the Pack's ruling says to count the Elves you control as the ability resolves, including Shaman of the Pack only if it's still on the battlefield [Shaman of the Pack ruling #0]. So every other Elf Annabelle still controls at that time is counted; Shaman of the Pack is not.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Deathsprout was cast and resolved while the Shaman of the Pack trigger was still on the stack (that's what "in response" means), so the trigger resolves after Shaman of the Pack is gone. If instead Deathsprout resolved after the Shaman of the Pack trigger had already resolved, Shaman of the Pack would have been on the battlefield during the count and would add 1 to the life loss.

Multiplayer: the ability says "target opponent," so only Nico loses life regardless of how many opponents Annabelle has; with more than two players, Annabelle chooses which opponent to target when the trigger is put on the stack, and the answer is otherwise the same [603.3d].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: 0. When Shaman of the Pack's trigger resolves, Annabelle controls no Elves.

entries.question: Can [Lava Spike] deal damage to [Nissa, Worldwaker]?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling as the reference: Lava Spike can target and deal 3 damage to a planeswalker like Nissa, Worldwaker directly (no redirection needed).
entries.answer:
Yes. Lava Spike's Oracle text reads "Lava Spike deals 3 damage to target player or planeswalker," so you may target Nissa, Worldwaker directly with it, even a Nissa, Worldwaker controlled by an opponent.

When Lava Spike resolves, the 3 damage dealt to Nissa, Worldwaker causes that many loyalty counters to be removed from Nissa, Worldwaker [120.3c, 306.8]. If Nissa, Worldwaker has only its starting 3 loyalty and no other loyalty counters have been added, all 3 counters come off and Nissa, Worldwaker is put into its owner's graveyard as a state-based action; if it has been activated with a +1 ability (or otherwise gained counters), it survives with that many fewer.

Two clarifications:
- You do not need any redirection effect. The old rule that let a player redirect noncombat damage aimed at an opponent onto that opponent's planeswalker has been removed, and cards like Lava Spike were given errata so they can hit planeswalkers directly [306.7].
- Planeswalkers are legal recipients of damage generally [120.1a, 115.4], so this works the same in a two-player game and in multiplayer — Lava Spike simply targets one player or one planeswalker, and in a multiplayer game you may choose any opponent's Nissa, Worldwaker (or your own) as that single target.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Lava Spike targets any player or planeswalker.

entries.question: Alison controls [Stoneforge Mystic] and uses it to put [Hero's Heirloom] onto the battlefield. Can Noel counter it with [Countermand]?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that Stoneforge Mystic's ability puts the Equipment onto the battlefield without it being a spell, so Countermand (which targets only spells) cannot counter it.
entries.answer:
No. Noel can't use Countermand on Hero's Heirloom, because Hero's Heirloom never becomes a spell. Stoneforge Mystic's second ability, "{1}{W}, {T}: You may put an Equipment card from your hand onto the battlefield," moves Hero's Heirloom directly from Alison's hand to the battlefield. It isn't cast, so it never exists as an artifact spell on the stack for Countermand to target (compare rule 301.1/301.2, where an artifact you cast uses the stack and is put onto the battlefield only when the artifact spell resolves). Countermand says "Counter target spell," and there is no spell here. Per Stoneforge Mystic ruling #0, Alison may put any Equipment card from hand onto the battlefield this way, and it enters unattached.

What Noel could respond to is Stoneforge Mystic's activated ability itself, which does use the stack (rule 602.2a). But rule 113.9 says activated abilities on the stack aren't spells and can't be countered by anything that counters only spells; only an effect that specifically counters abilities would work. Countermand counters only spells, so it can't be aimed at the ability either. Noel's realistic windows are to respond before the ability resolves by removing or tapping Stoneforge Mystic in response to its activation, or to deal with Hero's Heirloom after it's on the battlefield.

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; it's the same at a two-player or multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Putting an Equipment onto the battlefield with Stoneforge Mystic is an activated ability, not a spell.

entries.question: Can [Murder] destroy [Severed Legion]?
entries.reason: The candidate gives the same final ruling — Murder can target and destroy Severed Legion because it is a creature — so it matches the reference.
entries.answer:
Yes. Murder ("Destroy target creature.") can target and destroy Severed Legion.

Severed Legion is a 2/2 Zombie whose only ability is fear ("This creature can't be blocked except by artifact creatures and/or black creatures"). Fear only restricts which creatures may block Severed Legion in combat; it grants no hexproof, no protection, and no indestructible, so nothing stops Murder from choosing Severed Legion as its target or from destroying it. Murder uses the word "destroy," which is one of the ways a permanent can be destroyed [701.8b].

Things that would change this: if Severed Legion gained indestructible, it couldn't be destroyed at all and Murder would simply do nothing to it [702.12b]; if a regeneration shield were created for Severed Legion, that shield would replace the destruction event — instead, damage would be removed from Severed Legion, its controller would tap it, and it would be removed from combat if attacking or blocking [701.8c, 701.19a, 614.8]; and if Severed Legion somehow had hexproof or protection from everything, Murder couldn't target it at all [702.11e, 702.16j].

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players — Murder targets a single creature regardless of who controls it, so it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Murder targets creatures, and Severed Legion is a creature.

entries.question: Ari sacrifices [Beast Whisperer] to cast [Natural Order]. Does Ari draw a card?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line — Ari doesn't draw — and gives the same correct reasons: Natural Order isn't a creature and the sacrifice removes Beast Whisperer before the spell is cast.
entries.answer:
No, Ari draws no card.

Two independent reasons:

1. Beast Whisperer triggers only "whenever you cast a creature spell." Natural Order is a sorcery, not a creature spell, so Beast Whisperer's ability would never trigger on it even if Beast Whisperer were still on the battlefield.

2. Even for a creature spell, Beast Whisperer wouldn't be around. Sacrificing a green creature is an additional cost of Natural Order ([Natural Order ruling #0]), chosen as the spell is proposed and paid during the payment step ([601.2f], [601.2h]). The spell only "becomes cast" — and cast-triggers only trigger — after all costs are paid ([601.2i]). So Beast Whisperer has already left the battlefield before the trigger check happens. The "look back in time" exception in [603.10a] covers leaves-the-battlefield and sacrifice triggers; Beast Whisperer's is a cast trigger, so it gets no such exception.

Also note [Natural Order ruling #1]: no one can respond before the sacrifice, so there's no window to get a draw in.

This answer doesn't depend on player count — it's the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Natural Order is not a creature spell. Even if it were, Beast Whisperer isn't on the battlefield at the time when Natural Order becomes "cast".

entries.question: Alexia controls [Temple Garden] enchanted with [Utopia Sprawl], choosing "red". Nico controls [Damping Sphere]. If Alexia taps it for {G}, how much mana is produced in total?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference: Temple Garden produces {G} and Utopia Sprawl separately produces {R}, so total {G}{R}, and Damping Sphere doesn't apply because the land itself only produced one mana.
entries.answer:
Alexia gets two mana total: {G} from Temple Garden plus {R} from Utopia Sprawl. Damping Sphere does not turn anything into {C} here.

Why: "Tap [a permanent] for mana" means activating a mana ability of that permanent that includes {T} in its cost [106.12], and Damping Sphere's replacement effect only applies if a land "is tapped for two or more mana" — i.e., it modifies the mana production event of that land's own mana ability as it resolves and produces that amount [106.12b]. Temple Garden's own ability ("{T}: Add {G} or {W}") produces exactly one mana, {G}, so Damping Sphere's condition of "two or more mana" is never met and Temple Garden still produces {G}.

Utopia Sprawl's extra mana is not part of Temple Garden's production. Utopia Sprawl reads "Whenever enchanted Forest is tapped for mana, its controller adds an additional one mana of the chosen color" — that's a triggered mana ability that triggers when such a mana ability resolves and produces mana [106.12a, 603.1]. It doesn't use the stack; it resolves immediately after the mana ability that triggered it [605.4a], and its source is Utopia Sprawl, not Temple Garden [113.7, 106.3]. So the {R} is mana produced by Utopia Sprawl, and Temple Garden was never tapped for two or more mana.

Note Temple Garden has the Forest type (Land — Forest Plains), so Utopia Sprawl can legally enchant it [Temple Garden ruling #2].

Result by symbol: {G} (from Temple Garden) + {R} (from Utopia Sprawl) = 2 mana, no {C}. Nothing here depends on the number of players; the answer is the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table, since Damping Sphere's static ability applies to any land tapped for mana regardless of controller.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: {G}{R}. Damping Sphere only modifies the amount of mana produced by the land itself. Utopia Sprawl doesn't change how much mana Temple Garden produces, it just has a triggered ability that triggers when Temple Garden is tapped for mana and causes Utopia Sprawl to produce some mana as well.

entries.question: Autumn controls [Teferi, Time Raveler] and Nathalie flashes in [The Wandering Emperor] on Autumn's turn. Can Nathalie activate its abilities this turn?
entries.reason: The reference says the described flash cast can't occur due to Teferi, while the candidate allows activation assuming the planeswalker is on the battlefield, so they reach different final conclusions.
entries.answer:
Short answer: yes — assuming The Wandering Emperor is on the battlefield under Nathalie's control, Nathalie may activate one of her loyalty abilities during Autumn's turn. Teferi, Time Raveler's static ability restricts only *casting spells* ("Each opponent can cast spells only any time they could cast a sorcery"); it says nothing about activating abilities, and nothing in the priority rules stops a player from activating an ability whenever they have priority [117.1b].

Why the timing works: normally a loyalty ability can be activated only by its controller, with an empty stack, during a main phase of their own turn, and only if no loyalty ability of that permanent has been activated that turn [113.5], [606.1], [606.3]. The Wandering Emperor's own text overrides that general timing rule — "As long as The Wandering Emperor entered this turn, you may activate her loyalty abilities any time you could cast an instant" — and card text beats the general rule. The once-per-turn limit still applies: per [The Wandering Emperor ruling #0], Nathalie may still activate only one loyalty ability on the turn The Wandering Emperor entered. Also note The Wandering Emperor is a planeswalker, not a creature, so summoning-sickness rules [302.6] are irrelevant here.

Two caveats:

1. Getting her there. Teferi, Time Raveler does stop Nathalie from *casting* The Wandering Emperor with flash on Autumn's turn — casting is exactly what Teferi restricts, and per [Teferi, Time Raveler ruling #0] Teferi's restriction takes precedence over flash-style permissions. So I'm assuming she entered the battlefield some other way (put onto the battlefield by an effect, or cast on Nathalie's own turn — though "entered this turn" then wouldn't apply on Autumn's turn). If instead you mean Nathalie tried to hard-cast her with flash during Autumn's turn, that cast is illegal in the first place.
2. One unsettled wrinkle. The Wandering Emperor's permission is worded "any time you could cast an instant." A strict reading asks whether Nathalie could cast an instant at that moment, and Teferi, Time Raveler limits her to sorcery timing (never available on Autumn's turn). The rules and rulings provided here don't resolve that wording question, so if your group reads it strictly, Nathalie would be locked out on Autumn's turn.

Player count: Teferi, Time Raveler's restriction reads "each opponent," so it applies identically to every opponent whether the game is two-player or multiplayer; the answer doesn't change with more players. Note also that a player can't activate abilities of objects outside their range of influence [801.6], which matters only in formats with limited range.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: This can't happen as described. Nathalie cannot cast The Wandering Emperor on Autumn's turn due to Teferi, Time Raveler's effect.

entries.question: Arely casts [Replication Technique] targeting their [Death Watch]. They choose to make a copy of it, and Nico also gets a copy. Can Nico chose to have their copy stay targeting Death Watch?
entries.reason: Both say Nico may leave their copy targeting Arely's Death Watch, but that the copy will have an illegal target when it tries to resolve and therefore do nothing.
entries.answer:
Yes. Nico may leave their copy targeting Arely's Death Watch. Demonstrate says "Players may choose new targets for their copies" — an effect that lets a player "choose new targets" permits leaving any number of targets unchanged, even if those targets would be illegal for the copy (rules 115.7d and 707.10c). Only if Nico chooses to change the target must the new target be legal.

Why this matters here: Replication Technique reads "Create a token that's a copy of target permanent you control." Nico controls their copy, so Death Watch — a permanent Arely controls — is not a legal target for Nico's copy. Nico is still allowed to leave it there under 115.7d, but the copy will simply have an illegal target and won't do anything for Nico; if Nico wants a token, they must pick a permanent Nico controls.

Timing/order notes from the card: Arely chooses whether to copy as the demonstrate ability resolves, and then immediately chooses an opponent [Replication Technique ruling #1, #3]. Nico's copy goes on top of the stack, so Nico's copy resolves first, then Arely's copy, then the original spell [Replication Technique ruling #2]. Nico makes their targeting decision knowing the targets of Arely's original and Arely's copy [Replication Technique ruling #0].

Multiplayer: with more than two players, Arely picks which single opponent gets the copy; only that one opponent copies it. The targeting answer is the same either way. Also, if Arely declines to copy, no opponent copies at all [Replication Technique ruling #4].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Demonstrate doesn't require that the target is changed. ([702.144a]) However, when the copy tries to resolve, it will have an illegal target and be removed from the stack without resolving further.

entries.question: Ashley controls [Murktide Regent] and plays [Mystic Sanctuary] untapped, putting [Master Warcraft] on top of their library. Does this trigger Murktide Regent?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that moving Master Warcraft from Ashley's graveyard to the top of their library via Mystic Sanctuary's ability leaves the graveyard and therefore triggers Murktide Regent, so they reach the same ruling.
entries.answer:
Yes. When Mystic Sanctuary's triggered ability resolves and moves Master Warcraft from Ashley's graveyard to the top of their library, Master Warcraft — an instant card — has left Ashley's graveyard, so Murktide Regent's ability "Whenever an instant or sorcery card leaves your graveyard, put a +1/+1 counter on this creature" triggers, and Murktide Regent gets one +1/+1 counter.

A couple of supporting points:

- Abilities that trigger when a card leaves a graveyard are among the zone-change triggers that "look back in time" [603.10a], so the game uses how things looked immediately before the move; Master Warcraft being in a hidden zone (the library) afterward doesn't stop the trigger.
- Murktide Regent's ability doesn't try to do anything to Master Warcraft — it only puts a counter on Murktide Regent — so the rule about zone-change triggers failing when they can't find the moved object [603.6] costs you nothing here.
- Timing: Murktide Regent must already be on the battlefield when Mystic Sanctuary's ability resolves (it is, per your setup). Note also that Mystic Sanctuary's ability targets; if Master Warcraft had left the graveyard in response, the ability would do nothing and Murktide Regent would not trigger from it.
- Only one instant or sorcery card moves, so it's exactly one +1/+1 counter, and it triggers regardless of whether Master Warcraft was one of the cards delved away earlier (it wasn't — it's in the graveyard).

This works identically in a two-player game and in multiplayer; the ability cares only about Ashley's own graveyard.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes.

entries.question: Adonis controls [Sigarda's Aid] and is attacking with [Dormant Sliver]. After Nico chooses not to block, is Adonis able to cast [Sword of Light and Shadow] and attach it to Dormant Sliver?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude that after blockers are declared Adonis can cast Sword of Light and Shadow using Sigarda's Aid and have it attached to Dormant Sliver before combat damage is dealt.
entries.answer:
Yes. Sigarda's Aid lets Adonis cast Sword of Light and Shadow with flash, and Sigarda's Aid's second ability triggers when Sword of Light and Shadow enters, letting Adonis attach it to target creature he controls — Dormant Sliver, which is still an attacking creature. Since this happens during the declare blockers step (after Nico declined to block, with priority passing back to Adonis), the +2/+2 and protection from white and from black are in place before the combat damage step, so Dormant Sliver deals 4 damage and Sword of Light and Shadow's combat-damage trigger will also work.

Details:
- Sword of Light and Shadow's own Equip {2} ability could NOT be used here: equip means "[Cost]: Attach this permanent to target creature you control. Activate only as a sorcery" [702.6a]. Sigarda's Aid gets around that because it's a triggered ability that attaches the Equipment, not the equip ability. Card text (Sigarda's Aid) overrides the normal sorcery-speed timing you'd expect for Equipment.
- Dormant Sliver is a creature, so it's a legal thing to attach an Equipment to [301.5], [301.5a], [301.5b]. Sword of Light and Shadow enters the battlefield unattached first, then the trigger moves it [301.5b].
- Note Dormant Sliver gives all Slivers defender, so it can only be attacking if some other effect let it attack or put it onto the battlefield attacking; a creature put onto the battlefield attacking during the declare blockers step is unblocked [506.3d], [508.4d]. Either way, it's an attacking creature Adonis controls and a legal target.
- Timing assumption: I'm reading "after Nico chooses not to block" as the declare blockers step, blockers already declared. If instead Adonis waits until after the combat damage step, Sword of Light and Shadow can still be cast and attached, but the +2/+2 and its combat damage trigger would come too late to matter this combat.
- Multiplayer: nothing changes for the caster. With more than two players, only the defending player Dormant Sliver is attacking (or their planeswalker/battle) is relevant to blocking [508.4d]; the ability to cast and attach Sword of Light and Shadow is the same.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. After blockers are declared Adonis gets priority and has the ability to cast Sword of Light and Shadow before damage is dealt.

entries.question: Allison casts [Sorcerous Spyglass] naming [Spring-Loaded Sawblades]. Can Nico crew Spring-Loaded Sawblades?
entries.reason: The candidate concludes Nico can crew (arguing the name change allows it) while the reference says no because crew is an activated ability and thus prohibited, so their final rulings conflict.
entries.answer:
Yes — Nico can crew, because the crew ability lives on the back face, Bladewheel Chariot, and that face's name is not the name Allison chose.

Details:

1. The front face, Spring-Loaded Sawblades, is just an Artifact with flash, an enters-the-battlefield damage trigger, and a craft ability. It is not a Vehicle and has no crew ability at all, so there is nothing to crew while it's on that face.

2. Crew is an activated ability of Vehicle cards ([702.122a]), and a creature crews a Vehicle when it's tapped to pay that ability's cost ([702.122b]). That ability appears only on Bladewheel Chariot, the transformed face (Crew 1, plus the separate "tap two other untapped artifacts" ability).

3. Sorcerous Spyglass says activated abilities of sources with the chosen name can't be activated unless they're mana abilities. The chosen name here is Spring-Loaded Sawblades. Once the permanent is transformed via craft, the object's name is Bladewheel Chariot, not Spring-Loaded Sawblades — a card's name is determined by its Oracle wording for the face that's up ([108.1]). Since the source's name doesn't match the chosen name, Sorcerous Spyglass doesn't lock down Bladewheel Chariot's crew ability, and the prohibition in [602.5] (you can't begin to activate an ability that's prohibited) never applies.

4. What Sorcerous Spyglass naming Spring-Loaded Sawblades does shut off: the craft ability of Spring-Loaded Sawblades itself (it's an activated ability, not a mana ability). So Nico can't use craft to transform it into Bladewheel Chariot in the first place. If the permanent is already Bladewheel Chariot when Sorcerous Spyglass is cast naming Spring-Loaded Sawblades, crewing is unaffected.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Sorcerous Spyglass entered and named Spring-Loaded Sawblades while the permanent was still on its front face. If instead it was already transformed into Bladewheel Chariot, the naming is simply irrelevant to it and both its crew ability and its artifact-tapping ability work normally.

Multiplayer: the answer is the same with more than two players, except that Sorcerous Spyglass's "look at an opponent's hand" targets one chosen opponent while the name restriction applies to every source with that name; also, a player can never activate abilities of objects outside their range of influence ([801.6]), which only matters in formats with limited range.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Crew is an activated ability. ([702.122a])

entries.question: Nico has 7 life and controls two [Death's Shadow]s. August uses [Luminate Primordial] to exile one of the Death's Shadows. What happens next?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final result as the reference: Nico gains 6 life (to 13) and the remaining Death's Shadow becomes a 0/0 and is put into his graveyard by state-based actions.
entries.answer:
Nico gains 6 life (going from 7 to 13), and then Nico's remaining Death's Shadow becomes 0/0 and is put into the graveyard.

Details:

1. While on the battlefield with Nico at 7 life, each Death's Shadow is a 6/6 (13/13 with -7/-7). Death's Shadow's ability only applies on the battlefield; in exile its printed power/toughness is 13/13 [Death's Shadow ruling #1].
2. Luminate Primordial's trigger exiles the targeted Death's Shadow and then has that player gain life equal to its power. Because the Death's Shadow is no longer on the battlefield, the ability uses its last existence there 	o determine its power \u2014 6 \u2014 not the 13 it shows in exile [400.7] [603.6c]. So Nico, the opponent whose creature was exiled, gains 6 life.
3. Nico's life total is now 13, so the second Death's Shadow gets -13/-13 and is a 0/0. It's put into Nico's graveyard the next time state-based actions are checked. (The specific state-based-action rule for 0-toughness creatures isn't among the rules provided here, but the power/toughness math follows from the card itself.)

Multiplayer note: Luminate Primordial says "for each opponent, exile up to one target creature that player controls," so at a table with more than two players August also targets a creature controlled by each other opponent, and each of those players gains life equal to their own exiled creature's power. That doesn't change what happens to Nico here.

Timing assumption: I'm assuming the life gain is part of the same resolving Luminate Primordial trigger, immediately after the exile \u2014 which is how the card is worded. Nothing that changes Nico's life total in between is present in the question; if something raised or lowered Nico's life before the trigger resolved, the exiled Death's Shadow's power (and thus the life gained) would have been calculated from its last board state anyway.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Death's Shadow is a 6/6 when it gets exiled, so Nico gains 6 life. Before August receives priority again, state-based actions are checked, and the game sees that the remaining Death's Shadow now has 0 toughness, and it will be put into Nico's graveyard.

entries.question: Ashley activates [Boseiju, Who Endures] targeting Nikolai's [Skyshroud Forest]. Can Nikolai put a [Wastes] onto the battlefield from their library?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same conclusion as the reference — Wastes is a basic land card but has no basic land type, so it doesn't meet Boseiju, Who Endures's requirement to search for "a land card with a basic land type."
entries.answer:
No. Boseiju, Who Endures lets the affected player search for "a land card with a basic land type," and Wastes has no land type at all — it's a basic land card, but "Wastes" is not a land type (the basic land types are Plains, Island, Swamp, Mountain, Forest). So Nikolai can't find Wastes with Boseiju, Who Endures.

Details:
- Boseiju, Who Endures destroys the targeted Skyshroud Forest (a nonbasic land Nikolai controls), and then Nikolai "may search their library for a land card with a basic land type, put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle." Being a basic land card and having a basic land type are two different things; Wastes is the former but not the latter (Wastes ruling #0).
- Nikolai could still find a card like Forest, Island, or any nonbasic land that has a basic land type printed on its type line (e.g., a dual land with Forest Island). A land such as Skyshroud Forest, which has no land types, would not qualify.
- The search is optional in two ways: Nikolai may decline to search at all, and even when searching a hidden zone for cards with a stated quality, a player isn't required to find them (rule 701.23b). If Nikolai searches and finds nothing, they still shuffle.

This works the same in two-player and multiplayer games; Boseiju, Who Endures targets a permanent an opponent controls, and only that one opponent searches.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Wastes has no basic land types.

entries.question: Ainsley controls [Allosaurus Shepherd] and casts [Gnarlroot Pallbearer]. What happens if Nathaly targets it with [Remand]?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling — Remand resolves but can't counter the green spell due to Allosaurus Shepherd, the controller still draws, and Gnarlroot Pallbearer remains on the stack to resolve.
entries.answer:
Remand resolves, but it can't counter Gnarlroot Pallbearer, so Gnarlroot Pallbearer stays on the stack and is not returned to Ainsley's hand. Nathaly still draws a card from Remand.

Why: Allosaurus Shepherd's second ability reads "Green spells you control can't be countered." Gnarlroot Pallbearer is a green spell (mana cost {4}{G}{G}) controlled by Ainsley, so that card text overrides the general expectation that Remand's "counter target spell" works. Remand itself is not countered and is not removed from the stack: Gnarlroot Pallbearer is still a legal target (it's still a spell on the stack), so Remand resolves normally under the target-legality check [608.2b]. Its counter effect simply does nothing. Remand's second sentence is conditional — "If that spell is countered this way, put it into its owner's hand instead" — and since Gnarlroot Pallbearer was never countered, it isn't bounced. The last line, "Draw a card," still happens.

Then Gnarlroot Pallbearer, having been cast before Remand, resolves afterward [117.7]. It has no targets as a spell, so it becomes a permanent and enters the battlefield [608.3a]; its "When this creature enters" ability is a separate targeted triggered ability [115.1a], and Ainsley chooses a target creature for +X/+X at the time that trigger goes on the stack.

Timing note: I'm assuming Allosaurus Shepherd was already on the battlefield when Remand resolved. If Allosaurus Shepherd left the battlefield before Remand resolved, nothing would stop the counter and Gnarlroot Pallbearer would go to Ainsley's hand.

This works the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer; nothing here depends on the number of opponents.
