entries.answer_gold: Remand resolves, but can't counter Gnarlroot Pallbearer. Nathaly draws a card, and then Gnarlroot Pallbearer will resolve.

entries.question: For the third chapter ability of [Fall of Gil-galad], will the targeted creature fight immediately or when it dies?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the creature fights immediately during the chapter III resolution and that the "when this creature dies" effect is a separate triggered ability that happens later.
entries.answer:
The fight happens immediately, during the resolution of Fall of Gil-galad's chapter III ability. The two parts resolve in order: first the target creature you control gains "When this creature dies, draw two cards" until end of turn, and then, still during that same resolution, that creature fights up to one other target creature (each deals damage equal to its power to the other). Nothing waits for the creature to die.

The granted "When this creature dies, draw two cards" is a separate triggered ability with its own trigger condition ([603.1]). It only does something later, if and when that creature dies this turn. Note that the ability is granted before the fight damage, so it's already in place when the fight occurs — the order matters because a replacement/triggered setup must exist before the event ([614.4] makes the same point for replacement effects: they can't go back in time).

If the fight damage is lethal, the creature dies as a state-based action after Fall of Gil-galad's chapter ability finishes resolving, the death trigger then goes on the stack, and you draw two cards ([704.4]). Fight damage itself is dealt on resolution, not as combat damage in the combat damage step ([510.2] covers only combat damage), so no player gets priority in between granting the ability and the fight ([117.1], [608.1]).

This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table; the chapter ability targets creatures, not players.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: The targeted creature will fight immediately. While the text instructing the creature to fight is after the dies trigger, it's not inside the quotation marks, and therefore not part of the dies trigger.

entries.question: Ashley attacks with [Krallenhorde Killer]. Nickolas blocks with an animated [Mishra's Factory]. Can they tap it after blockers are declared to give itself +1/+1?
entries.reason: The candidate gives the same correct ruling — Mishra's Factory can tap after blockers are declared to pump itself (so it remains a blocker and deals combat damage) and correctly notes the summoning-sickness/timing restriction.
entries.answer:
Yes — assuming Nickolas has controlled Mishra's Factory continuously since the beginning of his most recent turn, he can activate its "{T}: Target Assembly-Worker creature gets +1/+1 until end of turn" ability after blockers are declared, targeting Mishra's Factory itself, and it will still deal and receive combat damage as a blocker of Krallenhorde Killer.

Details:
- Mishra's Factory animated by its {1} ability is a 2/2 Assembly-Worker artifact creature land, and it keeps all its other abilities [Mishra's Factory ruling #0], so it's a legal target for its own +1/+1 ability, making it a 3/3 blocking Krallenhorde Killer.
- Tapping a creature that has already been declared as a blocker doesn't remove it from combat and doesn't prevent its combat damage [506.4b]. Mishra's Factory remains a blocking creature until it's removed from combat or the combat phase ends [509.1g].
- Timing: after blockers are declared, the active player (Ashley) gets priority first in the declare blockers step, with any triggers put on the stack [509.2a]; Nickolas can activate the ability once he receives priority, still in the declare blockers step, before combat damage.
- The one real restriction is "summoning sickness": a {T} ability of a creature can't be activated unless its controller has controlled the permanent since the start of their most recent turn [602.5a], and it doesn't matter how long it has been a creature — if Mishra's Factory entered the battlefield this turn (or on Ashley's turn, i.e., after Nickolas's last turn began), the {T} ability can't be activated [Mishra's Factory ruling #1]. Note the {1} animation ability has no {T}, so it can always be activated to block; only the tap abilities are restricted.
- Number of players doesn't matter here: nothing in this interaction depends on there being exactly two players — Nickolas is the defending player who declared the block, and the priority rules cited apply the same at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes.

entries.question: Nasir controls [Phyrexian Revoker] naming "[Lightning Storm]". Can Aspen cast Lightning Storm? If so, can they discard land cards to put charge counters on it?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Aspen can cast Lightning Storm but cannot activate its discard-a-land ability because Phyrexian Revoker prevents activation of abilities of sources with that name.
entries.answer:
Yes, Aspen can cast Lightning Storm; no, nobody can activate its discard-a-land ability while Phyrexian Revoker naming "Lightning Storm" is on the battlefield.

Phyrexian Revoker reads "Activated abilities of sources with the chosen name can't be activated," and its ruling confirms this applies to sources in any zone, not just the battlefield [Phyrexian Revoker ruling #1]. Casting a spell is not activating an ability, so the naming does nothing to stop Lightning Storm from being cast for {1}{R}{R}.

Once Lightning Storm is on the stack, though, it is a source named Lightning Storm, and "Discard a land card: Put two charge counters on Lightning Storm..." is an activated ability of that source — exactly what Phyrexian Revoker shuts off. A player can't even begin to activate an ability that's prohibited from being activated [602.5c]. That prohibition applies to every player, not just Aspen, since Lightning Storm's ability says any player may activate it while it's on the stack [Lightning Storm ruling #3]. So Lightning Storm will simply resolve dealing 3 damage (X = 3 plus zero charge counters) to its target.

This works the same in a two-player game and at a multiplayer table: no opponent, and no teammate, can pump it either. Note also that Phyrexian Revoker's effect is a continuous effect from a static ability that applies moment by moment [611.3a] — if Phyrexian Revoker leaves the battlefield or the Revoker's controller changes nothing about it, the restriction ends and players holding priority while Lightning Storm is still on the stack could then start discarding lands. Because it's a static prohibition on activation rather than something on the stack, timing of when Phyrexian Revoker entered relative to the cast doesn't matter: what matters is whether Phyrexian Revoker is on the battlefield at the moment someone tries to activate the ability.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Aspen can cast Lightning Storm, but cannot discard a land card to put charge counters on it. Discarding a land card is an activated ability, while casting a spell is not.

entries.question: Aubrielle casts [King Macar, the Gold-Cursed], then casts [Word of Seizing] at their first opportunity. Does Nico have an opportunity to counter King Macar, the Gold-Cursed with [Ooze Spill]?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Nico cannot act while Word of Seizing (with split second) is on the stack but can cast Ooze Spill to counter King Macar after Word of Seizing resolves.
entries.answer:
Yes — but not until Word of Seizing has finished resolving.

Sequence: When Aubrielle casts King Macar, the Gold-Cursed, Aubrielle receives priority again immediately (601.2i), so Aubrielle can cast Word of Seizing before Nico ever gets priority. Casting a spell while another is on the stack is casting it "in response" (117.7, "In Response To"/"Respond"), and the later spell resolves first.

Word of Seizing has split second, which means that as long as Word of Seizing is on the stack, players can't cast spells or activate abilities that aren't mana abilities — only mana abilities and special actions are allowed (702.61b). So while Word of Seizing sits on the stack, Nico cannot cast Ooze Spill, an instant.

However, split second only applies while Word of Seizing is on the stack. Once Word of Seizing finishes resolving and is put into its owner's graveyard (608.2n), the restriction ends. King Macar, the Gold-Cursed is still a spell on the stack at that point (spells on the stack resolve one at a time, and no player had a chance to let King Macar, the Gold-Cursed resolve first). Players then receive priority again, and Nico — with priority and holding an instant (304.1, 117.1a) — can cast Ooze Spill targeting King Macar, the Gold-Cursed and counter it.

Note also that Word of Seizing targets a permanent ("Untap target permanent and gain control of it"), so it cannot target King Macar, the Gold-Cursed while King Macar, the Gold-Cursed is still a spell on the stack; it must have targeted some permanent already on the battlefield.

Two players vs. more: with only Aubrielle and Nico, Nico simply gets priority after Word of Seizing resolves. At a multiplayer table, priority passes in turn order starting after the active player, so other opponents may act before Nico, but Nico still gets the same opportunity to respond to King Macar, the Gold-Cursed once the split second spell has left the stack.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Nico can't cast any spells while Word of Seizing is on the stack, but Nico can wait for it to resolve and then cast a spell before King Macar, the Gold-Cursed resolves.

entries.question: Can Autumn evoke [Solitude] by exiling [Myrkul, Lord of Bones]?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same bottom-line ruling that Myrkul is white (even if multicolored) and may be exiled from hand to pay Solitude’s evoke cost.
entries.answer:
Yes — assuming Myrkul, Lord of Bones is in Autumn's hand, it can be exiled to pay Solitude's evoke cost.

Why: Solitude's evoke cost is "Exile a white card from your hand." Evoke is an alternative cost — "You may cast this card by paying [cost] rather than paying its mana cost" — plus a triggered ability, "When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it" [702.74a]. Autumn announces the intent to pay the evoke cost as part of casting Solitude, following the alternative-cost rules [601.2b, 601.2f, 118.9b].

The cost only requires a *white* card, not a mono-white one. Myrkul, Lord of Bones has {W} in its mana cost ({4}{W}{B}{G}), so it is a white card (it is also black and green). Being multicolored doesn't disqualify it.

Sequence: Solitude is cast for its evoke cost (Myrkul, Lord of Bones is exiled from hand as the cost), Solitude resolves and enters the battlefield, its enters trigger goes on the stack to exile up to one other target creature (that creature's controller gains life equal to its power), and the evoke sacrifice trigger also goes on the stack. Both triggers are controlled by Autumn, so Autumn stacks them; typically you let the exile trigger resolve, then Solitude is sacrificed. In a multiplayer game nothing changes here — the target of Solitude's trigger can be any creature, and only Autumn is paying costs and sacrificing.

Note the two Myrkul, Lord of Bones abilities on the card are battlefield abilities; a Myrkul, Lord of Bones exiled from hand as a cost does nothing.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. Myrkul, Lord of Bones is white, regardless of what other colors it has.

entries.question: Anastasia controls [Uglúk of the White Hand] and their [Mauhúr, Uruk-hai Captain] dies. How many +1/+1 counters does Uglúk of the White Hand get?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Uglúk gets two +1/+1 counters because Mauhúr's replacement effect isn't on the battlefield to modify the counters when the triggered ability resolves.
entries.answer:
Uglúk of the White Hand gets two +1/+1 counters.

Mauhúr, Uruk-hai Captain is an Orc, so Uglúk of the White Hand's triggered ability ("Whenever another creature you control dies, put a +1/+1 counter on Uglúk. If that creature was a Goblin or Orc, put two +1/+1 counters on Uglúk instead.") sees a dying Orc and places two counters rather than one.

Mauhúr, Uruk-hai Captain's own replacement effect ("If one or more +1/+1 counters would be put on an Army, Goblin, or Orc you control, that many plus one +1/+1 counters are put on it instead") does not add a third counter here, because that is a static ability of a permanent and it only functions while Mauhúr, Uruk-hai Captain is on the battlefield. By the time Uglúk of the White Hand's ability resolves and the counters are actually placed, Mauhúr, Uruk-hai Captain is already in the graveyard, so there is no effect to modify the counter placement. The "look back in time" exception of rule 603.10a only governs whether abilities trigger on the death event, not which continuous/replacement effects apply later when counters are placed.

If instead Mauhúr, Uruk-hai Captain were still on the battlefield (for example, some other Orc died), Uglúk of the White Hand — itself an Orc — would get 2 + 1 = 3 counters.

This answer doesn't depend on the number of players; it works the same in a two-player game or at a multiplayer table.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Two. Uglúk of the White Hand has a triggered ability, which triggers when Mauhúr, Uruk-hai Captain dies and doesn't resolve until later. Mauhúr, Uruk-hai Captain would need to be on the battlefield while Uglúk of the White Hand's trigger is resolving in order for its replacement effect to apply.

entries.question: Angelo casts [Lightning Storm], targeting Nico's [Spellskite]. Angelo then discards 27 lands to Lightning Storm, changing its target to Nico. Can Nico change its target back to Spellskite?
entries.reason: The candidate reaches the same final ruling as the reference — Nico can activate Spellskite to change Lightning Storm's target back to Spellskite while the spell is on the stack.
entries.answer:
Yes. Nico can activate Spellskite's ability ({U/P}, paid with {U} or 2 life) targeting the Lightning Storm spell on the stack, and when that ability resolves it changes Lightning Storm's target from Nico to Spellskite.

Why it works:
- A spell's targets can't be changed except by something that explicitly says so ([115.1]). Spellskite says exactly that: "Change a target of target spell or ability to this creature." Lightning Storm deals damage to "any target," and Spellskite (a creature) is a legal choice for that, so the change is legal ([115.7b], [115.7a]).
- Spellskite's ability itself targets the Lightning Storm spell. If Spellskite leaves the battlefield or otherwise becomes an illegal target for Lightning Storm before Spellskite's ability resolves, no target is changed [Spellskite ruling #1]. Note also that Spellskite's ability can be activated even when it isn't a legal target, in which case nothing changes [Spellskite ruling #2].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming Angelo's 27 discards are separate activations of Lightning Storm's ability that have all resolved (each resolution is when the new target is actually chosen [Lightning Storm ruling #3]), and Lightning Storm itself hasn't resolved yet. Nico gets priority between those activations and after the last one, since after each instance of the ability resolves the active player receives priority and then priority passes normally [Lightning Storm ruling #1], [Lightning Storm ruling #0]. Spellskite's ability must resolve while Lightning Storm is still on the stack; once Lightning Storm resolves, nothing can redirect it.

Angelo's counterplay: Lightning Storm's ability may be activated by any player while Lightning Storm is on the stack, so Angelo can respond to Spellskite's ability (or act after it resolves) by discarding another land card and, on resolution of that ability, choosing a new target again — moving it back to Nico. Whoever gets the last such effect to resolve before Lightning Storm resolves sets the final target. If Spellskite is the only other legal target available at that moment, Angelo would have to leave the target unchanged [Lightning Storm ruling #4].

Multiplayer note: nothing here depends on the game having exactly two players — any player at the table may activate Lightning Storm's ability, and the priority order after each resolution starts with the active player [Lightning Storm ruling #1], [Lightning Storm ruling #3].

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Yes. There's nothing that would prevent that from happening.

entries.question: In their main phase, Autumn creates a token copy of [Nylea's Forerunner] with [Reflection of Kiki-Jiki]. After that resolves, Natalee casts [Time Stop]. What happens to the token?
entries.reason: Both conclude the token survives Time Stop and the delayed ability will remove it at the beginning of the next end step (not this turn), so they reach the same final ruling.
entries.answer:
The token copy of Nylea's Forerunner survives Time Stop and stays on the battlefield — it is not sacrificed this turn.

Why: Reflection of Kiki-Jiki's ability creates a token that's a copy of another target nonlegendary creature you control (here Nylea's Forerunner), with haste, and sets up a delayed triggered ability: "Sacrifice it at the beginning of the next end step." Time Stop ends the turn: the current phase or step ends, all creatures and planeswalkers are removed from combat, and the game skips straight to the cleanup step, skipping every phase and step in between [724.1d]. That means this turn's end step never happens, so the delayed trigger never gets a chance to trigger this turn.

The cleanup step doesn't help kill it either. In cleanup, damage is removed from permanents and all "until end of turn" and "this turn" effects end [514.2, 703.4p] — but the token isn't an "until end of turn" effect; it's a permanent on the battlefield, and nothing makes tokens cease to exist while they're on the battlefield (the state-based action only kills tokens in other zones) [704.5d, 111.7, 704.1].

The delayed triggered ability isn't destroyed by ending the turn — Time Stop exiles spells and abilities on the stack, and this delayed ability was never on the stack. It's still waiting, so it will trigger at the beginning of the next end step (the next turn's end step) and Autumn will sacrifice the token copy of Nylea's Forerunner then. In the meantime, Autumn keeps a 5/3 hasty token copy of Nylea's Forerunner granting trample to their other creatures.

Assumption on timing: I'm reading it as Reflection of Kiki-Jiki's ability fully resolving (the token already on the battlefield) before Time Stop is cast, as stated. If instead Time Stop were cast while Reflection of Kiki-Jiki's activated ability was still on the stack, that ability would be exiled along with everything else on the stack and no token would ever be created.

Two players vs. multiplayer: nothing here changes. Ending the turn and the token's fate work the same regardless of the number of players; the delayed trigger simply waits for the next end step, which is whichever turn comes next in turn order.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: It's exiled at the beginning of the next end step, which will probably be Natalee's end step on their next turn. Ending the turn skips straight to the cleanup step, with no end step.

entries.question: Ari casts [Archon of Cruelty], and before it resolves Neil casts [Veil of Summer]. What happens when the Archon resolves?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Archon enters the battlefield but Veil of Summer gives hexproof that prevents the ETB trigger from being placed on the stack (so with only Neil as an opponent the trigger does nothing and Ari doesn't draw or gain life).
entries.answer:
Archon of Cruelty itself resolves normally and enters the battlefield — Veil of Summer does nothing to stop the creature spell, because Archon of Cruelty doesn't target anything (115.10a). What Veil of Summer stops is the enters-the-battlefield trigger.

Details:

1. Veil of Summer resolves first. Since Ari cast Archon of Cruelty, a black spell, Neil draws a card, and Neil plus his permanents gain hexproof from black until end of turn. "Hexproof from black" means Neil and his permanents can't be the targets of black spells or abilities his opponents control (702.11b, 702.11c, 702.11e; Veil of Summer text).

2. Archon of Cruelty resolves and enters the battlefield. Its triggered ability triggers and Ari must choose a target opponent as it goes on the stack. Archon of Cruelty is black, so its ability is a black ability controlled by Neil's opponent — Neil is not a legal target.

3. If the game is just Ari and Neil, Ari has no legal target for the trigger. An ability with no legal targets can't be put on the stack, and even if the situation changed, on resolution a trigger whose only target is illegal is removed from the stack and does nothing (608.2b). So no sacrifice, no discard, no 3 life loss — and Ari also does not draw a card or gain 3 life, since the whole ability fails to resolve.

4. In a multiplayer game, Ari may simply choose a different opponent who doesn't have hexproof from black; that opponent sacrifices a creature or planeswalker of their choice, discards, and loses 3 life, and Ari draws and gains 3 life as normal. Only Neil (and Neil's permanents) are shielded.

Timing note: I'm assuming Neil cast Veil of Summer while Archon of Cruelty was still on the stack, as stated, so the hexproof is already in place when the enters trigger picks targets. If Veil of Summer were instead cast after the trigger was already on the stack with Neil targeted, the target would become illegal on resolution and the trigger would still do nothing (608.2b).

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Archon of Cruelty's ability triggers but is not placed onto the stack, since there are no legal targets for it. Ari will not draw a card or gain life.

entries.question: Ariel cast [Commandeer] targeting Nova's [The One Ring]. Does Ariel get protection from everything?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude the triggered ability doesn't trigger because Ariel didn't cast The One Ring, so no one gains protection.
entries.answer:
No. Neither Ariel nor Nova gets protection from everything.

How it plays out: Commandeer says "Gain control of target noncreature spell... (If that spell is an artifact, enchantment, or planeswalker, the permanent enters under your control.)" The One Ring is an artifact spell, so once Commandeer resolves, the The One Ring spell is controlled by Ariel and the resulting artifact permanent enters the battlefield under Ariel's control (Ariel is its controller by default as the player under whose control it entered; Nova remains its owner, per 110.2b).

The One Ring's trigger reads: "When The One Ring enters, if you cast it, you gain protection from everything until your next turn." The "you" here is the controller of the ability — Ariel. But Ariel did not cast The One Ring; Nova did. That intervening "if" clause is false, so the ability doesn't trigger at all and no one gains protection. Nova can't get it either, since Nova doesn't control The One Ring or its triggered ability.

For reference, had it triggered, protection from everything would mean all damage dealt to that player is prevented, Auras can't be attached to them, and they can't be the target of spells or abilities (The One Ring rulings #0 and #2); a spell already on the stack targeting them would have an illegal target (ruling #1). None of that applies here.

Ariel does keep The One Ring itself, with its indestructibility, upkeep life loss, and {T} draw ability. This answer is the same whether the game is two-player or multiplayer — the "if you cast it" clause fails regardless of how many opponents are at the table. One multiplayer-only wrinkle from the provided rules: if a control-changing effect on an object ends and the object's default controller has left the game, the object is exiled (800.4c); Commandeer's control change is permanent, so that isn't a concern here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. Ariel didn't cast The One Ring.

entries.question: Andres casts [Blood Feud], can Andres choose Nathalia's [Colorful Feiyi Sparrow] for both targets?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude "No" and explain that the word "another" is an explicit targeting restriction that prevents the same creature from being chosen for both targets.
entries.answer:
No. Andres can't choose Nathalia's Colorful Feiyi Sparrow for both of Blood Feud's targets — Blood Feud needs two different creatures.

Why: Blood Feud reads "Target creature fights another target creature." Although Blood Feud uses the word "target" in two places (and normally the same object may be chosen once for each instance of "target" — see rules 115.3 and 601.2c), the word "another" is an explicit targeting restriction that requires the second target to be a different creature from the first. Colorful Feiyi Sparrow can legally be one of the two targets, but Andres must pick some other creature for the remaining target.

Andres does not need the two creatures to have different controllers, though: Blood Feud can target two creatures with the same controller (Blood Feud ruling #0), so Andres could target Colorful Feiyi Sparrow plus another creature Nathalia controls, or one of his own, or a third player's — targets are declared as Blood Feud is put on the stack and can't later be changed except by an effect that says so (rule 115.1). If Andres tried to announce Colorful Feiyi Sparrow twice, the casting would be illegal and the game would rewind to before Blood Feud was proposed (rules 601.2c, 733.1).

This is the same in two-player and multiplayer games; the only difference in multiplayer is the wider pool of creatures Andres may pick from for the second target.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No. The word "another" here retains its normal English meaning, and means that both targets cannot be the same creature.

entries.question: Ainsley uses [Living End] to return both [Breathless Knight] and [Lantern Kami] from their graveyard to the battlefield. How many +1/+1 counters will Breathless Knight get?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Breathless Knight gets zero counters because Living End exiles the cards before returning them, so they enter from exile (not a graveyard) and the Knight's "entered from a graveyard" condition isn't met.
entries.answer:
Zero +1/+1 counters. Living End says "Each player exiles all creature cards from their graveyard, then sacrifices all creatures they control, then puts all cards they exiled this way onto the battlefield." So Breathless Knight and Lantern Kami leave the graveyard for exile first, and they enter the battlefield from exile — not from a graveyard.

Breathless Knight's trigger reads "Whenever this creature or another creature you control enters, if that creature entered from a graveyard or you cast it from a graveyard, put a +1/+1 counter on this creature." That's an intervening-"if" style condition on the zone the creature came from. Since both Breathless Knight and Lantern Kami come from exile under Living End, and neither was cast from a graveyard, the condition isn't met for either entry, so no counters are placed. The card's own wording governs here.

For contrast: if an effect had returned both creatures directly from the graveyard to the battlefield at the same time, Breathless Knight would see its own entry and Lantern Kami's entry (the ability covers "this creature or another creature you control"), giving it two +1/+1 counters. Also note that if Breathless Knight somehow had two instances of this triggered ability, each instance would trigger separately, in line with how the game treats duplicated triggered keyword abilities (see, e.g., [702.108b]).

Player count doesn't matter here — Living End affects each player, but Breathless Knight's ability only cares about creatures Ainsley controls, so the answer is the same in a two-player or multiplayer game.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: Zero. Living End exiles the cards from the graveyard before putting them on the battlefield, and Breathless Knight only gets counters if it entered from a graveyard.

entries.question: Aryan controls [Frontline Heroism] and casts [Resounding Roar] targeting the token. If they choose to copy Resounding Roar and target the new token that's been created, will Aryan create another token?
entries.reason: Both the candidate and the reference conclude that only one token is created because the copied Resounding Roar is not cast and thus cannot trigger Frontline Heroism, so the ability triggers only once.
entries.answer:
No — Aryan gets exactly one new token, the one Frontline Heroism's own ability creates. The copy of Resounding Roar does not cause a second trigger, so no additional token is made.

Why: When Aryan casts Resounding Roar targeting only a single creature they control, Frontline Heroism's last ability triggers. Note that the ability isn't optional and isn't really a choice: as it resolves, Aryan creates a 1/1 red Soldier creature token with haste, then copies Resounding Roar, and the copy targets that token ([Frontline Heroism ruling #5], card text of Frontline Heroism). That's the one token.

The copy of Resounding Roar is put directly onto the stack and is therefore not cast ([707.10], [Frontline Heroism ruling #1]). Frontline Heroism's ability only triggers on casting a spell, so the copy can't trigger it again — no second token, no infinite loop. The copy is still a spell in its own right and will resolve to give the token +3/+3 until end of turn ([112.1a]).

Timing note: Frontline Heroism's ability resolves before the original Resounding Roar, so the token exists and gets +3/+3 from the copy first; the original Resounding Roar then resolves and gives +3/+3 to its original target. The trigger resolves even if the original Resounding Roar is countered ([Frontline Heroism ruling #2]).

This works identically at a two-player table or in multiplayer — Frontline Heroism only cares about spells you cast targeting a single creature you control, and the provided rules give no opponent-dependent variation here.

Card data from Scryfall (scryfall.com).
entries.answer_gold: No, the event Frontline Heroism's trigger is watching for is Aryan casting a spell that targets one of their creatures, copying a spell does not constitute casting it.
